abstract: This paper outlines a schema for movement control based on two stages of signal processing. The higher stage is a neural network model that treats the cerebellum as an array of adjustable motor pattern generators. This network uses sensory input to preset and to trigger elemental pattern generators and to evaluate their performance. The actual patterned outputs, however, are produced by intrin(cid:173) sic circuitry that includes recurrent loops and is thus capable of self-sustained activity. These patterned outputs are sent as motor commands to local feedback systems called motor servos. The latter control the forces and lengths of individual muscles. Overall control is thus achieved in two stages: (1) an adaptive cerebellar network generates an array of feedforward motor commands and (2) a set of local feedback systems translates these commands into actual movements.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a movement-control architecture that divides the task between generating motor patterns and carrying them out. Its higher stage models the cerebellum as a collection of adjustable pattern generators. Its lower stage consists of local feedback controllers that regulate the forces and lengths of individual muscles.

Sensory information helps prepare and trigger the higher-level generators, and also provides a way to evaluate their performance. Once activated, the generators produce patterned activity through their own internal circuitry. Recurrent loops allow that activity to sustain itself, so the temporal pattern comes from the network’s internal dynamics.

The resulting patterns become feedforward motor commands sent to the local muscle controllers, called motor servos. Those controllers translate the commands into movement through feedback. The architecture therefore assigns different responsibilities to two interacting stages: an adaptive network organizes the motor commands, while local systems regulate their physical execution. Its contribution is a proposed way to combine internally generated movement patterns with sensory evaluation and muscle-level feedback.
summary.tldr: A proposed cerebellar controller generates adaptive motor patterns that local muscle feedback systems translate into movement.

title: Schema for Motor Control Utilizing a Network Model of the Cerebellum

abstract: This paper describes the construction of a system that recognizes hand-printed digits, using a combination of classical techniques and neural-net methods. The system has been trained and tested on real-world data, derived from zip codes seen on actual U.S. Mail. The system rejects a small percentage of the examples as unclassifiable, and achieves a very low error rate on the remaining examples. The system compares favorably with other state-of-the art recognizers. While some of the methods are specific to this task, it is hoped that many of the techniques will be applicable to a wide range of recognition tasks.

paragraphs: The paper describes a system for recognizing hand-printed digits using classical recognition techniques together with neural-network methods. Its training and testing data come from ZIP codes on actual U.S. mail. This grounds the task in handwriting encountered in a real application, connecting the system design to practical recognition needs.

The recognizer can reject examples that it treats as unclassifiable. It rejects a small portion of the data and achieves a very low error rate on the examples it accepts. These two outcomes belong together: the reported accuracy concerns the retained examples, while rejection allows the system to leave some inputs unresolved.

The authors report favorable comparisons with other leading recognizers. Their contribution is the combined recognition system, including its ability to distinguish accepted classifications from rejected cases. They also suggest that many of the techniques could apply to other recognition tasks, while acknowledging that some methods are specific to handwritten digits. That broader usefulness is presented as a prospect for transfer beyond the demonstrated application.
summary.tldr: A hybrid recognizer achieves very low error on accepted handwritten ZIP-code digits while rejecting a small share of difficult examples.

title: Neural Network Recognizer for Hand-Written Zip Code Digits

abstract: The goal has been to construct a supervised artificial neural network that learns incrementally an unknown mapping. As a result a network con(cid:173) sisting of a combination of ART2 and backpropagation is proposed and is called an "ART2/BP" network. The ART2 network is used to build and focus a supervised backpropagation network. The ART2/BP network has the advantage of being able to dynamically expand itself in response to input patterns containing new information. Simulation results show that the ART2/BP network outperforms a classical maximum likelihood method for the estimation of a discrete dynamic and nonlinear transfer function.

paragraphs: This paper addresses supervised learning when an unknown mapping must be learned incrementally. The proposed network combines ART2 with backpropagation and is called ART2/BP. Its central feature is that the network can change its structure as it encounters input patterns containing new information, allowing learning to include expansion of the model itself.

ART2 is used to build and focus the supervised backpropagation network. The two components therefore have connected roles: one helps organize the network used for learning, while the other learns the supervised mapping. Dynamic expansion makes the architecture responsive to information arriving during learning instead of requiring all of its representational capacity to be settled beforehand.

The authors evaluate the approach through simulations involving estimation of a discrete dynamic, nonlinear transfer function. ART2/BP performs better than a classical maximum likelihood method in that comparison. The stated result supports the usefulness of combining incremental network construction with supervised estimation for the dynamic process studied, linking structural adaptation to improved estimation performance.
summary.tldr: ART2/BP combines incremental network growth with supervised learning and improves nonlinear dynamic-process estimation in simulations.

title: ART2/BP architecture for adaptive estimation of dynamic processes

abstract: Networks for reconstructing a sparse or noisy function often use an edge field to segment the function into homogeneous regions, This approach assumes that these regions do not overlap or have disjoint parts, which is often false. For example, images which contain regions split by an occlud(cid:173) ing object can't be properly reconstructed using this type of network. We have developed a network that overcomes these limitations, using support maps to represent the segmentation of a signal. In our approach, the sup(cid:173) port of each region in the signal is explicitly represented. Results from an initial implementation demonstrate that this method can reconstruct images and motion sequences which contain complicated occlusion.

For example, images which contain regions split by an occlud(cid:173) ing object can't be properly reconstructed using this type of network. We have developed a network that overcomes these limitations, using support maps to represent the segmentation of a signal. In our approach, the sup(cid:173) port of each region in the signal is explicitly represented. Results from an initial implementation demonstrate that this method can reconstruct images and motion sequences which contain complicated occlusion.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image or another function from sparse or noisy observations often involves dividing it into relatively homogeneous regions. The paper challenges approaches that represent this division using an edge field. As described in the abstract, those approaches assume that regions do not overlap or consist of separated pieces, which becomes problematic when an object blocks part of another region.

The proposed network uses multiple support maps to represent segmentation. A support map explicitly records where a particular region is present in the signal. This representation lets the model describe a region through its membership across locations, including pieces separated by an occluding object.

Results from an initial implementation show reconstruction of images and motion sequences containing complicated occlusion. The significance is the connection between representation and reconstruction: if segmentation cannot express the scene's organization, reconstruction is constrained from the start. Explicit region supports address the particular overlap and disconnected-region restrictions identified in the paper.
summary.tldr: Explicit support maps let a reconstruction network represent overlapping or separated regions and handle complicated occlusion.

title: Against Edges: Function Approximation with Multiple Support Maps
On Learning µ-Perceptron Networks with Binary Weights

abstract: In this paper, recursive estimation algorithms for dynamic modular networks are developed. The models are based on Gaussian RBF networks and the gating network is considered in two stages: At first, it is simply a time-varying scalar and in the second, it is based on the state, as in the mixture of local experts scheme. The resulting algorithm uses Kalman filter estimation for the model estimation and the gating probability estimation. Both, 'hard' and 'soft' competition based estimation schemes are developed where in the former, the most probable network is adapted and in the latter all networks are adapted by appropriate weighting of the data.
originalAbstract: In this paper, recursive estimation algorithms for dynamic modular networks are developed. The models are based on Gaussian RBF networks and the gating network is considered in two stages: At first, it is simply a time-varying scalar and in the second, it is based on the state, as in the mixture of local experts scheme. The resulting algorithm uses Kalman filter estimation for the model estimation and the gating probability estimation. Both, 'hard' and 'soft' competition based estimation schemes are developed where in the former, the most probable network is adapted and in the latter all networks are adapted by appropriate weighting of the data.

paragraphs: This paper develops recursive estimation algorithms for dynamic models built from multiple Gaussian radial basis function networks. A gating mechanism determines how the component networks participate. The authors consider two forms of gating: a scalar that changes with time and a state-dependent mechanism resembling a mixture of local experts.

The estimation procedure uses Kalman filtering both for the component models and for the gating probabilities. Learning therefore includes two connected tasks: adjusting the models and estimating which model is appropriate. Considering both time-varying and state-dependent gating gives the framework different ways to express changes in the relevance of its components.

The paper develops hard and soft competition variants. Under hard competition, only the network judged most probable is adapted. Under soft competition, every network is updated, with data weighted according to its responsibility. This distinction determines how learning experience is distributed among the components. The contribution is a set of recursive algorithms that jointly address model adaptation and the changing allocation of data to local models.
summary.tldr: Kalman-filter-based algorithms jointly adapt modular RBF models and their gating probabilities using hard or weighted competition.

title: Recursive Estimation of Dynamic Modular RBF Networks

abstract: Statistically independent features can be extracted by finding a fac(cid:173) torial representation of a signal distribution. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) accomplishes this for linear correlated and Gaus(cid:173) sian distributed signals. Independent Component Analysis (ICA), formalized by Comon (1994), extracts features in the case of lin(cid:173) ear statistical dependent but not necessarily Gaussian distributed signals. Nonlinear Component Analysis finally should find a facto(cid:173) rial representation for nonlinear statistical dependent distributed signals. This paper proposes for this task a novel feed-forward, information conserving, nonlinear map - the explicit symplectic transformations. It also solves the problem of non-Gaussian output distributions by considering single coordinate higher order statis(cid:173) tics.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA), formalized by Comon (1994), extracts features in the case of lin(cid:173) ear statistical dependent but not necessarily Gaussian distributed signals. paragraphs: This paper seeks a representation in which a signal's components are statistically independent. Such a factorial representation expresses the joint distribution through separate component distributions. The problem becomes more demanding when the statistical relationships between signal components are nonlinear, because a linear transformation may not capture the structure that connects them.

The authors position the task as an extension of principal component analysis and independent component analysis. In their account, PCA handles linear correlations in Gaussian signals, while ICA addresses linear dependencies without requiring Gaussian distributions. Nonlinear component analysis targets the further case in which dependencies themselves require a nonlinear transformation.

The proposed solution is a feed-forward nonlinear map built from explicit symplectic transformations and designed to conserve information. The method also handles non-Gaussian output distributions by considering higher-order statistics of individual coordinates. These two elements address different aspects of the goal: transforming nonlinear relationships and describing output components beyond Gaussian behavior. The contribution is a proposed information-conserving route to extracting statistically independent features from nonlinearly dependent signals.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes information-conserving symplectic transformations to extract independent components from nonlinearly dependent signals.

title: Symplectic Nonlinear Component Analysis

abstract: The additive clustering (ADCL US) model (Shepard & Arabie, 1979) treats the similarity of two stimuli as a weighted additive measure of their common features. Inspired by recent work in unsupervised learning with multiple cause models, we propose anew, statistically well-motivated algorithm for discovering the structure of natural stimulus classes using the ADCLUS model, which promises substan(cid:173) tial gains in conceptual simplicity, practical efficiency, and solution quality over earlier efforts. We also present preliminary results with artificial data and two classic similarity data sets.
originalAbstract: The additive clustering (ADCL US) model (Shepard & Arabie, 1979) treats the similarity of two stimuli as a weighted additive measure of their common features. Inspired by recent work in unsupervised learning with multiple cause models, we propose anew, statistically well-motivated algorithm for discovering the structure of natural stimulus classes using the ADCLUS model, which promises substan(cid:173) tial gains in conceptual simplicity, practical efficiency, and solution quality over earlier efforts. We also present preliminary results with artificial data and two classic similarity data sets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover the features underlying judgments of similarity. It uses the additive clustering model, in which two stimuli are similar to the extent that they share features. Each common feature contributes a weight, and the combined contributions determine the modeled similarity.

The authors propose a statistically motivated algorithm for learning this structure, drawing inspiration from unsupervised models with multiple causes. The task is to uncover a feature organization that accounts for the similarities among stimuli. Because several shared features can contribute to a pair's similarity, the model can describe structure through overlapping contributions.

The proposed algorithm promises simpler concepts, greater practical efficiency, and better solutions than earlier approaches to the model. The paper presents preliminary results on artificial data and two established similarity datasets. These results explore the proposed learning procedure in both constructed and existing examples. The contribution is a new route to fitting an interpretable account of similarity in terms of weighted shared features.
summary.tldr: A statistically motivated additive-clustering algorithm learns weighted shared features that explain similarities among stimuli.

title: Learning the Structure of Similarity

abstract: This paper discusses a probabilistic model-based approach to clus(cid:173) tering sequences, using hidden Markov models (HMMs) . The prob(cid:173) lem can be framed as a generalization of the standard mixture model approach to clustering in feature space. Two primary issues are addressed. First, a novel parameter initialization procedure is proposed, and second, the more difficult problem of determining the number of clusters K, from the data, is investigated. Experi(cid:173) mental results indicate that the proposed techniques are useful for revealing hidden cluster structure in data sets of sequences.

The prob(cid:173) lem can be framed as a generalization of the standard mixture model approach to clustering in feature space. Two primary issues are addressed. First, a novel parameter initialization procedure is proposed, and second, the more difficult problem of determining the number of clusters K, from the data, is investigated. Experi(cid:173) mental results indicate that the proposed techniques are useful for revealing hidden cluster structure in data sets of sequences.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to discover groups in a collection of sequences. It uses hidden Markov models as the basis for a probabilistic clustering method, extending the mixture-model view ordinarily used for points in a feature space. This makes sequence modeling part of the description of each group.

Two practical questions receive particular attention. The first is how to initialize the model parameters before fitting, for which the authors propose a new procedure. The second is how to determine the number of clusters from the data. The abstract identifies this second question as more difficult, since it concerns the grouping structure itself rather than just a starting parameter setting.

Experimental results indicate that the proposed techniques can reveal hidden cluster structure in sequence datasets. The contribution therefore includes both a modeling framework and methods for making it usable: choosing starting values and investigating how many groups the observations support. Together, these address the process of discovering sequence categories when those categories are not supplied in advance.
summary.tldr: The paper clusters sequences with hidden Markov models and develops methods for initialization and determining the number of clusters.

title: Clustering Sequences with Hidden Markov Models

abstract: The popular K-means clustering partitions a data set by minimiz(cid:173) ing a sum-of-squares cost function. A coordinate descend method is then used to find local minima. In this paper we show that the minimization can be reformulated as a trace maximization problem associated with the Gram matrix of the data vectors. Furthermore, we show that a relaxed version of the trace maximization problem possesses global optimal solutions which can be obtained by com(cid:173) puting a partial eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix, and the cluster assignment for each data vectors can be found by comput(cid:173) ing a pivoted QR decomposition of the eigenvector matrix. As a by-product we also derive a lower bound for the minimum of the sum-of-squares cost function.
originalAbstract: The popular K-means clustering partitions a data set by minimiz(cid:173) ing a sum-of-squares cost function. A coordinate descend method is then used to find local minima. In this paper we show that the minimization can be reformulated as a trace maximization problem associated with the Gram matrix of the data vectors. Furthermore, we show that a relaxed version of the trace maximization problem possesses global optimal solutions which can be obtained by com(cid:173) puting a partial eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix, and the cluster assignment for each data vectors can be found by comput(cid:173) ing a pivoted QR decomposition of the eigenvector matrix. As a by-product we also derive a lower bound for the minimum of the sum-of-squares cost function.

paragraphs: K-means groups observations by minimizing a sum of squared distances, commonly using coordinate descent to reach a local minimum. This paper reformulates that objective as a trace maximization problem involving the data's Gram matrix. The reformulation connects a familiar clustering objective with a matrix optimization problem.

The authors then relax the trace maximization problem. They show that this relaxed version has globally optimal solutions obtainable through a partial eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix. Cluster assignments are recovered using a pivoted QR decomposition of the eigenvector matrix, providing a sequence of matrix operations that leads from the relaxation to a partition.

The analysis also yields a lower bound on the minimum achievable sum-of-squares cost. This supplies theoretical information about the original clustering objective in addition to the assignment procedure. The central qualification is that the global optimality guarantee applies to the relaxed problem; it should not be read as a guarantee that every recovered discrete clustering globally minimizes the original K-means objective.
summary.tldr: A spectral relaxation of K-means has globally optimal matrix solutions and yields cluster assignments plus a cost lower bound.

title: Spectral Relaxation for K-means Clustering

abstract: In this paper, we study a special kind of learning problem in which each training instance is given a set of (or distribution over) candidate class labels and only one of the candidate labels is the correct one. Such a problem can occur, e.g., in an information retrieval setting where a set of words is associated with an image, or if classes labels are organized hierarchically. We propose a novel discriminative approach for handling the ambiguity of class labels in the training examples. The experiments with the proposed approach over five different UCI datasets show that our approach is able to find the correct label among the set of candidate labels and actually achieve performance close to the case when each training instance is given a single correct label. In contrast, naIve methods degrade rapidly as more ambiguity is introduced into the labels.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study a special kind of learning problem in which each training instance is given a set of (or distribution over) candidate class labels and only one of the candidate labels is the correct one. Such a problem can occur, e.g., in an information retrieval setting where a set of words is associated with an image, or if classes labels are organized hierarchically. We propose a novel discriminative approach for handling the ambiguity of class labels in the training examples. The experiments with the proposed approach over five different UCI datasets show that our approach is able to find the correct label among the set of candidate labels and actually achieve performance close to the case when each training instance is given a single correct label. In contrast, naIve methods degrade rapidly as more ambiguity is introduced into the labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies training data in which each example has several candidate class labels, but exactly one is correct. The candidates may be supplied as a set or as a probability distribution. This is a problem of ambiguity in supervision: the learner must resolve which candidate applies while learning how to classify examples.

The authors propose a discriminative approach designed to handle that ambiguity. The setting can arise when words are associated with an image or when labels have a hierarchical organization. These examples motivate learning from partially informative labels, where the supplied candidates constrain the answer without directly identifying it.

Experiments on five UCI datasets show that the method can identify the correct label among the candidates and achieve performance close to training with a single correct label per example. In contrast, the naive methods examined deteriorate rapidly as label ambiguity increases. These findings support the value of modeling the ambiguity explicitly, under the paper's assumption that one candidate is the correct class.
summary.tldr: A discriminative method learns from ambiguous candidate labels and approaches fully labeled performance on five reported datasets.

title: Learning with Multiple Labels

abstract: Speech dereverberation is desirable with a view to achieving, for exam- ple, robust speech recognition in the real world. However, it is still a chal- lenging problem, especially when using a single microphone. Although blind equalization techniques have been exploited, they cannot deal with speech signals appropriately because their assumptions are not satisﬁed by speech signals. We propose a new dereverberation principle based on an inherent property of speech signals, namely quasi-periodicity. The present methods learn the dereverberation ﬁlter from a lot of speech data with no prior knowledge of the data, and can achieve high quality speech dereverberation especially when the reverberation time is long.

However, it is still a chal- lenging problem, especially when using a single microphone. Although blind equalization techniques have been exploited, they cannot deal with speech signals appropriately because their assumptions are not satisﬁed by speech signals. We propose a new dereverberation principle based on an inherent property of speech signals, namely quasi-periodicity. The present methods learn the dereverberation ﬁlter from a lot of speech data with no prior knowledge of the data, and can achieve high quality speech dereverberation especially when the reverberation time is long.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the removal of reverberation from speech recorded with a single microphone. Reverberation complicates uses such as robust real-world speech recognition, and a single recording channel makes the problem especially challenging. The authors identify a mismatch between speech and the assumptions used by existing blind equalization techniques.

Their proposed principle instead relies on speech’s quasi-periodicity: its approximately repeating structure. The methods learn a dereverberation filter from a large amount of speech data without prior knowledge of those data. Quasi-periodicity supplies the speech-specific property guiding this learning, replacing assumptions that the abstract says are unsuitable for speech.

The authors state that the methods can achieve high-quality dereverberation, particularly when reverberation lasts a long time. This makes the contribution both a new principle for recovering speech and a data-driven way to learn the required filter. The claimed effectiveness is especially associated with long reverberation times, and the learning approach explicitly draws on substantial speech data.
summary.tldr: A single-microphone dereverberation method learns from speech’s quasi-periodicity and can produce high-quality results, especially with long reverberation times.

title: One Microphone Blind Dereverberation Based on Quasi-periodicity of Speech Signals

abstract: In this paper we introduce a new underlying probabilistic model for prin- cipal component analysis (PCA). Our formulation interprets PCA as a particular Gaussian process prior on a mapping from a latent space to the observed data-space. We show that if the prior’s covariance func- tion constrains the mappings to be linear the model is equivalent to PCA, we then extend the model by considering less restrictive covariance func- tions which allow non-linear mappings. This more general Gaussian pro- cess latent variable model (GPLVM) is then evaluated as an approach to the visualisation of high dimensional data for three different data-sets. Additionally our non-linear algorithm can be further kernelised leading to ‘twin kernel PCA’ in which a mapping between feature spaces occurs.
originalAbstract: In this paper we introduce a new underlying probabilistic model for prin- cipal component analysis (PCA). Our formulation interprets PCA as a particular Gaussian process prior on a mapping from a latent space to the observed data-space. We show that if the prior’s covariance func- tion constrains the mappings to be linear the model is equivalent to PCA, we then extend the model by considering less restrictive covariance func- tions which allow non-linear mappings. This more general Gaussian pro- cess latent variable model (GPLVM) is then evaluated as an approach to the visualisation of high dimensional data for three different data-sets. paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic interpretation of principal component analysis through a mapping from a latent space to the observed data. A Gaussian process prior describes that mapping. When its covariance function restricts the mapping to be linear, the authors show that the resulting model is equivalent to PCA.

This equivalence provides a route to a nonlinear extension. By choosing less restrictive covariance functions, the model can allow nonlinear mappings between latent representations and observations. The resulting Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model preserves the probabilistic mapping viewpoint while broadening the kinds of relationships it can represent.

The authors evaluate the more general model as a method for visualizing high-dimensional data on three datasets. They also describe an additional kernelization of the nonlinear algorithm, producing what they call twin kernel PCA, where the mapping occurs between feature spaces. The contribution connects PCA, nonlinear latent representations, and kernel mappings within one probabilistic construction, with visualization serving as the stated application.
summary.tldr: The paper recasts PCA as a Gaussian process latent-variable model and extends it to nonlinear mappings for high-dimensional data visualization.

title: Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models for Visualisation of High Dimensional Data

abstract: The detection and pose estimation of people in images and video is made challenging by the variability of human appearance, the complexity of natural scenes, and the high dimensionality of articulated body mod- els. To cope with these problems we represent the 3D human body as a graphical model in which the relationships between the body parts are represented by conditional probability distributions. We formulate the pose estimation problem as one of probabilistic inference over a graphi- cal model where the random variables correspond to the individual limb parameters (position and orientation). Because the limbs are described by 6-dimensional vectors encoding pose in 3-space, discretization is im- practical and the random variables in our model must be continuous- valued. To approximate belief propagation in such a graph we exploit a recently introduced generalization of the particle ﬁlter. This framework facilitates the automatic initialization of the body-model from low level cues and is robust to occlusion of body parts and scene clutter.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's pose is difficult because appearance varies, scenes contain clutter, and an articulated body has many possible configurations. This paper represents the three-dimensional body as a graphical model. Each limb has variables describing its position and orientation, while conditional probability distributions express relationships between body parts.

Pose estimation becomes a problem of probabilistic inference: evidence about individual parts must be combined with the relationships connecting them. Each limb requires six continuous coordinates. The authors argue that discretizing this space is impractical, so the inference method must handle continuous variables rather than enumerate a fixed collection of limb positions.

The method approximates belief propagation using a generalization of particle filtering. This supplies a way to exchange uncertain information between connected body parts while retaining continuous pose descriptions. The authors state that the framework supports automatic initialization from low-level image cues and is robust to occluded parts and scene clutter. Its importance lies in combining local evidence with a probabilistic model of the assembled body.
summary.tldr: A continuous graphical body model uses approximate belief propagation to assemble human poses from uncertain image evidence.

title: Attractive People: Assembling Loose-Limbed Models using Non-parametric Belief Propagation

abstract: We investigate the problem of reducing the complexity of a graphical model (G, PG ) by finding a subgraph H of G, chosen from a class of subgraphs H, such that H is optimal with respect to KL-divergence. We do this by first defining a decomposition tree representation for G, which is closely related to the junction-tree representation for G. We then give an algorithm which uses this representation to compute the optimal H ∈ H. Gavril [2] and Tarjan [3] have used graph separation properties to solve several combinatorial optimization problems when the size of the minimal separators in the graph is bounded. We present an extension of this technique which applies to some important choices of H even when the size of the minimal separators of G are arbitrarily large. In particular, this applies to problems such as finding an optimal subgraphical model over a (k − 1)-tree of a graphical model over a k-tree (for arbitrary k) and selecting an optimal subgraphical model with (a constant) d fewer edges with respect to KL-divergence can be solved in time polynomial in |V (G)| using this formulation.
originalAbstract: We investigate the problem of reducing the complexity of a graphical model (G, PG ) by finding a subgraph H of G, chosen from a class of subgraphs H, such that H is optimal with respect to KL-divergence. We do this by first defining a decomposition tree representation for G, which is closely related to the junction-tree representation for G. We then give an algorithm which uses this representation to compute the optimal H ∈ H. Gavril [2] and Tarjan [3] have used graph separation properties to solve several combinatorial optimization problems when the size of the minimal separators in the graph is bounded. We present an extension of this technique which applies to some important choices of H even when the size of the minimal separators of G are arbitrarily large. In particular, this applies to problems such as finding an optimal subgraphical model over a (k − 1)-tree of a graphical model over a k-tree (for arbitrary k) and selecting an optimal subgraphical model with (a constant) d fewer edges with respect to KL-divergence can be solved in time polynomial in |V (G)| using this formulation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to simplify a graphical model while preserving its probability distribution as well as possible. It searches a specified class of subgraphs for the one that is optimal under KL divergence. The goal is therefore a principled choice of reduced model, with optimality defined relative to the allowed subgraph class.

The authors introduce a decomposition-tree representation closely related to a junction tree and use it to compute the optimal subgraph. Their approach extends graph-separation techniques previously used for combinatorial optimization. For some important subgraph classes, the extension works even when the original graph’s minimal separators are arbitrarily large.

The stated applications include finding an optimal model over a (k − 1)-tree within a model over a k-tree, and optimally removing a constant number of edges. The formulation gives polynomial-time solutions in the number of vertices for these problems. The significance is that useful optimal simplifications remain computationally accessible beyond settings requiring small minimal separators.
summary.tldr: A decomposition-tree method finds KL-optimal subgraphical models for important classes, including cases with arbitrarily large minimal separators.

title: Optimal sub-graphical models

abstract: We present new theoretical and empirical results with the iLSTD algorithm for policy evaluation in reinforcement learning with linear function approximation. iLSTD is an incremental method for achieving results similar to LSTD, the dataefficient, least-squares version of temporal difference learning, without incurring the full cost of the LSTD computation. LSTD is O(n2 ), where n is the number of parameters in the linear function approximator, while iLSTD is O(n). In this paper, we generalize the previous iLSTD algorithm and present three new results: (1) the first convergence proof for an iLSTD algorithm; (2) an extension to incorporate eligibility traces without changing the asymptotic computational complexity; and (3) the first empirical results with an iLSTD algorithm for a problem (mountain car) with feature vectors large enough (n = 10, 000) to show substantial computational advantages over LSTD.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy evaluation in reinforcement learning with a linear function approximator. Least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, is data efficient, but its computational cost grows quadratically with the number of parameters. Incremental LSTD aims to obtain similar results with a cost that grows linearly, making larger representations more practical.

The authors generalize the existing incremental algorithm and provide its first convergence proof for an iLSTD algorithm. They also extend it to include eligibility traces, which allow learning updates to incorporate information associated with earlier experience. The extension preserves the algorithm's asymptotic computational complexity, so this added capability does not change its stated linear scaling.

The empirical study uses mountain car with 10,000 features, a representation large enough to demonstrate substantial computational advantages over LSTD. The contribution combines theoretical support, an expanded learning mechanism, and evidence at a scale where the computational distinction matters. The convergence result applies to an iLSTD algorithm as established in the paper, while the reported practical advantage is demonstrated on the specified evaluation problem.
summary.tldr: The paper adds a convergence proof and eligibility traces to iLSTD while retaining linear computational scaling and demonstrating advantages with 10,000 features.

title: iLSTD: Eligibility Traces and Convergence Analysis

abstract: In this paper we introduce and experiment with a framework for learning local perceptual distance functions for visual recognition. We learn a distance function for each training image as a combination of elementary distances between patch-based visual features. We apply these combined local distance functions to the tasks of image retrieval and classification of novel images. On the Caltech 101 object recognition benchmark, we achieve 60.3% mean recognition across classes using 15 training images per class, which is better than the best published performance by Zhang, et al.
originalAbstract: In this paper we introduce and experiment with a framework for learning local perceptual distance functions for visual recognition. We learn a distance function for each training image as a combination of elementary distances between patch-based visual features. We apply these combined local distance functions to the tasks of image retrieval and classification of novel images. On the Caltech 101 object recognition benchmark, we achieve 60.3% mean recognition across classes using 15 training images per class, which is better than the best published performance by Zhang, et al.

paragraphs: This paper learns how to measure visual similarity for image retrieval and classification. Its central choice is to learn a local distance function for each training image. Similarity is therefore adapted around individual training examples, giving each image its own learned way of comparing visual content.

Each local function combines elementary distances between visual features extracted from image patches. These combined functions are then used to retrieve images and classify previously unseen ones. The approach places the learning effort in the comparison rule: patch-based measurements provide the ingredients, and their learned combination determines the distance associated with a training image.

On the Caltech 101 object recognition benchmark, the method achieves 60.3% mean recognition across classes with 15 training images per class. The authors report that this exceeds the best previously published result they compare against. That finding supports the usefulness of learning image-specific combinations of feature distances for recognition. The stated numerical result concerns classification, while the framework is also applied to image retrieval.
summary.tldr: Learning a separate patch-feature distance function for each training image achieves 60.3% mean recognition on Caltech 101 with 15 examples per class.

title: Image Retrieval and Classification Using Local Distance Functions

abstract: A novel approach to measure the interdependence of two time series is proposed, referred to as “stochastic event synchrony” (SES); it quantiﬁes the alignment of two point processes by means of the following parameters: time delay, variance of the timing jitter, fraction of “spurious” events, and average similarity of events. SES may be applied to generic one-dimensional and multi-dimensional point pro- cesses, however, the paper mainly focusses on point processes in time-frequency domain. The average event similarity is in that case described by two parameters: the average frequency offset between events in the time-frequency plane, and the variance of the frequency offset (“frequency jitter”); SES then consists of ﬁve pa- rameters in total. Those parameters quantify the synchrony of oscillatory events, and hence, they provide an alternative to existing synchrony measures that quan- tify amplitude or phase synchrony. The pairwise alignment of point processes is cast as a statistical inference problem, which is solved by applying the max- product algorithm on a graphical model. The SES parameters are determined from the resulting pairwise alignment by maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. The proposed interdependence measure is applied to the problem of detecting anoma- lies in EEG synchrony of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) patients; the results indicate that SES signiﬁcantly improves the sensitivity of EEG in detecting MCI.

paragraphs: Stochastic event synchrony measures relationships between two time series by aligning their events. It describes timing delay, timing variability, the fraction of spurious events, and average event similarity. This provides a description of how events correspond, allowing the measure to distinguish several aspects of synchrony instead of expressing their relationship through a single timing quantity.

The paper focuses on events in the time-frequency plane. There, event similarity is represented by average frequency offset and frequency variability, producing five parameters overall. These describe synchronization between oscillatory events and offer an alternative to measures based on amplitude or phase. The framework also permits more general one-dimensional and multidimensional point processes.

The authors formulate event alignment as statistical inference on a graphical model and solve it with max-product message passing. They then estimate the synchrony parameters from the alignment using maximum a posteriori estimation. In an application to EEG abnormalities associated with mild cognitive impairment, the reported results indicate significantly improved detection sensitivity. This is evidence from the studied application rather than a universal diagnostic guarantee.
summary.tldr: Stochastic event synchrony uses graphical-model alignment to characterize neural events and shows improved EEG sensitivity for detecting mild cognitive impairment.

title: Measuring Neural Synchrony by Message Passing

abstract: Neuroimaging datasets often have a very large number of voxels and a very small number of training cases, which means that overfitting of models for this data can become a very serious problem. Working with a set of fMRI images from a study on stroke recovery, we consider a classification task for which logistic regression performs poorly, even when L1- or L2- regularized. We show that much better discrimination can be achieved by fitting a generative model to each separate condition and then seeing which model is most likely to have generated the data. We compare discriminative training of exactly the same set of models, and we also consider convex blends of generative and discriminative training.
originalAbstract: Neuroimaging datasets often have a very large number of voxels and a very small number of training cases, which means that overfitting of models for this data can become a very serious problem. Working with a set of fMRI images from a study on stroke recovery, we consider a classification task for which logistic regression performs poorly, even when L1- or L2- regularized. We show that much better discrimination can be achieved by fitting a generative model to each separate condition and then seeing which model is most likely to have generated the data. We compare discriminative training of exactly the same set of models, and we also consider convex blends of generative and discriminative training.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to classify fMRI images when each image contains many voxel measurements but only a small number of training examples is available. This imbalance makes overfitting a serious concern: a model can fit the available examples without learning patterns that reliably distinguish new ones. The study uses images collected in research on stroke recovery.

Its central approach is to fit a separate generative model for each condition. Classification then depends on which model makes an observed image most likely. This gives the models a task beyond directly separating labels: they must describe the image data associated with their respective conditions.

For the classification task studied, logistic regression performs poorly even with either L1 or L2 regularization. The authors report substantially better discrimination using the separate generative models. This finding shows that, in this setting, modeling the data within each condition can provide a more effective basis for classification than the tested logistic regression approaches.

The paper also compares generative and discriminative training of exactly the same models and considers weighted blends of the two training objectives. Holding the models fixed allows the comparison to focus on how they are trained. The abstract reports the advantage over logistic regression but does not state which training blend performs best.
summary.tldr: On a stroke-recovery fMRI classification task, separate generative models for each condition achieve much better discrimination than logistic regression, even with L1 or L2 regularization.

title: Generative versus discriminative training of RBMs for classification of fMRI images

abstract: The stochastic approximation method is behind the solution to many important, actively-studied problems in machine learning. Despite its far-reaching application, there is almost no work on applying stochastic approximation to learning problems with constraints. The reason for this, we hypothesize, is that no robust, widely-applicable stochastic approximation method exists for handling such problems. We propose that interior-point methods are a natural solution. We establish the stability of a stochastic interior-point approximation method both analytically and empirically, and demonstrate its utility by deriving an on-line learning algorithm that also performs feature selection via L1 regularization.
originalAbstract: The stochastic approximation method is behind the solution to many important, actively-studied problems in machine learning. Despite its far-reaching application, there is almost no work on applying stochastic approximation to learning problems with constraints. The reason for this, we hypothesize, is that no robust, widely-applicable stochastic approximation method exists for handling such problems. We propose that interior-point methods are a natural solution. We establish the stability of a stochastic interior-point approximation method both analytically and empirically, and demonstrate its utility by deriving an on-line learning algorithm that also performs feature selection via L1 regularization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to learn through stochastic approximation when the learning problem also has constraints. Stochastic approximation underlies many machine learning methods, but the authors identify comparatively little work on its constrained use. They suggest that the absence of a robust, broadly applicable method may help explain this gap; that explanation is presented as a hypothesis.

Their proposed solution combines stochastic approximation with an interior-point approach to handling constraints. The central contribution is a stability result for this combined method, supported both by mathematical analysis and by empirical investigation. Stability matters here because a method for constrained learning must do more than propose updates: its behavior under those updates also needs justification.

The authors demonstrate the method’s usefulness by deriving an online learning algorithm with L1 regularization. This algorithm performs feature selection alongside learning, connecting the general constrained optimization proposal to a concrete learning task. The paper therefore contributes both an analyzed method and an example of how it can support learning with feature selection.
summary.tldr: A stochastic interior-point method supports constrained online learning, with stability analysis and an L1-regularized feature-selection application.

title: An interior-point stochastic approximation method and an L1-regularized delta rule

abstract: Dependent Dirichlet processes (DPs) are dependent sets of random measures, each being marginally Dirichlet process distributed. They are used in Bayesian nonparametric models when the usual exchangebility assumption does not hold. We propose a simple and general framework to construct dependent DPs by marginalizing and normalizing a single gamma process over an extended space. The result is a set of DPs, each located at a point in a space such that neighboring DPs are more dependent. We describe Markov chain Monte Carlo inference, involving the typical Gibbs sampling and three different Metropolis-Hastings proposals to speed up convergence. We report an empirical study of convergence speeds on a synthetic dataset and demonstrate an application of the model to topic modeling through time.
originalAbstract: Dependent Dirichlet processes (DPs) are dependent sets of random measures, each being marginally Dirichlet process distributed. They are used in Bayesian nonparametric models when the usual exchangebility assumption does not hold. We propose a simple and general framework to construct dependent DPs by marginalizing and normalizing a single gamma process over an extended space. The result is a set of DPs, each located at a point in a space such that neighboring DPs are more dependent. We describe Markov chain Monte Carlo inference, involving the typical Gibbs sampling and three different Metropolis-Hastings proposals to speed up convergence. We report an empirical study of convergence speeds on a synthetic dataset and demonstrate an application of the model to topic modeling through time.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to construct related Dirichlet processes for Bayesian nonparametric models. These models are useful when observations cannot be treated as exchangeable, meaning that their placement or ordering matters. The goal is to let distributions vary across a space while retaining dependence between nearby locations.

The construction starts from one gamma process defined over an extended space. Marginalizing and normalizing it produces a collection of random measures, each individually distributed as a Dirichlet process. Their shared construction introduces dependence, with processes at neighboring locations more strongly related. This supplies a general mechanism for combining local variation with shared statistical structure.

The authors describe Markov chain Monte Carlo inference using Gibbs sampling and three Metropolis-Hastings proposals intended to improve convergence speed. They study convergence empirically on synthetic data and demonstrate the model through topic modeling over time. In that application, time provides the space across which topic models are related. The contribution brings together a dependent-process construction, an inference procedure, and an example of modeling distributions that evolve across locations.
summary.tldr: A shared gamma process generates dependent Dirichlet processes that connect nearby locations, with an application to topics over time.

title: Spatial Normalized Gamma Processes

abstract: Automated recovery from failures is a key component in the management of large data centers. Such systems typically employ a hand-made controller created by an expert. While such controllers capture many important aspects of the recovery process, they are often not systematically optimized to reduce costs such as server downtime. In this paper we explain how to use data gathered from the interactions of the hand-made controller with the system, to create an optimized controller. We suggest learning an indefinite horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process, a model for decision making under uncertainty, and solve it using a point-based algorithm. We describe the complete process, starting with data gathering, model learning, model checking procedures, and computing a policy. While our paper focuses on a specific domain, our method is applicable to other systems that use a hand-coded, imperfect controllers.
originalAbstract: Automated recovery from failures is a key component in the management of large data centers. Such systems typically employ a hand-made controller created by an expert. While such controllers capture many important aspects of the recovery process, they are often not systematically optimized to reduce costs such as server downtime. In this paper we explain how to use data gathered from the interactions of the hand-made controller with the system, to create an optimized controller. We suggest learning an indefinite horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process, a model for decision making under uncertainty, and solve it using a point-based algorithm. We describe the complete process, starting with data gathering, model learning, model checking procedures, and computing a policy. While our paper focuses on a specific domain, our method is applicable to other systems that use a hand-coded, imperfect controllers.

paragraphs: Large data centers often recover from failures using controllers written by experts. Such controllers encode useful operational knowledge, but their choices may not be systematically optimized for costs such as server downtime. This paper proposes using records of an existing controller's interactions with the system to build an optimized recovery policy.

The approach learns an indefinite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process. This model represents decision making when the system's state is uncertain and recovery unfolds over a sequence of actions. A point-based algorithm then solves the learned decision problem to compute a policy, connecting the collected operational data to future recovery decisions.

The paper describes the complete workflow, including collecting data, learning the model, checking it, and computing the policy. That full sequence matters because the proposed controller depends on a model inferred from the existing controller's experience. Although the application concerns fault recovery, the authors state that the method also applies to other systems operated by imperfect hand-coded controllers. The contribution is a systematic path from existing control behavior to model-based optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper turns data from an existing fault-recovery controller into a learned decision model and an optimized recovery policy.

title: Improving Existing Fault Recovery Policies

abstract: Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) is a widely used greedy algorithm for recovering sparse vectors from linear measurements. A well-known analysis of Tropp and Gilbert shows that OMP can recover a k-sparse n-dimensional real vector from m = 4k log(n) noise-free random linear measurements with a probability that goes to one as n goes to infinity. This work shows strengthens this result by showing that a lower number of measurements, m = 2k log(n-k), is in fact sufficient for asymptotic recovery. Moreover, this number of measurements is also sufficient for detection of the sparsity pattern (support) of the vector with measurement errors provided the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales to infinity. The scaling m = 2k log(n-k) exactly matches the number of measurements required by the more complex lasso for signal recovery.
originalAbstract: Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) is a widely used greedy algorithm for recovering sparse vectors from linear measurements. A well-known analysis of Tropp and Gilbert shows that OMP can recover a k-sparse n-dimensional real vector from m = 4k log(n) noise-free random linear measurements with a probability that goes to one as n goes to infinity. This work shows strengthens this result by showing that a lower number of measurements, m = 2k log(n-k), is in fact sufficient for asymptotic recovery. Moreover, this number of measurements is also sufficient for detection of the sparsity pattern (support) of the vector with measurement errors provided the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales to infinity. The scaling m = 2k log(n-k) exactly matches the number of measurements required by the more complex lasso for signal recovery.

paragraphs: Orthogonal matching pursuit is a greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from linear measurements. A k-sparse vector has only k nonzero entries among its n coordinates. The paper sharpens an existing analysis of how many random measurements are sufficient for recovery with probability approaching one as the dimension grows.

The earlier result used 4k log(n) noise-free measurements. The new analysis shows that 2k log(n-k) measurements suffice for asymptotic recovery. This is a stronger sufficient guarantee for the algorithm, reducing the measurement count justified by the theory. It does not establish that this count is necessary for every recovery problem.

The same measurement scaling also suffices to identify the nonzero coordinates in the presence of measurement errors, provided the signal-to-noise ratio tends to infinity. That condition is central to the noisy result. The scaling matches the stated measurement requirement for the more complex lasso, showing that this greedy algorithm can attain the same asymptotic measurement scaling under the analyzed conditions.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis shows that 2k log(n-k) random measurements suffice for asymptotic OMP recovery, including noisy support recovery when SNR diverges.

title: Orthogonal Matching Pursuit From Noisy Random Measurements: A New Analysis

abstract: In this paper we present a novel approach to learn directed acyclic graphs (DAG) and factor models within the same framework while also allowing for model comparison between them. For this purpose, we exploit the connection between factor models and DAGs to propose Bayesian hierarchies based on spike and slab priors to promote sparsity, heavy-tailed priors to ensure identifiability and predictive densities to perform the model comparison. We require identifiability to be able to produce variable orderings leading to valid DAGs and sparsity to learn the structures. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on artificial and biological data showing that our approach outperform a number of state of the art methods.
originalAbstract: In this paper we present a novel approach to learn directed acyclic graphs (DAG) and factor models within the same framework while also allowing for model comparison between them. For this purpose, we exploit the connection between factor models and DAGs to propose Bayesian hierarchies based on spike and slab priors to promote sparsity, heavy-tailed priors to ensure identifiability and predictive densities to perform the model comparison. We require identifiability to be able to produce variable orderings leading to valid DAGs and sparsity to learn the structures. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on artificial and biological data showing that our approach outperform a number of state of the art methods.

paragraphs: The paper brings directed acyclic graphs and factor models into a common Bayesian learning framework. These provide different ways to describe relationships among variables, and the authors also want to compare them within the same approach. Their starting point is a connection between the two model families that supports shared machinery for inference.

The framework assigns distinct roles to several modeling choices. Spike-and-slab priors encourage sparse structures, helping determine which relationships should be present. Heavy-tailed priors provide identifiability, which the authors require to obtain variable orderings that lead to valid directed acyclic graphs. Predictive densities then supply the basis for comparing the models.

This combination makes structure learning and model comparison parts of one procedure rather than disconnected decisions. Sparsity concerns the relationships retained, while identifiability supports the ordering needed for a valid graph. Experiments on artificial and biological data demonstrate the approach's effectiveness and report better performance than several state-of-the-art methods. Those results provide empirical support for the framework across the two kinds of data examined.
summary.tldr: A shared Bayesian framework learns sparse factor models and directed acyclic graphs and compares them through predictive densities.

title: Bayesian Sparse Factor Models and DAGs Inference and Comparison

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of minimizing a convex, Lipschitz function $f$ over a convex, compact set $X$ under a stochastic bandit feedback model. In this model, the algorithm is allowed to observe noisy realizations of the function value $f(x)$ at any query point $x \in X$. We demonstrate a generalization of the ellipsoid algorithm that incurs $O(\poly(d)\sqrt{T})$ regret. Since any algorithm has regret at least $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ on this problem, our algorithm is optimal in terms of the scaling with $T$.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the problem of minimizing a convex, Lipschitz function $f$ over a convex, compact set $X$ under a stochastic bandit feedback model. In this model, the algorithm is allowed to observe noisy realizations of the function value $f(x)$ at any query point $x \in X$. We demonstrate a generalization of the ellipsoid algorithm that incurs $O(\poly(d)\sqrt{T})$ regret. Since any algorithm has regret at least $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ on this problem, our algorithm is optimal in terms of the scaling with $T$.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization when the learner can query a point and receive only a noisy observation of the function's value there. The objective is convex and Lipschitz, and the allowed query points form a compact convex set. These assumptions describe the optimization problem studied; the feedback does not directly provide the function's gradient or its values elsewhere.

The authors develop a generalization of the ellipsoid algorithm for this stochastic bandit-feedback setting. They analyze cumulative regret, which captures the cost of the points selected while searching for a good solution. The resulting upper bound grows with the square root of the number of rounds T, multiplied by a factor polynomial in the dimension d.

A corresponding lower bound shows that any algorithm must incur regret of at least square-root order in T on this problem. The proposed method therefore achieves optimal scaling with the time horizon. That optimality statement specifically concerns dependence on T: the reported upper bound also includes a polynomial dependence on dimension. The result establishes the achievable time scaling despite noisy, value-only feedback.
summary.tldr: A generalized ellipsoid algorithm achieves optimal square-root dependence on time for stochastic convex optimization with noisy value-only feedback.

title: Stochastic convex optimization with bandit feedback

abstract: In stochastic multi--armed bandits the objective is to solve the exploration--exploitation dilemma and ultimately maximize the expected reward. Nonetheless, in many practical problems, maximizing the expected reward is not the most desirable objective. In this paper, we introduce a novel setting based on the principle of risk--aversion where the objective is to compete against the arm with the best risk--return trade--off. This setting proves to be intrinsically more difficult than the standard multi-arm bandit setting due in part to an exploration risk which introduces a regret associated to the variability of an algorithm. Using variance as a measure of risk, we introduce two new algorithms, we investigate their theoretical guarantees, and we report preliminary empirical results.
originalAbstract: In stochastic multi--armed bandits the objective is to solve the exploration--exploitation dilemma and ultimately maximize the expected reward. Nonetheless, in many practical problems, maximizing the expected reward is not the most desirable objective. In this paper, we introduce a novel setting based on the principle of risk--aversion where the objective is to compete against the arm with the best risk--return trade--off. This setting proves to be intrinsically more difficult than the standard multi-arm bandit setting due in part to an exploration risk which introduces a regret associated to the variability of an algorithm. Using variance as a measure of risk, we introduce two new algorithms, we investigate their theoretical guarantees, and we report preliminary empirical results.

paragraphs: The paper changes the objective of a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem to account for risk. Standard formulations seek high expected reward while balancing exploration with exploitation. Here, the learner instead competes with the arm offering the best balance between return and risk, using variance as the measure of risk.

This objective makes exploration more complicated. The authors identify an exploration risk that produces regret associated with the algorithm's own variability. Thus, evaluating a learning strategy requires accounting for the risk introduced by its behavior during learning as well as the risk–return qualities of the available arms. The resulting setting is intrinsically harder than the standard bandit problem.

The authors introduce two algorithms for this formulation and investigate their theoretical guarantees. They also report preliminary empirical results. The contribution is both a new decision criterion and methods for pursuing it, with analysis showing why a concern for variability changes the learning problem. The empirical evidence is presented as preliminary support alongside that theoretical investigation.
summary.tldr: A variance-based risk-averse bandit formulation exposes additional exploration risk and motivates two new learning algorithms.

title: Risk-Aversion in Multi-armed Bandits

abstract: We present a new variational inference algorithm for Gaussian processes with non-conjugate likelihood functions. This includes binary and multi-class classification, as well as ordinal regression. Our method constructs a convex lower bound, which can be optimized by using an efficient fixed point update method. We then show empirically that our new approach is much faster than existing methods without any degradation in performance.
originalAbstract: We present a new variational inference algorithm for Gaussian processes with non-conjugate likelihood functions. This includes binary and multi-class classification, as well as ordinal regression. Our method constructs a convex lower bound, which can be optimized by using an efficient fixed point update method. We then show empirically that our new approach is much faster than existing methods without any degradation in performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses inference for Gaussian processes whose likelihood functions are non-conjugate. The supported settings include binary classification, multiclass classification, and ordinal regression. These tasks motivate an inference procedure that can handle the likelihoods used for their outputs while retaining the Gaussian process modeling framework.

The proposed solution is a variational inference algorithm built around a convex lower bound. Instead of directly carrying out the original inference calculation, the method optimizes this bound using efficient fixed-point updates. The bound and update procedure are the central computational contributions: together they provide a tractable optimization route for the non-conjugate cases covered by the method.

The authors report that the approach is much faster than existing methods in their empirical comparisons, with no degradation in performance. This is an experimental finding about the evaluated settings, rather than a universal speed guarantee. Its practical significance is that the reported computational savings do not require sacrificing the measured predictive performance, making inference efficiency the principal benefit highlighted by the paper.
summary.tldr: A convex-bound variational algorithm speeds up non-conjugate Gaussian process inference without performance loss in the reported experiments.

title: Fast Bayesian Inference for Non-Conjugate Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: This paper considers the problem of transferring experimental findings learned from multiple heterogeneous domains to a target environment, in which only limited experiments can be performed. We reduce questions of transportability from multiple domains and with limited scope to symbolic derivations in the do-calculus, thus extending the treatment of transportability from full experiments introduced in Pearl and Bareinboim (2011). We further provide different graphical and algorithmic conditions for computing the transport formula for this setting, that is, a way of fusing the observational and experimental information scattered throughout different domains to synthesize a consistent estimate of the desired effects.
originalAbstract: This paper considers the problem of transferring experimental findings learned from multiple heterogeneous domains to a target environment, in which only limited experiments can be performed. We reduce questions of transportability from multiple domains and with limited scope to symbolic derivations in the do-calculus, thus extending the treatment of transportability from full experiments introduced in Pearl and Bareinboim (2011). We further provide different graphical and algorithmic conditions for computing the transport formula for this setting, that is, a way of fusing the observational and experimental information scattered throughout different domains to synthesize a consistent estimate of the desired effects.

paragraphs: Experimental findings from one environment may be useful in another, but differences between environments complicate that transfer. This paper studies how to combine findings from several heterogeneous domains to estimate causal effects in a target environment where only limited experiments can be conducted. The available evidence includes both observations and experiments spread across domains.

The authors translate transportability questions into symbolic derivations using do-calculus, a formal system for reasoning about interventions. This extends treatment of transportability based on full experiments to settings with restricted experimental scope and multiple sources. The approach makes the reasoning about which evidence can be transferred an explicit part of constructing an estimate.

The paper provides graphical and algorithmic conditions for computing a transport formula. Such a formula specifies how information from the different domains can be combined to obtain a consistent estimate of the desired effect. The contribution is a formal route to evidence fusion when the relevant conditions hold, addressing differences between environments and limits on experimentation within the same framework.
summary.tldr: Do-calculus provides conditions and formulas for combining evidence across heterogeneous environments when experiments are limited.

title: Transportability from Multiple Environments with Limited Experiments

abstract: When a probabilistic model and its prior are given, Bayesian learning offers inference with automatic parameter tuning. However, Bayesian learning is often obstructed by computational difficulty: the rigorous Bayesian learning is intractable in many models, and its variational Bayesian (VB) approximation is prone to suffer from local minima. In this paper, we overcome this difficulty for low-rank subspace clustering (LRSC) by providing an exact global solver and its efficient approximation. LRSC extracts a low-dimensional structure of data by embedding samples into the union of low-dimensional subspaces, and its variational Bayesian variant has shown good performance. We first prove a key property that the VB-LRSC model is highly redundant. Thanks to this property, the optimization problem of VB-LRSC can be separated into small subproblems, each of which has only a small number of unknown variables. Our exact global solver relies on another key property that the stationary condition of each subproblem is written as a set of polynomial equations, which is solvable with the homotopy method. For further computational efficiency, we also propose an efficient approximate variant, of which the stationary condition can be written as a polynomial equation with a single variable. Experimental results show the usefulness of our approach.

However, Bayesian learning is often obstructed by computational difficulty: the rigorous Bayesian learning is intractable in many models, and its variational Bayesian (VB) approximation is prone to suffer from local minima. In this paper, we overcome this difficulty for low-rank subspace clustering (LRSC) by providing an exact global solver and its efficient approximation. LRSC extracts a low-dimensional structure of data by embedding samples into the union of low-dimensional subspaces, and its variational Bayesian variant has shown good performance. We first prove a key property that the VB-LRSC model is highly redundant. Thanks to this property, the optimization problem of VB-LRSC can be separated into small subproblems, each of which has only a small number of unknown variables. Our exact global solver relies on another key property that the stationary condition of each subproblem is written as a set of polynomial equations, which is solvable with the homotopy method. For further computational efficiency, we also propose an efficient approximate variant, of which the stationary condition can be written as a polynomial equation with a single variable. Experimental results show the usefulness of our approach.

paragraphs: Low-rank subspace clustering represents data through a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Its variational Bayesian formulation has shown good performance, but optimization can get trapped in local minima. This paper develops an exact global solver for that formulation, together with a more computationally efficient approximation, addressing a specific obstacle to Bayesian learning in this model.

The authors first prove that the variational Bayesian model contains substantial redundancy. Exploiting this property separates the optimization into small subproblems with few unknowns. Each subproblem's stationary conditions can be expressed as polynomial equations, allowing the exact solver to use a homotopy method to solve them.

For greater efficiency, the approximate variant reduces its stationary condition to a polynomial equation in a single variable. Experiments show the usefulness of the approach. The key contribution is the model-specific mathematical reduction: redundancy that might appear to complicate learning instead enables a global solution strategy. The exactness applies to the variational Bayesian optimization problem, whose formulation is itself an approximation to full Bayesian inference.
summary.tldr: Model redundancy enables an exact global solver and an efficient approximate solver for variational Bayesian low-rank subspace clustering.

title: Global Solver and Its Efficient Approximation for Variational Bayesian Low-rank Subspace Clustering

abstract: In this paper we introduce a novel method that can efficiently estimate a family of hierarchical dense sets in high-dimensional distributions. Our method can be regarded as a natural extension of the one-class SVM (OCSVM) algorithm that finds multiple parallel separating hyperplanes in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We call our method q-OCSVM, as it can be used to estimate $q$ quantiles of a high-dimensional distribution. For this purpose, we introduce a new global convex optimization program that finds all estimated sets at once and show that it can be solved efficiently. We prove the correctness of our method and present empirical results that demonstrate its superiority over existing methods.

We call our method q-OCSVM, as it can be used to estimate $q$ quantiles of a high-dimensional distribution. For this purpose, we introduce a new global convex optimization program that finds all estimated sets at once and show that it can be solved efficiently.
