paragraphs: Describing a high-dimensional distribution can involve identifying a hierarchy of dense regions rather than just one boundary around typical data. This paper introduces q-OCSVM to estimate such a family of sets efficiently. The method can be used to estimate multiple quantiles of a high-dimensional distribution.

The construction extends the one-class support vector machine by finding several parallel separating hyperplanes in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These hyperplanes provide the structure for the multiple estimated sets. Instead of treating each set as a separate optimization task, the authors formulate one global convex program that finds all of them together.

The paper shows that this joint program can be solved efficiently and proves the method's correctness. Empirical comparisons also report superiority over existing methods. The contribution is a coordinated way to estimate several levels of a distribution's dense structure, combining a convex formulation with theoretical justification and experimental evidence for the resulting estimates.
summary.tldr: q-OCSVM jointly estimates hierarchical dense regions of a high-dimensional distribution through one efficient convex optimization problem.

title: q-OCSVM: A q-Quantile Estimator for High-Dimensional Distributions

abstract: Consider the problem of minimizing the sum of a smooth (possibly non-convex) and a convex (possibly nonsmooth) function involving a large number of variables. A popular approach to solve this problem is the block coordinate descent (BCD) method whereby at each iteration only one variable block is updated while the remaining variables are held fixed. With the recent advances in the developments of the multi-core parallel processing technology, it is desirable to parallelize the BCD method by allowing multiple blocks to be updated simultaneously at each iteration of the algorithm. In this work, we propose an inexact parallel BCD approach where at each iteration, a subset of the variables is updated in parallel by minimizing convex approximations of the original objective function. We investigate the convergence of this parallel BCD method for both randomized and cyclic variable selection rules. We analyze the asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence behavior of the algorithm for both convex and non-convex objective functions. The numerical experiments suggest that for a special case of Lasso minimization problem, the cyclic block selection rule can outperform the randomized rule.

paragraphs: The paper studies large optimization problems whose objective combines a smooth, possibly nonconvex function with a convex, possibly nonsmooth function. Block coordinate descent addresses such problems by updating one group of variables while keeping the others fixed. The authors seek to exploit parallel processors by allowing several groups to change simultaneously.

Their proposed inexact parallel method updates a subset of variables by minimizing convex approximations of the original objective. These local optimization problems provide a way to organize parallel updates even when the overall objective is nonconvex. The paper considers both randomized selection of variable blocks and cyclic selection according to an ordered schedule.

The analysis covers asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence behavior for convex and nonconvex objectives, addressing both eventual behavior and behavior before the limit. Numerical experiments on a special case of Lasso minimization suggest that cyclic selection can outperform randomized selection. That comparison is specific to the examined case; the broader contribution is an analyzed framework for parallel block updates through successive convex approximations.
summary.tldr: Parallel block updates based on convex approximations support large nonsmooth optimization problems, with convergence analyses for randomized and cyclic selection.

title: Parallel Successive Convex Approximation for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Recommender systems involve an inherent trade-off between accuracy of recommendations and the extent to which users are willing to release information about their preferences. In this paper, we explore a two-tiered notion of privacy where there is a small set of public'' users who are willing to share their preferences openly, and a large set of private'' users who require privacy guarantees. We show theoretically and demonstrate empirically that a moderate number of public users with no access to private user information already suffices for reasonable accuracy. Moreover, we introduce a new privacy concept for gleaning relational information from private users while maintaining a first order deniability. We demonstrate gains from controlled access to private user preferences.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems benefit from information about users' preferences, creating a tension between prediction accuracy and willingness to disclose those preferences. This paper considers a population with two privacy expectations: a small group openly shares its preferences, while a much larger group requires privacy guarantees. This separation gives the authors a way to study how different sources of information contribute.

The first result concerns what can be achieved using public information alone. Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence show that a moderate number of public users can suffice for reasonable recommendation accuracy without accessing private users' information. The stated result is about obtaining useful accuracy, rather than eliminating every accuracy cost associated with privacy.

The authors then introduce a privacy concept that permits extracting relational information from private users while preserving what they call first order deniability. They demonstrate gains from this controlled access to preferences. Together, the results examine both the usefulness of openly shared data and the additional benefit available under a more selective form of private information access.
summary.tldr: A two-tier privacy framework studies useful recommendations from public users and further gains from controlled access to private preferences.

title: Controlling privacy in recommender systems

abstract: We combine supervised learning with unsupervised learning in deep neural networks. The proposed model is trained to simultaneously minimize the sum of supervised and unsupervised cost functions by backpropagation, avoiding the need for layer-wise pre-training. Our work builds on top of the Ladder network proposed by Valpola (2015) which we extend by combining the model with supervision. We show that the resulting model reaches state-of-the-art performance in semi-supervised MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification in addition to permutation-invariant MNIST classification with all labels.
originalAbstract: We combine supervised learning with unsupervised learning in deep neural networks. The proposed model is trained to simultaneously minimize the sum of supervised and unsupervised cost functions by backpropagation, avoiding the need for layer-wise pre-training. Our work builds on top of the Ladder network proposed by Valpola (2015) which we extend by combining the model with supervision. We show that the resulting model reaches state-of-the-art performance in semi-supervised MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification in addition to permutation-invariant MNIST classification with all labels.

paragraphs: The paper combines supervised and unsupervised learning within a deep neural network. Supervised learning supplies a task-related objective, while unsupervised learning supplies an additional objective that does not depend on class labels. The authors extend an existing Ladder network by incorporating supervision, making both forms of learning part of the same model.

Training minimizes the sum of the supervised and unsupervised costs through backpropagation. This allows the objectives to shape the network simultaneously and avoids the need for separate layer-by-layer pretraining. The central methodological choice is therefore how learning signals are combined during training, with supervision integrated into the Ladder network rather than added only after a preliminary training phase.

The resulting model achieves state-of-the-art results on semi-supervised MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification. It also achieves state-of-the-art performance on permutation-invariant MNIST classification with all labels available. Together, the reported results show benefits in both the evaluated semi-supervised tasks and a fully labeled setting, supporting the usefulness of jointly optimizing the two kinds of cost.
summary.tldr: Ladder networks jointly optimize supervised and unsupervised objectives, achieving state-of-the-art results on the reported classification benchmarks without layer-wise pretraining.

title: Semi-supervised Learning with Ladder Networks

abstract: In personalized recommendation systems, it is important to predict preferences of a user on items that have not been seen by that user yet. Similarly, in revenue management, it is important to predict outcomes of comparisons among those items that have never been compared so far. The MultiNomial Logit model, a popular discrete choice model, captures the structure of the hidden preferences with a low-rank matrix. In order to predict the preferences, we want to learn the underlying model from noisy observations of the low-rank matrix, collected as revealed preferences in various forms of ordinal data. A natural approach to learn such a model is to solve a convex relaxation of nuclear norm minimization. We present the convex relaxation approach in two contexts of interest: collaborative ranking and bundled choice modeling. In both cases, we show that the convex relaxation is minimax optimal. We prove an upper bound on the resulting error with finite samples, and provide a matching information-theoretic lower bound.

paragraphs: Recommendation and choice prediction often require estimating preferences for items that a person has never evaluated. The available evidence may consist of rankings or choices rather than numerical ratings. This paper studies how to recover hidden preference structure from such noisy ordinal observations so that unseen preferences and comparisons can be predicted.

The model represents preferences with a low-rank matrix within a MultiNomial Logit formulation. Low rank supplies shared structure across otherwise incomplete observations. The authors develop a convex relaxation based on nuclear norm minimization and examine it in two settings: collaborative ranking and bundled choice modeling. Both settings use observed relative preferences to learn the underlying model.

For each setting, the paper proves a finite-sample upper bound on estimation error and a matching information-theoretic lower bound. Together, these establish minimax optimality in the studied formulations: the method attains the best worst-case error behavior characterized by the bounds. This gives a statistical justification for the convex approach beyond its role as a convenient optimization strategy.
summary.tldr: Convex learning of low-rank preference models achieves minimax-optimal error guarantees for collaborative ranking and bundled choice modeling.

title: Collaboratively Learning Preferences from Ordinal Data

abstract: We introduce the Stochastic Asynchronous Proximal Alternating Linearized Minimization (SAPALM) method, a block coordinate stochastic proximal-gradient method for solving nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization problems. SAPALM is the first asynchronous parallel optimization method that provably converges on a large class of nonconvex, nonsmooth problems. We prove that SAPALM matches the best known rates of convergence --- among synchronous or asynchronous methods --- on this problem class. We provide upper bounds on the number of workers for which we can expect to see a linear speedup, which match the best bounds known for less complex problems, and show that in practice SAPALM achieves this linear speedup. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on several matrix factorization problems.
originalAbstract: We introduce the Stochastic Asynchronous Proximal Alternating Linearized Minimization (SAPALM) method, a block coordinate stochastic proximal-gradient method for solving nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization problems. SAPALM is the first asynchronous parallel optimization method that provably converges on a large class of nonconvex, nonsmooth problems. We prove that SAPALM matches the best known rates of convergence --- among synchronous or asynchronous methods --- on this problem class. We provide upper bounds on the number of workers for which we can expect to see a linear speedup, which match the best bounds known for less complex problems, and show that in practice SAPALM achieves this linear speedup. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on several matrix factorization problems.

paragraphs: This paper introduces SAPALM for optimization problems that are both nonconvex and nonsmooth. The method uses stochastic proximal-gradient updates on blocks of variables and allows parallel workers to operate asynchronously. It addresses how to gain parallel speed while retaining convergence guarantees for this challenging class of objectives.

The authors prove convergence on a broad class of such problems and show that the convergence rates match the best known rates among synchronous and asynchronous methods for that class. They also derive upper bounds on the number of workers for which linear speedup can be expected. These bounds match the best known bounds for less complex problems.

The experiments demonstrate linear speedup in practice and state-of-the-art performance on several matrix-factorization problems. The worker bounds give a theoretical scope for expecting gains proportional to added parallel resources, while the empirical results show that such gains can occur in implementation. The contribution combines asynchronous computation with optimization guarantees and practical evidence on the stated applications.
summary.tldr: SAPALM provides asynchronous optimization for a broad nonsmooth, nonconvex problem class, with convergence guarantees and demonstrated linear parallel speedup.

title: The Sound of APALM Clapping: Faster Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Stochastic Asynchronous PALM

abstract: We consider the weakly supervised binary classification problem where the labels are randomly flipped with probability $1-\alpha$. Although there exist numerous algorithms for this problem, it remains theoretically unexplored how the statistical accuracies and computational efficiency of these algorithms depend on the degree of supervision, which is quantified by $\alpha$. In this paper, we characterize the effect of $\alpha$ by establishing the information-theoretic and computational boundaries, namely, the minimax-optimal statistical accuracy that can be achieved by all algorithms, and polynomial-time algorithms under an oracle computational model. For small $\alpha$, our result shows a gap between these two boundaries, which represents the computational price of achieving the information-theoretic boundary due to the lack of supervision. Interestingly, we also show that this gap narrows as $\alpha$ increases. In other words, having more supervision, i.e., more correct labels, not only improves the optimal statistical accuracy as expected, but also enhances the computational efficiency for achieving such accuracy.

In other words, having more supervision, i.e., more correct labels, not only improves the optimal statistical accuracy as expected, but also enhances the computational efficiency for achieving such accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary classification when labels are randomly flipped with probability 1 − α. The parameter α measures the degree of supervision. The central question is how changing label reliability affects both the best possible statistical accuracy and the computational effort needed to reach that accuracy.

The authors establish two boundaries: the minimax accuracy achievable by algorithms without computational restrictions, and the accuracy achievable by polynomial-time algorithms under an oracle computational model. Comparing these boundaries separates what the data makes statistically possible from what computationally efficient procedures can attain within that model.

For small α, the analysis finds a gap between the boundaries, representing a computational price associated with weak supervision. The gap narrows as α increases. Thus, in the studied setting, more correct labels improve the optimal statistical accuracy and make that accuracy more accessible computationally. The result gives a theoretical account of why additional supervision can provide benefits beyond simply reducing label noise.
summary.tldr: Under an oracle computational model, stronger supervision narrows the gap between statistically optimal classification and what polynomial-time algorithms can achieve.

title: More Supervision, Less Computation: Statistical-Computational Tradeoffs in Weakly Supervised Learning

abstract: For testing two vector random variables for independence, we propose testing whether the distance of one vector from an arbitrary center point is independent from the distance of the other vector from another arbitrary center point by a univariate test. We prove that under minimal assumptions, it is enough to have a consistent univariate independence test on the distances, to guarantee that the power to detect dependence between the random vectors increases to one with sample size. If the univariate test is distribution-free, the multivariate test will also be distribution-free. If we consider multiple center points and aggregate the center-specific univariate tests, the power may be further improved, and the resulting multivariate test may be distribution-free for specific aggregation methods (if the univariate test is distribution-free). We show that certain multivariate tests recently proposed in the literature can be viewed as instances of this general approach. Moreover, we show in experiments that novel tests constructed using our approach can have better power and computational time than competing approaches.

paragraphs: Testing whether two random vectors are independent can be harder than testing two scalar variables. This paper reduces the problem by measuring each vector's distance from a chosen center point, then applying a univariate independence test to those two distances. The approach turns an existing scalar test into a tool for detecting multivariate dependence.

Under minimal assumptions, the authors prove that a consistent univariate test is sufficient for the resulting test's probability of detecting dependence to approach one as sample size grows. If the scalar test is distribution-free, the multivariate construction retains that property. These guarantees explain why the distance reduction can preserve useful testing behavior.

Using several centers and combining their tests may improve power further. Distribution-free behavior is retained for specific aggregation methods when the underlying test is distribution-free. The authors also show that some existing multivariate tests fit this framework. Experiments demonstrate that newly constructed tests can improve both detection power and computational time over competing approaches.
summary.tldr: Testing distances from chosen centers converts univariate independence tests into consistent multivariate tests under minimal assumptions.

title: Multivariate tests of association based on univariate tests

abstract: We present a data-efficient reinforcement learning method for continuous state-action systems under significant observation noise. Data-efficient solutions under small noise exist, such as PILCO which learns the cartpole swing-up task in 30s. PILCO evaluates policies by planning state-trajectories using a dynamics model. However, PILCO applies policies to the observed state, therefore planning in observation space. We extend PILCO with filtering to instead plan in belief space, consistent with partially observable Markov decisions process (POMDP) planning. This enables data-efficient learning under significant observation noise, outperforming more naive methods such as post-hoc application of a filter to policies optimised by the original (unfiltered) PILCO algorithm. We test our method on the cartpole swing-up task, which involves nonlinear dynamics and requires nonlinear control.

However, PILCO applies policies to the observed state, therefore planning in observation space. We extend PILCO with filtering to instead plan in belief space, consistent with partially observable Markov decisions process (POMDP) planning. This enables data-efficient learning under significant observation noise, outperforming more naive methods such as post-hoc application of a filter to policies optimised by the original (unfiltered) PILCO algorithm. We test our method on the cartpole swing-up task, which involves nonlinear dynamics and requires nonlinear control.

paragraphs: Learning to control a continuous system becomes harder when observations are substantially noisy. The controller must act using an imperfect view of the underlying state. This paper extends PILCO, a data-efficient reinforcement learning method, to account for that uncertainty during policy planning in a Gaussian partially observable setting.

PILCO evaluates policies through trajectories predicted by a learned dynamics model, but its original policies act on observed states. The proposed extension incorporates filtering and plans in belief space: a representation of uncertainty about the state. This makes the planning process consistent with the information available to a controller operating under partial observability.

The distinction matters because adding a filter after optimizing a policy leaves that optimization unaware of the filtering process. The authors report that integrating filtering into planning enables data-efficient learning under significant observation noise and outperforms such post-hoc approaches. Their test uses cartpole swing-up, a task involving nonlinear dynamics and nonlinear control, demonstrating the benefit in the continuous-control problem examined.
summary.tldr: Integrating filtering into PILCO's policy planning improves data-efficient cartpole learning under significant observation noise.

title: Data-Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Continuous State-Action Gaussian-POMDPs

abstract: We consider the problem of accurately estimating the reliability of workers based on noisy labels they provide, which is a fundamental question in crowdsourcing. We propose a novel lower bound on the minimax estimation error which applies to any estimation procedure. We further propose Triangular Estimation (TE), an algorithm for estimating the reliability of workers. TE has low complexity, may be implemented in a streaming setting when labels are provided by workers in real time, and does not rely on an iterative procedure. We prove that TE is minimax optimal and matches our lower bound. We conclude by assessing the performance of TE and other state-of-the-art algorithms on both synthetic and real-world data.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of accurately estimating the reliability of workers based on noisy labels they provide, which is a fundamental question in crowdsourcing. We propose a novel lower bound on the minimax estimation error which applies to any estimation procedure. We further propose Triangular Estimation (TE), an algorithm for estimating the reliability of workers. TE has low complexity, may be implemented in a streaming setting when labels are provided by workers in real time, and does not rely on an iterative procedure. We prove that TE is minimax optimal and matches our lower bound. We conclude by assessing the performance of TE and other state-of-the-art algorithms on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can be noisy, so assessing the people who provide them is a central statistical problem. This paper studies how accurately worker reliability can be estimated from their labels. It first establishes a lower bound on minimax estimation error: a limit on the best worst-case accuracy that any estimation procedure can achieve in the problem considered.

The authors then introduce Triangular Estimation, or TE, and prove that it matches this lower bound. This establishes minimax optimality, connecting an achievable algorithm to the fundamental estimation limit. The claim concerns worst-case estimation error in the studied setting, rather than saying that TE must outperform every alternative on each individual dataset.

TE also has practical computational properties: it has low complexity, avoids an iterative procedure, and can operate as workers supply labels in real time. The paper evaluates it alongside other leading algorithms on synthetic and real-world data. Together, the results connect statistical optimality with an implementation suitable for streaming crowdsourcing workflows.
summary.tldr: Triangular Estimation estimates worker reliability with low computational complexity and provably optimal worst-case error.

title: A Minimax Optimal Algorithm for Crowdsourcing

abstract: Estimating treatment effects from observational data is challenging due to the missing counterfactuals. Matching is an effective strategy to tackle this problem. The widely used matching estimators such as nearest neighbor matching (NNM) pair the treated units with the most similar control units in terms of covariates, and then estimate treatment effects accordingly. However, the existing matching estimators have poor performance when the distributions of control and treatment groups are unbalanced. Moreover, theoretical analysis suggests that the bias of causal effect estimation would increase with the dimension of covariates. In this paper, we aim to address these problems by learning low-dimensional balanced and nonlinear representations (BNR) for observational data. In particular, we convert counterfactual prediction as a classification problem, develop a kernel learning model with domain adaptation constraint, and design a novel matching estimator. The dimension of covariates will be significantly reduced after projecting data to a low-dimensional subspace. Experiments on several synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

However, the existing matching estimators have poor performance when the distributions of control and treatment groups are unbalanced. The dimension of covariates will be significantly reduced after projecting data to a low-dimensional subspace. paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data requires dealing with missing counterfactuals: the alternative outcome for a unit is unobserved. Matching addresses this by comparing treated units with similar untreated units. However, matching can perform poorly when the two groups have different covariate distributions, and theoretical analysis links increasing covariate dimension with greater estimation bias.

The paper learns a lower-dimensional, nonlinear representation in which the treatment and control groups are balanced. It formulates counterfactual prediction as a classification problem and develops a kernel learning model with a domain adaptation constraint. A new matching estimator then uses the resulting representation, bringing dimensionality reduction and distribution balancing into the matching procedure.

Projecting the data into a smaller space substantially reduces the number of covariate dimensions used for comparison. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a representation-learning strategy tailored to two stated difficulties in observational matching: imbalance between groups and the challenges associated with comparing units across many covariates.
summary.tldr: The method improves observational treatment-effect matching by learning low-dimensional nonlinear representations that balance treatment and control groups.

title: Matching on Balanced Nonlinear Representations for Treatment Effects Estimation

abstract: We revisit isotonic regression on linear orders, the problem of fitting monotonic functions to best explain the data, in an online setting. It was previously shown that online isotonic regression is unlearnable in a fully adversarial model, which lead to its study in the fixed design model. Here, we instead develop the more practical random permutation model. We show that the regret is bounded above by the excess leave-one-out loss for which we develop efficient algorithms and matching lower bounds. We also analyze the class of simple and popular forward algorithms and recommend where to look for algorithms for online isotonic regression on partial orders.
originalAbstract: We revisit isotonic regression on linear orders, the problem of fitting monotonic functions to best explain the data, in an online setting. It was previously shown that online isotonic regression is unlearnable in a fully adversarial model, which lead to its study in the fixed design model. Here, we instead develop the more practical random permutation model. We show that the regret is bounded above by the excess leave-one-out loss for which we develop efficient algorithms and matching lower bounds. We also analyze the class of simple and popular forward algorithms and recommend where to look for algorithms for online isotonic regression on partial orders.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression fits predictions that respect an ordering: as inputs move along the order, fitted values must remain monotonic. This paper studies the online version, where predictions are made sequentially. Earlier work found the problem unlearnable under a fully adversarial model, motivating alternatives that restrict how the sequence is presented.

The authors develop a random permutation model as an alternative to the previously studied fixed-design setting. Their analysis bounds regret by excess leave-one-out loss, connecting online performance to a quantity based on leaving observations out in turn. They develop efficient algorithms for this quantity and establish matching lower bounds.

The paper also examines simple, commonly used forward algorithms and offers directions for online isotonic regression on partial orders. Its main contribution is a different framework for understanding when sequential monotonic prediction can be analyzed effectively. The random permutation assumption is essential context for the guarantees: the results address this model rather than overturning the earlier impossibility for fully adversarial sequences.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes online isotonic regression under random presentation order, relating regret to excess leave-one-out loss.

title: Random Permutation Online Isotonic Regression

abstract: The Euclidean k-means problem is arguably the most widely-studied clustering problem in machine learning. While the k-means objective is NP-hard in the worst-case, practitioners have enjoyed remarkable success in applying heuristics like Lloyd's algorithm for this problem. To address this disconnect, we study the following question: what properties of real-world instances will enable us to design efficient algorithms and prove guarantees for finding the optimal clustering? We consider a natural notion called additive perturbation stability that we believe captures many practical instances of Euclidean k-means clustering. Stable instances have unique optimal k-means solutions that does not change even when each point is perturbed a little (in Euclidean distance). This captures the property that k-means optimal solution should be tolerant to measurement errors and uncertainty in the points. We design efficient algorithms that provably recover the optimal clustering for instances that are additive perturbation stable. When the instance has some additional separation, we can design a simple, efficient algorithm with provable guarantees that is also robust to outliers. We also complement these results by studying the amount of stability in real datasets, and demonstrating that our algorithm performs well on these benchmark datasets.

To address this disconnect, we study the following question: what properties of real-world instances will enable us to design efficient algorithms and prove guarantees for finding the optimal clustering? We consider a natural notion called additive perturbation stability that we believe captures many practical instances of Euclidean k-means clustering. Stable instances have unique optimal k-means solutions that does not change even when each point is perturbed a little (in Euclidean distance). This captures the property that k-means optimal solution should be tolerant to measurement errors and uncertainty in the points. We design efficient algorithms that provably recover the optimal clustering for instances that are additive perturbation stable. When the instance has some additional separation, we can design a simple, efficient algorithm with provable guarantees that is also robust to outliers. We also complement these results by studying the amount of stability in real datasets, and demonstrating that our algorithm performs well on these benchmark datasets.

This paper investigates whether a property of the data can help explain that gap and support stronger algorithms. It studies additive perturbation stability: the optimal clustering is unique and remains unchanged when each point moves a little in Euclidean distance.

That condition formalizes tolerance to small measurement errors or uncertainty in point locations. For instances satisfying it, the authors design efficient algorithms that provably recover the optimal clustering. With an additional separation condition, they also obtain a simple, efficient algorithm that has theoretical guarantees and tolerates outliers.

The paper complements its theory by examining stability in real datasets and reporting good algorithmic performance on benchmark data. Its guarantees are tied to the stated stability and separation properties. The contribution is therefore a connection between a concrete form of data robustness and exact recovery, alongside evidence that studying this property can be relevant to practical clustering.
summary.tldr: Small-perturbation stability enables efficient, provably optimal k-means clustering, with outlier robustness under an additional separation condition.

title: Clustering Stable Instances of Euclidean k-means.

abstract: It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive, there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations. Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

It measures similarity through matches between subspaces of neuron activations.

The authors develop a theory characterizing the structure of these matches. The contribution combines a precise comparison framework with algorithms and empirical evidence, giving researchers a systematic way to investigate how much representational agreement identical architectures actually produce.
summary.tldr: A theory and algorithms for activation-subspace matching suggest that differently initialized networks learn less similar representations than often expected.

title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation

abstract: Graph-structured data arise in wide applications, such as computer vision, bioinformatics, and social networks. Quantifying similarities among graphs is a fundamental problem. In this paper, we develop a framework for computing graph kernels, based on return probabilities of random walks. The advantages of our proposed kernels are that they can effectively exploit various node attributes, while being scalable to large datasets. We conduct extensive graph classification experiments to evaluate our graph kernels. The experimental results show that our graph kernels significantly outperform other state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

This is a foundational problem when data are represented by connected entities, as in computer vision, bioinformatics, and social networks. The paper develops graph kernels, which provide similarity measures that can be used for tasks such as assigning whole graphs to categories.

The framework bases those kernels on the probabilities that random walks return to their starting nodes. This connects the similarity measure to how movement through a graph reflects its structure. The proposed kernels can also exploit different kinds of node attributes, allowing information attached to individual nodes to contribute alongside the graph’s connectivity. Scalability to large datasets is another stated advantage.

The authors evaluate their kernels through extensive graph classification experiments. They report significantly better accuracy and computational efficiency than other state-of-the-art approaches in those comparisons. The findings support return probabilities as a useful basis for graph comparison, with the tested framework combining structural information, node attributes, and efficient computation.
summary.tldr: RetGK compares graphs through random-walk return probabilities and node attributes, improving classification accuracy and computational efficiency in experiments.

title: RetGK: Graph Kernels based on Return Probabilities of Random Walks

abstract: This paper investigates the ability of generative networks to convert their input noise distributions into other distributions. Firstly, we demonstrate a construction that allows ReLU networks to increase the dimensionality of their noise distribution by implementing a ``space-filling'' function based on iterated tent maps. We show this construction is optimal by analyzing the number of affine pieces in functions computed by multivariate ReLU networks. Secondly, we provide efficient ways (using polylog$(1/\epsilon)$ nodes) for networks to pass between univariate uniform and normal distributions, using a Taylor series approximation and a binary search gadget for computing function inverses. Lastly, we indicate how high dimensional distributions can be efficiently transformed into low dimensional distributions.

paragraphs: A generative network transforms input noise into an output distribution. This paper examines what such transformations require from the network, focusing on the relationship between network size, noise dimensionality, and the distributions being produced. Its contributions are explicit constructions and analyses of their efficiency.

First, the authors construct ReLU networks that increase noise dimensionality using a space-filling function built from iterated tent maps. They establish optimality of this construction by studying how many affine pieces multivariate ReLU networks can produce. This connects the complexity of the distributional transformation to the piecewise-affine structure of the functions computed by the network.

Second, they give efficient transformations between one-dimensional uniform and normal distributions using a number of nodes polynomial in log(1/ε). These constructions use Taylor approximation and a binary-search component for computing inverse functions. Finally, the paper indicates how high-dimensional distributions can be transformed efficiently into lower-dimensional ones. Together, the results clarify several ways network structure can compensate for differences in the form and dimensionality of input noise.
summary.tldr: Explicit network constructions characterize efficient transformations of noise distributions, including an optimal ReLU construction for increasing dimensionality.

title: Size-Noise Tradeoffs in Generative Networks

abstract: Temporal-difference learning (TD), coupled with neural networks, is among the most fundamental building blocks of deep reinforcement learning. However, due to the nonlinearity in value function approximation, such a coupling leads to nonconvexity and even divergence in optimization. As a result, the global convergence of neural TD remains unclear. In this paper, we prove for the first time that neural TD converges at a sublinear rate to the global optimum of the mean-squared projected Bellman error for policy evaluation. In particular, we show how such global convergence is enabled by the overparametrization of neural networks, which also plays a vital role in the empirical success of neural TD. Beyond policy evaluation, we establish the global convergence of neural (soft) Q-learning, which is further connected to that of policy gradient algorithms.

The objective being optimized is therefore specified precisely, rather than being an unrestricted claim about optimal decision-making. The analysis identifies neural-network overparameterization as what enables this convergence result in the setting studied.

The paper also establishes global convergence for neural soft Q-learning and connects that result to policy-gradient algorithms. This extends the theoretical discussion beyond evaluating a fixed policy. The contribution is a convergence analysis explaining how sufficiently rich neural parameterizations can support successful learning, while the abstract's initial warning about nonlinearity remains relevant outside the scope of the established results.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how overparameterization enables global convergence guarantees for neural temporal-difference learning and neural soft Q-learning.

title: Neural Temporal-Difference Learning Converges to Global Optima

abstract: This paper discusses one of the most fundamental issues about point processes that what is the best sampling method for point processes. We propose \textit{thinning} as a downsampling method for accelerating the learning of point processes. We find that the thinning operation preserves the structure of intensity, and is able to estimate parameters with less time and without much loss of accuracy. Theoretical results including intensity, parameter and gradient estimation on a thinned history are presented for point processes with decouplable intensities. A stochastic optimization algorithm based on the thinned gradient is proposed. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of thinning in the tasks of parameter and gradient estimation, as well as stochastic optimization.

paragraphs: Point processes describe events occurring over time, and learning from their histories can be computationally expensive. This paper proposes thinning as a downsampling strategy to accelerate that learning. The objective is to use a reduced event history while retaining enough information to estimate the process effectively.

The authors find that thinning preserves the structure of the intensity, which describes the process’s event rate. They develop theoretical results for estimating intensities, parameters, and gradients from a thinned history. Those results apply to point processes with decouplable intensities, a stated condition on the class of models covered by the theory.

The paper also introduces a stochastic optimization algorithm driven by the thinned gradient. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support thinning for parameter estimation, gradient estimation, and optimization. The reported outcome is reduced estimation time without much accuracy loss. Together, the structural results and experiments explain how downsampling can serve as a computational tool for learning these processes, rather than merely reducing the amount of stored data.
summary.tldr: Thinning accelerates point-process estimation and optimization with little reported accuracy loss, with theory for decouplable intensities.

title: Thinning for Accelerating the Learning of Point Processes

abstract: We investigate a sequential optimization procedure to minimize the empirical risk functional $f_{\hat\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{2}\|G_{\hat\theta}(x) - y\|^2$ for certain families of deep networks $G_{\theta}(x)$. The approach is to optimize a sequence of objective functions that use network parameters obtained during different stages of the training process. When initialized with random parameters $\theta_0$, we show that the objective $f_{\theta_0}(x)$ is ``nice'' and easy to optimize with gradient descent. As learning is carried out, we obtain a sequence of generative networks $x \mapsto G_{\theta_t}(x)$ and associated risk functions $f_{\theta_t}(x)$, where $t$ indicates a stage of stochastic gradient descent during training. Since the parameters of the network do not change by very much in each step, the surface evolves slowly and can be incrementally optimized. The algorithm is formalized and analyzed for a family of expansive networks. We call the procedure {\it surfing} since it rides along the peak of the evolving (negative) empirical risk function, starting from a smooth surface at the beginning of learning and ending with a wavy nonconvex surface after learning is complete. Experiments show how surfing can be used to find the global optimum and for compressed sensing even when direct gradient descent on the final learned network fails.

paragraphs: The paper studies finding an input to a deep network whose output matches a target, measured by squared error. Optimizing this objective on a fully trained network can be difficult because its surface is nonconvex. The proposed surfing procedure instead follows a sequence of objectives defined by network parameters from successive stages of training.

For the network families considered, the authors show that the objective at random initialization is easy to optimize with gradient descent. As training progresses, small parameter changes make the objective surface evolve gradually. Surfing incrementally updates the input solution along this evolution, carrying it from the initial landscape toward the final learned one.

The algorithm is formalized and analyzed for a family of expansive networks. Experiments demonstrate cases where surfing finds the global optimum and succeeds in compressed sensing even when direct gradient descent on the final network fails. These findings support using the training trajectory as an optimization resource, with the theoretical analysis tied to the specified network family.
summary.tldr: Surfing optimizes an input across successive network training stages, succeeding in experiments where direct optimization of the final network fails.

title: Surfing: Iterative Optimization Over Incrementally Trained Deep Networks

abstract: We propose a new family of neural networks to predict the behaviors of physical systems by learning their underpinning constraints. A neural projection operator lies at the heart of our approach, composed of a lightweight network with an embedded recursive architecture that interactively enforces learned underpinning constraints and predicts the various governed behaviors of different physical systems. Our neural projection operator is motivated by the position-based dynamics model that has been used widely in game and visual effects industries to unify the various fast physics simulators. Our method can automatically and effectively uncover a broad range of constraints from observation point data, such as length, angle, bending, collision, boundary effects, and their arbitrary combinations, without any connectivity priors. We provide a multi-group point representation in conjunction with a configurable network connection mechanism to incorporate prior inputs for processing complex physical systems. We demonstrated the efficacy of our approach by learning a set of challenging physical systems all in a unified and simple fashion including: rigid bodies with complex geometries, ropes with varying length and bending, articulated soft and rigid bodies, and multi-object collisions with complex boundaries.

This paper predicts physical behavior by learning those constraints from observed points. Its approach is motivated by position-based dynamics, a framework used in fast simulation, and makes constraint enforcement the central operation of a neural model.

The core component is a lightweight neural projection operator with a recursive architecture. It repeatedly enforces learned constraints as part of predicting the system's behavior. The authors report learning individual constraint types and their combinations without supplied connectivity information, allowing the model to infer relevant structure from observations rather than requiring that structure as an input.

For complex systems, the method also offers a representation using multiple point groups and configurable network connections that can incorporate prior information. Demonstrations cover rigid objects with complex shapes, ropes with different lengths and bending behavior, articulated soft and rigid bodies, and collisions involving multiple objects and boundaries. These results support using a shared constraint-learning approach across varied physical systems.
summary.tldr: A recursive neural projection operator learns physical constraints from point observations and uses them to predict varied physical systems.

title: Learning Physical Constraints with Neural Projections

abstract: A recent technique of randomized smoothing has shown that the worst-case (adversarial) l2-robustness can be transformed into the average-case Gaussian-robustness by "smoothing" a classifier, i.e., by considering the averaged prediction over Gaussian noise. In this paradigm, one should rethink the notion of adversarial robustness in terms of generalization ability of a classifier under noisy observations. We found that the trade-off between accuracy and certified robustness of smoothed classifiers can be greatly controlled by simply regularizing the prediction consistency over noise. This relationship allows us to design a robust training objective without approximating a non-existing smoothed classifier, e.g., via soft smoothing. Our experiments under various deep neural network architectures and datasets show that the "certified" l2-robustness can be dramatically improved with the proposed regularization, even achieving better or comparable results to the state-of-the-art approaches with significantly less training costs and hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing builds a classifier by averaging predictions over Gaussian noise. This connects average behavior under noisy inputs to a guarantee against worst-case adversarial changes measured in l2 distance. The paper examines how to train the underlying classifier so that this smoothing procedure produces stronger certified robustness.

The proposed approach regularizes prediction consistency across noise realizations. In plain terms, training encourages the classifier to respond similarly when different Gaussian disturbances are applied to an input. The authors find that this consistency strongly influences the trade-off between ordinary accuracy and certified robustness. They use the relationship to construct a robust training objective without relying on a soft approximation of the smoothed classifier.

Experiments across multiple network architectures and datasets show substantial improvements in certified l2 robustness. The method achieves results better than or comparable to the evaluated state-of-the-art approaches while requiring significantly less training cost and fewer hyperparameters. The contribution is a training principle: making predictions agree under noise can improve the robustness guarantees obtained through smoothing.
summary.tldr: Encouraging consistent predictions under Gaussian noise improves the certified robustness of smoothed classifiers with comparatively low training cost.

title: Consistency Regularization for Certified Robustness of Smoothed Classifiers

abstract: The increasing impact of black box models, and particularly of unsupervised ones, comes with an increasing interest in tools to understand and interpret them. In this paper, we consider in particular how to characterise visual groupings discovered automatically by deep neural networks, starting with state-of-the-art clustering methods. In some cases, clusters readily correspond to an existing labelled dataset. However, often they do not, yet they still maintain an "intuitive interpretability''. We introduce two concepts, visual learnability and describability, that can be used to quantify the interpretability of arbitrary image groupings, including unsupervised ones. The idea is to measure (1) how well humans can learn to reproduce a grouping by measuring their ability to generalise from a small set of visual examples (learnability) and (2) whether the set of visual examples can be replaced by a succinct, textual description (describability). By assessing human annotators as classifiers, we remove the subjective quality of existing evaluation metrics. For better scalability, we finally propose a class-level captioning system to generate descriptions for visual groupings automatically and compare it to human annotators using the describability metric.

That creates an evaluation problem: agreement with known categories cannot capture every understandable grouping. This paper introduces two measures intended to assess the interpretability of arbitrary visual groups, including automatically discovered ones.

Visual learnability measures whether people can infer a grouping from a small set of examples and apply it to new images. Describability asks whether a short textual description can replace those examples. Both turn interpretation into a task with observable classification behavior, instead of relying on an annotator's general impression that a cluster seems meaningful.

The authors also propose a captioning system that generates descriptions for entire visual classes to make the approach more scalable. They compare its descriptions with human descriptions using the describability measure. The framework separates two useful questions: whether a visual distinction can be learned from examples, and whether that distinction can be communicated concisely through language.
summary.tldr: The paper measures visual-group interpretability through people's ability to learn groupings from examples or recognize them from concise descriptions.

title: Quantifying Learnability and Describability of Visual Concepts Emerging in Representation Learning

abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of interest in representation learning in hyperbolic spaces, driven by their ability to represent hierarchical data with significantly fewer dimensions than standard Euclidean spaces. However, the viability and benefits of hyperbolic spaces for downstream machine learning tasks have received less attention. In this paper, we present, to our knowledge, the first theoretical guarantees for learning a classifier in hyperbolic rather than Euclidean space. Specifically, we consider the problem of learning a large-margin classifier for data possessing a hierarchical structure. Our first contribution is a hyperbolic perceptron algorithm, which provably converges to a separating hyperplane. We then provide an algorithm to efficiently learn a large-margin hyperplane, relying on the careful injection of adversarial examples. Finally, we prove that for hierarchical data that embeds well into hyperbolic space, the low embedding dimension ensures superior guarantees when learning the classifier directly in hyperbolic space.

This paper asks whether that representational advantage also benefits classification performed directly in hyperbolic space. It develops theoretical guarantees for learning large-margin classifiers on data with hierarchical structure, extending attention from the embedding itself to the downstream learning task.

The first contribution is a hyperbolic perceptron algorithm with a proof of convergence to a separating hyperplane. The authors then introduce an efficient algorithm for learning a large-margin hyperplane. Its construction carefully injects adversarial examples into learning, using them as part of the procedure for obtaining the desired classifier.

The final theoretical result links classification guarantees to embedding dimension. For hierarchical data that embeds well in hyperbolic space, the lower dimension yields superior guarantees when classification is learned directly there. That condition is central to the result: the advantage is tied to data whose hierarchy has a suitable hyperbolic representation. The paper thus supplies a theoretical connection between compact hierarchical embeddings and subsequent classification.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes hyperbolic classification guarantees, including large-margin learning and advantages for hierarchical data that embeds well in low-dimensional hyperbolic space.

title: Robust large-margin learning in hyperbolic space

abstract: Group fairness is measured via parity of quantitative metrics across different protected demographic groups. In this paper, we investigate the problem of reliably assessing group fairness metrics when labeled examples are few but unlabeled examples are plentiful. We propose a general Bayesian framework that can augment labeled data with unlabeled data to produce more accurate and lower-variance estimates compared to methods based on labeled data alone. Our approach estimates calibrated scores (for unlabeled examples) of each group using a hierarchical latent variable model conditioned on labeled examples. This in turn allows for inference of posterior distributions for an array of group fairness metrics with a notion of uncertainty. We demonstrate that our approach leads to significant and consistent reductions in estimation error across multiple well-known fairness datasets, sensitive attributes, and predictive models. The results clearly show the benefits of using both unlabeled data and Bayesian inference in assessing whether a prediction model is fair or not.

paragraphs: Fairness assessments often compare numerical measures across protected demographic groups. When only a small number of examples have labels, those comparisons can be uncertain. This paper asks how abundant unlabeled examples can help estimate group fairness more reliably, rather than relying exclusively on the limited labeled sample.

The proposed Bayesian framework uses a hierarchical latent-variable model conditioned on labeled examples to estimate calibrated scores for unlabeled examples within each group. These scores support inference about several fairness metrics. Instead of returning only a single estimate, the framework produces posterior distributions that express uncertainty about the values of those metrics.

Across multiple fairness datasets, sensitive attributes, and predictive models, the authors report significant, consistent reductions in estimation error. They also describe estimates as more accurate and less variable than methods using labeled data alone. The contribution concerns the reliability of fairness measurement: combining the two kinds of data can provide stronger evidence about a model's group-level behavior while retaining an explicit representation of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework combines scarce labeled examples with abundant unlabeled data to estimate group fairness more accurately and quantify uncertainty.

title: Can I Trust My Fairness Metric? Assessing Fairness with Unlabeled Data and Bayesian Inference

abstract: Estimating the per-state expected cumulative rewards is a critical aspect of reinforcement learning approaches, however the experience is obtained, but standard deep neural-network function-approximation methods are often inefficient in this setting. An alternative approach, exemplified by value iteration networks, is to learn transition and reward models of a latent Markov decision process whose value predictions fit the data. This approach has been shown empirically to converge faster to a more robust solution in many cases, but there has been little theoretical study of this phenomenon. In this paper, we explore such implicit representations of value functions via theory and focused experimentation. We prove that, for a linear parametrization, gradient descent converges to global optima despite non-linearity and non-convexity introduced by the implicit representation. Furthermore, we derive convergence rates for both cases which allow us to identify conditions under which stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with this implicit representation converges substantially faster than its explicit counterpart. Finally, we provide empirical results in some simple domains that illustrate the theoretical findings.
originalAbstract: Estimating the per-state expected cumulative rewards is a critical aspect of reinforcement learning approaches, however the experience is obtained, but standard deep neural-network function-approximation methods are often inefficient in this setting. An alternative approach, exemplified by value iteration networks, is to learn transition and reward models of a latent Markov decision process whose value predictions fit the data. This approach has been shown empirically to converge faster to a more robust solution in many cases, but there has been little theoretical study of this phenomenon. In this paper, we explore such implicit representations of value functions via theory and focused experimentation. We prove that, for a linear parametrization, gradient descent converges to global optima despite non-linearity and non-convexity introduced by the implicit representation. Furthermore, we derive convergence rates for both cases which allow us to identify conditions under which stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with this implicit representation converges substantially faster than its explicit counterpart. Finally, we provide empirical results in some simple domains that illustrate the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often requires estimating the expected cumulative reward from each state. One approach predicts those values directly with a neural network. Another learns transition and reward models for a latent Markov decision process, then uses the values implied by that process to fit the data. This paper investigates why the second representation can learn faster.

The authors study this implicit representation through theory and focused experiments. For a linear parameterization, they prove that gradient descent reaches global optima despite the nonlinearity and nonconvexity introduced by representing values indirectly. This establishes a convergence result within a specific parameterization rather than for arbitrary deep networks.

They also derive convergence rates for implicit and explicit representations. Comparing those rates identifies conditions under which stochastic gradient descent is substantially faster with the implicit approach. Experiments in simple domains illustrate the theoretical findings. The contribution explains how the choice of value-function representation can affect optimization, even when both approaches ultimately aim to predict cumulative rewards.
summary.tldr: For a linear parameterization, implicit model-based value representations admit global convergence and can accelerate stochastic gradient descent under identified conditions.

title: Understanding End-to-End Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Methods as Implicit Parameterization

abstract: Policy gradient (PG) gives rise to a rich class of reinforcement learning (RL) methods. Recently, there has been an emerging trend to augment the existing PG methods such as REINFORCE by the \emph{variance reduction} techniques. However, all existing variance-reduced PG methods heavily rely on an uncheckable importance weight assumption made for every single iteration of the algorithms. In this paper, a simple gradient truncation mechanism is proposed to address this issue. Moreover, we design a Truncated Stochastic Incremental Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient (TSIVR-PG) method, which is able to maximize not only a cumulative sum of rewards but also a general utility function over a policy's long-term visiting distribution. We show an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity for TSIVR-PG to find an $\epsilon$-stationary policy. By assuming the \emph{overparameterization} of policy and exploiting the \emph{hidden convexity} of the problem, we further show that TSIVR-PG converges to global $\epsilon$-optimal policy with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ samples.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient algorithms improve reinforcement-learning policies using estimated gradients. Variance reduction can make these estimates more useful, but the paper identifies a theoretical obstacle: existing variance-reduced methods rely on an importance-weight assumption that must hold at every iteration and cannot be checked. The authors introduce a simple gradient-truncation mechanism to address this issue.

Their algorithm, TSIVR-PG, supports both cumulative reward maximization and more general utilities defined over a policy’s long-term visiting distribution. The latter describes where the policy spends its time. This broadens the optimization target beyond a sum of rewards while retaining a variance-reduced policy-gradient approach.

The stronger global result therefore depends on extra structure beyond the stationarity guarantee.
summary.tldr: TSIVR-PG uses gradient truncation to address an uncheckable importance-weight assumption and establishes stationary-point and conditional global-optimality sample bounds.

title: On the Convergence and Sample Efficiency of Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient Method

abstract: We propose a new framework for Imitation Learning (IL) via density estimation of the expert's occupancy measure followed by Maximum Occupancy Entropy Reinforcement Learning (RL) using the density as a reward. Our approach maximizes a non-adversarial model-free RL objective that provably lower bounds reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence between occupancy measures of the expert and imitator. We present a practical IL algorithm, Neural Density Imitation (NDI), which obtains state-of-the-art demonstration efficiency on benchmark control tasks.

paragraphs: Imitation learning uses expert demonstrations to guide an agent's behavior. This paper organizes that problem around the expert's occupancy measure, a distribution describing where the expert spends its experience. The proposed framework first estimates the density of that distribution, giving the learning process an explicit model of the expert's pattern of occupancy.

The estimated density then serves as a reward for Maximum Occupancy Entropy Reinforcement Learning. This creates a two-stage route from demonstrations to an imitation policy: learn the expert density, then use it within a model-free reinforcement learning objective. The objective is non-adversarial. The authors also prove a lower-bound relationship between it and reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence between expert and imitator occupancy measures.

The practical algorithm implementing this framework is Neural Density Imitation, or NDI. It achieves state-of-the-art demonstration efficiency on the evaluated benchmark control tasks. The result supports density estimation as a useful foundation for imitation, with the empirical contribution centered on learning effectively from demonstrations and the theoretical contribution connecting the objective to occupancy-distribution comparison.
summary.tldr: Neural Density Imitation learns an expert occupancy density and uses it as a reward, achieving leading demonstration efficiency on benchmark control tasks.

title: Imitation with Neural Density Models

abstract: Bayesian model averaging, obtained as the expectation of a likelihood function by a posterior distribution, has been widely used for prediction, evaluation of uncertainty, and model selection. Various approaches have been developed to efficiently capture the information in the posterior distribution; one such approach is the optimization of a set of models simultaneously with interaction to ensure the diversity of the individual models in the same way as ensemble learning. A representative approach is particle variational inference (PVI), which uses an ensemble of models as an empirical approximation for the posterior distribution. PVI iteratively updates each model with a repulsion force to ensure the diversity of the optimized models. However, despite its promising performance, a theoretical understanding of this repulsion and its association with the generalization ability remains unclear. In this paper, we tackle this problem in light of PAC-Bayesian analysis. First, we provide a new second-order Jensen inequality, which has the repulsion term based on the loss function. Thanks to the repulsion term, it is tighter than the standard Jensen inequality. Then, we derive a novel generalization error bound and show that it can be reduced by enhancing the diversity of models. Finally, we derive a new PVI that optimizes the generalization error bound directly. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the performance of the proposed PVI compares favorably with existing methods in the experiment.

paragraphs: Particle variational inference represents a Bayesian posterior using an ensemble of models. Its updates include repulsion between models to preserve diversity, but the connection between that repulsion and generalization has been unclear. This paper studies the connection through PAC-Bayesian analysis, seeking a theoretical explanation for why maintaining different models can help.

The authors derive a second-order version of Jensen’s inequality with a repulsion term defined through the loss function. This term makes the inequality tighter than the standard version. They then use it to obtain a generalization-error bound that can be reduced by increasing model diversity, giving repulsion a direct role in the theoretical objective.

The contribution joins a mathematical refinement with an inference procedure: diversity becomes something connected explicitly to the bound being optimized, rather than only a feature of the update dynamics.
summary.tldr: A tighter Jensen inequality links model repulsion to a generalization bound and yields a new particle variational inference method.

title: Loss function based second-order Jensen inequality and its application to particle variational inference

abstract: Recent improvements in the performance of state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods for Graph Representational Learning (GRL) have come at the cost of significant computational resource requirements for training, e.g., for calculating gradients via backprop over many data epochs. Meanwhile, Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) can find closed-form solutions to convex problems, using merely a handful of epochs. In this paper, we make GRL more computationally tractable for those with modest hardware. We design a framework that computes SVD of *implicitly* defined matrices, and apply this framework to several GRL tasks. For each task, we derive first-order approximation of a SOTA model, where we design (expensive-to-store) matrix $\mathbf{M}$ and train the model, in closed-form, via SVD of $\mathbf{M}$, without calculating entries of $\mathbf{M}$. By converging to a unique point in one step, and without calculating gradients, our models show competitive empirical test performance over various graphs such as article citation and biological interaction networks. More importantly, SVD can initialize a deeper model, that is architected to be non-linear almost everywhere, though behaves linearly when its parameters reside on a hyperplane, onto which SVD initializes. The deeper model can then be fine-tuned within only a few epochs. Overall, our algorithm trains hundreds of times faster than state-of-the-art methods, while competing on test empirical performance. We open-source our implementation at: https://github.com/samihaija/isvd

paragraphs: Learning graph representations can require many rounds of gradient computation and substantial hardware resources. This paper develops a cheaper route based on singular value decomposition, or SVD. The key challenge is that the matrices needed for this route would themselves be expensive to store if constructed explicitly.

Their framework performs the decomposition without calculating that matrix's entries. The resulting models have closed-form training solutions, avoiding gradient-based optimization while producing competitive test performance on graphs including citation and biological interaction networks.

The SVD solution can also initialize a deeper network designed to behave linearly on a particular parameter hyperplane and nonlinearly almost everywhere else. After initialization on that hyperplane, the network can be fine-tuned for only a few epochs. Overall, the authors report training hundreds of times faster than state-of-the-art methods while remaining competitive empirically, making computational accessibility a central part of the contribution.
summary.tldr: Implicit SVD trains approximations to graph learning models without materializing large matrices, achieving competitive results with much faster training.

title: Implicit SVD for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: This paper investigates the problem of best arm identification in {\sl contaminated} stochastic multi-arm bandits. In this setting, the rewards obtained from any arm are replaced by samples from an adversarial model with probability $\varepsilon$. A fixed confidence (infinite-horizon) setting is considered, where the goal of the learner is to identify the arm with the largest mean. Owing to the adversarial contamination of the rewards, each arm's mean is only partially identifiable. This paper proposes two algorithms, a gap-based algorithm and one based on the successive elimination, for best arm identification in sub-Gaussian bandits. These algorithms involve mean estimates that achieve the optimal error guarantee on the deviation of the true mean from the estimate asymptotically. Furthermore, these algorithms asymptotically achieve the optimal sample complexity. Specifically, for the gap-based algorithm, the sample complexity is asymptotically optimal up to constant factors, while for the successive elimination-based algorithm, it is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to illustrate the gains of the algorithms compared to the existing baselines.

paragraphs: The paper studies choosing the option with the highest mean reward when observed rewards may be corrupted. Each reward is replaced by a sample from an adversarial model with probability epsilon. The learner works in a fixed-confidence setting, aiming to identify the best option without a predetermined finite sampling horizon.

Contamination introduces a fundamental difficulty: an option's true mean is only partially identifiable from the observations. For sub-Gaussian bandits, the authors propose a gap-based algorithm and a successive-elimination algorithm. Both rely on mean estimators whose deviation from the true mean satisfies an asymptotically optimal error guarantee.

The sampling guarantees distinguish the two approaches. The gap-based algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal sample complexity up to constant factors, while the elimination-based algorithm achieves it up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments illustrate improvements over existing baselines. The contribution combines robust estimation with efficient option selection, while explicitly accounting for the uncertainty about true means that adversarial contamination leaves unresolved.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms identify high-mean bandit arms under adversarial reward contamination with asymptotically near-optimal sampling guarantees.

title: Mean-based Best Arm Identification in Stochastic Bandits under Reward Contamination

abstract: Neural networks are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks -- slight but carefully constructed perturbations of the inputs which can drastically impair the network's performance. Many defense methods have been proposed for improving robustness of deep networks by training them on adversarially perturbed inputs. However, these models often remain vulnerable to new types of attacks not seen during training, and even to slightly stronger versions of previously seen attacks. In this work, we propose a novel approach to adversarial robustness, which builds upon the insights from the domain adaptation field. Our method, called Adversarial Feature Desensitization (AFD), aims at learning features that are invariant towards adversarial perturbations of the inputs. This is achieved through a game where we learn features that are both predictive and robust (insensitive to adversarial attacks), i.e. cannot be used to discriminate between natural and adversarial data. Empirical results on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach against a wide range of attack types and attack strengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/BashivanLab/afd.
