paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning problems involve choosing a multidimensional allocation from a very large set of discrete, unordered possibilities. Security-resource placement and emergency-response allocation are examples in the paper. These problems can also require randomized policies and validity rules that are difficult to express as a compact mathematical formula.

The proposed approach represents a stochastic policy with a state-conditioned normalizing flow. The network produces one sampled action together with its log probability, which an actor-critic method uses for learning. This provides a compact way to represent policy behavior in the large categorical action space described by the authors.

To enforce constraints, the method uses an oracle that checks whether an action is valid and rejects invalid actions. A modified policy gradient enables updates to the underlying policy through this rejection mechanism. Experiments demonstrate scalability relative to prior methods and enforcement of arbitrary state-dependent constraints on the action distribution's support. The availability of a validity oracle is central to how the method handles those constraints.
summary.tldr: A flow-based stochastic policy and oracle-guided action rejection address large discrete action spaces with state-dependent validity constraints.

title: Generative Modelling of Stochastic Actions with Arbitrary Constraints in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We focus on the weakly-supervised audio-visual video parsing task (AVVP), which aims to identify and locate all the events in audio/visual modalities. Previous works only concentrate on video-level overall label denoising across modalities, but overlook the segment-level label noise, where adjacent video segments (i.e., 1-second video clips) may contain different events. However, recognizing events on the segment is challenging because its label could be any combination of events that occur in the video. To address this issue, we consider tackling AVVP from the language perspective, since language could freely describe how various events appear in each segment beyond fixed labels. Specifically, we design language prompts to describe all cases of event appearance for each video. Then, the similarity between language prompts and segments is calculated, where the event of the most similar prompt is regarded as the segment-level label. In addition, to deal with the mislabeled segments, we propose to perform dynamic re-weighting on the unreliable segments to adjust their labels. Experiments show that our simple yet effective approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

paragraphs: Audio-visual video parsing identifies events and locates where they occur in sound and images. With weak supervision, labels describe an entire video even though adjacent one-second segments can contain different events. This paper focuses on the resulting segment-level label noise, which approaches centered on cleaning overall video labels can leave unresolved.

The authors use language to describe possible combinations of events within a segment. For each video, they construct prompts covering the different cases of event appearance and compare these prompts with individual segments. The events associated with the most similar prompt become the segment's provisional label. Language provides a flexible way to express combinations beyond a single fixed event label.

Because this matching can still mislabel segments, the method dynamically reweights unreliable ones to adjust their labels. The reported experiments show a large improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The result supports addressing weak supervision at the temporal scale where events actually change, with language-based matching and subsequent correction working together to produce more useful segment-level supervision.
summary.tldr: Language prompts and dynamic reweighting improve weakly supervised video parsing by assigning and correcting event labels for individual segments.

title: Revisit Weakly-Supervised Audio-Visual Video Parsing from the Language Perspective

abstract: Learning to represent and simulate the dynamics of physical systems is a crucial yet challenging task. Existing equivariant Graph Neural Network (GNN) based methods have encapsulated the symmetry of physics, \emph{e.g.}, translations, rotations, etc, leading to better generalization ability. Nevertheless, their frame-to-frame formulation of the task overlooks the non-Markov property mainly incurred by unobserved dynamics in the environment. In this paper, we reformulate dynamics simulation as a spatio-temporal prediction task, by employing the trajectory in the past period to recover the Non-Markovian interactions. We propose Equivariant Spatio-Temporal Attentive Graph Networks (ESTAG), an equivariant version of spatio-temporal GNNs, to fulfil our purpose. At its core, we design a novel Equivariant Discrete Fourier Transform (EDFT) to extract periodic patterns from the history frames, and then construct an Equivariant Spatial Module (ESM) to accomplish spatial message passing, and an Equivariant Temporal Module (ETM) with the forward attention and equivariant pooling mechanisms to aggregate temporal message. We evaluate our model on three real datasets corresponding to the molecular-, protein- and macro-level. Experimental results verify the effectiveness of ESTAG compared to typical spatio-temporal GNNs and equivariant GNNs.

paragraphs: A single observed frame may not contain enough information to predict a physical system’s next state. Unobserved environmental dynamics can make the observed process non-Markovian, meaning its history matters. This paper reframes physical simulation as prediction from a recent trajectory while retaining geometric symmetries such as translations and rotations.

The proposed ESTAG architecture combines spatial and temporal processing in an equivariant graph network. An Equivariant Discrete Fourier Transform extracts periodic patterns from historical frames. A spatial module passes information between graph elements, while a temporal module uses forward attention and equivariant pooling to combine information across time. These components incorporate history while respecting the model’s symmetry structure.

The authors evaluate ESTAG on three real datasets spanning molecular, protein, and macroscopic systems. Results show its effectiveness compared with typical spatiotemporal GNNs and equivariant GNNs. The findings support combining two sources of useful structure: the geometric rules that physical predictions should respect and the past observations needed to recover interactions that a frame-to-frame model can overlook.
summary.tldr: ESTAG combines symmetry-preserving graph computation with trajectory history to model physical dynamics affected by unobserved interactions.

title: Equivariant Spatio-Temporal Attentive Graph Networks to Simulate Physical Dynamics

abstract: We propose UTSP, an Unsupervised Learning (UL) framework for solving the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP). We train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) using a surrogate loss. The GNN outputs a heat map representing the probability for each edge to be part of the optimal path. We then apply local search to generate our final prediction based on the heat map. Our loss function consists of two parts: one pushes the model to find the shortest path and the other serves as a surrogate for the constraint that the route should form a Hamiltonian Cycle. Experimental results show that UTSP outperforms the existing data-driven TSP heuristics.Our approach is parameter efficient as well as data efficient: the model takes $\sim$ 10\% of the number of parameters and $\sim$ 0.2\% of training samples compared with Reinforcement Learning or Supervised Learning methods.

The GNN outputs a heat map representing the probability for each edge to be part of the optimal path. We then apply local search to generate our final prediction based on the heat map. Our loss function consists of two parts: one pushes the model to find the shortest path and the other serves as a surrogate for the constraint that the route should form a Hamiltonian Cycle. paragraphs: The travelling salesman problem asks for a short route that visits every location and returns to its starting point. UTSP approaches this problem with unsupervised learning, training a graph neural network to identify promising connections. Its output is a heat map representing the probability that each edge belongs to the optimal route.

Training uses a surrogate loss with two components. One encourages shorter routes, while the other approximates the requirement that the route form a Hamiltonian cycle, visiting every node once before returning. The heat map then guides local search to produce the final prediction. This separates learning which edges look promising from the subsequent search that assembles a route.

Experiments show UTSP outperforming existing data-driven TSP heuristics. The authors also report parameter and data efficiency: roughly 10% as many model parameters and 0.2% as many training samples as the compared reinforcement or supervised learning methods. These findings support combining an unsupervised structural objective with local search to obtain competitive routes using a relatively compact learned model.
summary.tldr: UTSP trains an unsupervised graph network to guide local search, outperforming evaluated data-driven TSP heuristics with fewer parameters and training samples.

title: Unsupervised Learning for Solving the Travelling Salesman Problem

abstract: We study causal representation learning, the task of inferring latent causal variables and their causal relations from high-dimensional functions (“mixtures”) of the variables. Prior work relies on weak supervision, in the form of counterfactual pre- and post-intervention views or temporal structure; places restrictive assumptions, such as linearity, on the mixing function or latent causal model; or requires partial knowledge of the generative process, such as the causal graph or intervention targets. We instead consider the general setting in which both the causal model and the mixing function are nonparametric. The learning signal takes the form of multiple datasets, or environments, arising from unknown interventions in the underlying causal model. Our goal is to identify both the ground truth latents and their causal graph up to a set of ambiguities which we show to be irresolvable from interventional data. We study the fundamental setting of two causal variables and prove that the observational distribution and one perfect intervention per node suffice for identifiability, subject to a genericity condition. This condition rules out spurious solutions that involve fine-tuning of the intervened and observational distributions, mirroring similar conditions for nonlinear cause-effect inference. For an arbitrary number of variables, we show that at least one pair of distinct perfect interventional domains per node guarantees identifiability. Further, we demonstrate that the strengths of causal influences among the latent variables are preserved by all equivalent solutions, rendering the inferred representation appropriate for drawing causal conclusions from new data. Our study provides the first identifiability results for the general nonparametric setting with unknown interventions, and elucidates what is possible and impossible for causal representation learning without more direct supervision.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden causal variables and their relationships from observations that mix those variables together. This paper allows both the mixing function and the causal model to be nonparametric. Its learning signal consists of datasets generated under interventions whose targets are unknown.

For two causal variables, the authors prove that observational data and one perfect intervention per variable are sufficient for identifiability under a genericity condition. That condition excludes finely tuned relationships between observational and intervened distributions that could create spurious solutions. For any number of variables, a pair of distinct perfect intervention environments per variable provides a sufficient guarantee.

Recovery is only up to ambiguities that the authors show cannot be resolved from interventional data. Nevertheless, all equivalent solutions preserve the strengths of causal influences, supporting causal conclusions from new observations. The results establish when hidden causal structure can be recovered in this general setting while explicitly accounting for what the available intervention evidence cannot distinguish.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sufficient intervention conditions for identifying nonparametric latent causal models up to unavoidable ambiguities.

title: Nonparametric Identifiability of Causal Representations from Unknown Interventions

abstract: The signaling capacity of a neural population depends on the scale and orientation of its covariance across trials. Estimating this "noise" covariance is challenging and is thought to require a large number of stereotyped trials. New approaches are therefore needed to interrogate the structure of neural noise across rich, naturalistic behaviors and sensory experiences, with few trials per condition. Here, we exploit the fact that conditions are smoothly parameterized in many experiments and leverage Wishart process models to pool statistical power from trials in neighboring conditions. We demonstrate that these models perform favorably on experimental data from the mouse visual cortex and monkey motor cortex relative to standard covariance estimators. Moreover, they produce smooth estimates of covariance as a function of stimulus parameters, enabling estimates of noise correlations in entirely unseen conditions as well as continuous estimates of Fisher information—a commonly used measure of signal fidelity. Together, our results suggest that Wishart processes are broadly applicable tools for quantification and uncertainty estimation of noise correlations in trial-limited regimes, paving the way toward understanding the role of noise in complex neural computations and behavior.

paragraphs: Neural populations vary in their responses even when experimental conditions repeat. The covariance of those fluctuations describes how neurons vary together and influences the population’s ability to carry signals. Estimating it separately for every condition can require many repeated trials, making rich experiments with few repetitions difficult to analyze.

The authors use Wishart process models to share statistical information across nearby conditions. Their approach exploits experiments in which conditions have a smooth parameterization, so neighboring settings can inform one another. Instead of obtaining isolated covariance estimates, the model produces a smoothly varying description of covariance across stimulus parameters.

On recordings from mouse visual cortex and monkey motor cortex, the models compare favorably with standard covariance estimators. They also support predictions of noise correlations at unobserved conditions and continuous estimates of Fisher information, a measure of signal fidelity. These results suggest a useful route to estimating neural variability and its uncertainty when trials are scarce, provided the structure across conditions can be exploited.
summary.tldr: Wishart process models estimate neural noise correlations with few trials by sharing information across smoothly varying experimental conditions.

title: Estimating Noise Correlations Across Continuous Conditions With Wishart Processes

abstract: The Landsat program is the longest-running Earth observation program in history, with 50+ years of data acquisition by 8 satellites. The multispectral imagery captured by sensors onboard these satellites is critical for a wide range of scientific fields. Despite the increasing popularity of deep learning and remote sensing, the majority of researchers still use decision trees and random forests for Landsat image analysis due to the prevalence of small labeled datasets and lack of foundation models. In this paper, we introduce SSL4EO-L, the first ever dataset designed for Self-Supervised Learning for Earth Observation for the Landsat family of satellites (including 3 sensors and 2 product levels) and the largest Landsat dataset in history (5M image patches). Additionally, we modernize and re-release the L7 Irish and L8 Biome cloud detection datasets, and introduce the first ML benchmark datasets for Landsats 4–5 TM and Landsat 7 ETM+ SR. Finally, we pre-train the first foundation models for Landsat imagery using SSL4EO-L and evaluate their performance on multiple semantic segmentation tasks. All datasets and model weights are available via the TorchGeo library, making reproducibility and experimentation easy, and enabling scientific advancements in the burgeoning field of remote sensing for a multitude of downstream applications.

paragraphs: Landsat has accumulated more than fifty years of multispectral Earth imagery, but small labeled datasets and a lack of foundation models have limited deep-learning adoption for its analysis. SSL4EO-L addresses these resource gaps with a dataset designed for self-supervised learning. It contains five million image patches covering three sensors and two product levels in the Landsat family.

The work also updates and re-releases the L7 Irish and L8 Biome cloud-detection datasets. It introduces machine learning benchmarks for Landsats 4–5 TM and Landsat 7 ETM+ SR. These contributions provide both pretraining material and task-specific evaluation resources, supporting the development and assessment of models across additional Landsat imagery.

The contribution is a coordinated set of data, benchmarks, and pretrained models that makes Landsat-focused experimentation more accessible. The abstract reports these evaluations without asserting a particular numerical improvement over previous analysis methods.
summary.tldr: SSL4EO-L provides five million Landsat patches, updated benchmarks, and pretrained foundation models for Earth-observation research.

title: SSL4EO-L: Datasets and Foundation Models for Landsat Imagery

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed learning approach that enables machine learning models to be trained on decentralized data without compromising end devices' personal, potentially sensitive data. However, the distributed nature and uninvestigated data intuitively introduce new security vulnerabilities, including backdoor attacks. In this scenario, an adversary implants backdoor functionality into the global model during training, which can be activated to cause the desired misbehaviors for any input with a specific adversarial pattern. Despite having remarkable success in triggering and distorting model behavior, prior backdoor attacks in FL often hold impractical assumptions, limited imperceptibility, and durability. Specifically, the adversary needs to control a sufficiently large fraction of clients or know the data distribution of other honest clients. In many cases, the trigger inserted is often visually apparent, and the backdoor effect is quickly diluted if the adversary is removed from the training process. To address these limitations, we propose a novel backdoor attack framework in FL, the Irreversible Backdoor Attack (IBA), that jointly learns the optimal and visually stealthy trigger and then gradually implants the backdoor into a global model. This approach allows the adversary to execute a backdoor attack that can evade both human and machine inspections. Additionally, we enhance the efficiency and durability of the proposed attack by selectively poisoning the model's parameters that are least likely updated by the main task's learning process and constraining the poisoned model update to the vicinity of the global model. Finally, we evaluate the proposed attack framework on several benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet, and achieved high success rates while simultaneously bypassing existing backdoor defenses and achieving a more durable backdoor effect compared to other backdoor attacks. Overall, IBA offers a more effective, stealthy, and durable approach to backdoor attacks in FL. The code associated with this paper is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/sail-research/iba).

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks on federated learning introduce hidden behavior into a shared model during distributed training. A particular input pattern later activates that behavior. The paper highlights weaknesses in earlier attacks, including conspicuous triggers, demanding assumptions about attacker access, and effects that fade after the attacker stops participating.

IBA combines learning a visually subtle trigger with gradually introducing the backdoor into the global model. Its design also targets model parameters that the main learning task is less likely to change and keeps malicious updates close to the global model. These mechanisms aim to make the attack harder to notice and less vulnerable to being overwritten by subsequent training.

Evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet report high attack success, evasion of existing defenses, and greater persistence than the compared attacks. These findings identify a security concern involving both detectability and durability. Despite the framework's name, the stated evidence supports a more durable backdoor effect, rather than a universal guarantee that the attack is irreversible.
summary.tldr: IBA produces stealthier, longer-lasting federated-learning backdoors and bypasses existing defenses in the reported benchmark evaluations.

title: IBA: Towards Irreversible Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning

abstract: We introduce a data-driven learning framework that assimilates two powerful ideas: ideal large eddy simulation (LES) from turbulence closure modeling and neural stochastic differential equations (SDE) for stochastic modeling. The ideal LES models the LES flow by treating each full-order trajectory as a random realization of the underlying dynamics, as such, the effect of small-scales is marginalized to obtain the deterministic evolution of the LES state. However, ideal LES is analytically intractable. In our work, we use a latent neural SDE to model the evolution of the stochastic process and an encoder-decoder pair for transforming between the latent space and the desired ideal flow field. This stands in sharp contrast to other types of neural parameterization of closure models where each trajectory is treated as a deterministic realization of the dynamics. We show the effectiveness of our approach (niLES – neural ideal LES) on two challenging chaotic dynamical systems: Kolmogorov flow at a Reynolds number of 20,000 and flow past a cylinder at Reynolds number 500. Compared to competing methods, our method can handle non-uniform geometries using unstructured meshes seamlessly. In particular, niLES leads to trajectories with more accurate statistics and enhances stability, particularly for long-horizon rollouts. (Source codes and datasets will be made publicly available.)

paragraphs: Large eddy simulation models turbulent flow while accounting for the effects of smaller scales. Ideal LES treats each full-resolution trajectory as a random realization of underlying dynamics and marginalizes small-scale effects to obtain deterministic evolution of the LES state. This formulation is analytically intractable, motivating a learned way to approximate its underlying stochastic description.

The proposed niLES framework uses a latent neural stochastic differential equation to model the evolving stochastic process. An encoder and decoder connect that latent representation to the desired ideal flow field. This differs from neural closure approaches that treat every trajectory as a deterministic realization. The distinction matters because the framework explicitly builds the randomness of full-order trajectories into its modeling approach.

The authors evaluate niLES on Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number 20,000 and flow around a cylinder at Reynolds number 500. They report more accurate trajectory statistics and improved stability compared with competing methods, especially over long rollouts. The framework also accommodates non-uniform geometries through unstructured meshes, supporting its use across the tested flow configurations.
summary.tldr: niLES combines ideal large eddy simulation with a latent neural SDE to improve turbulence statistics and long-rollout stability.

title: Neural Ideal Large Eddy Simulation: Modeling Turbulence with Neural Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Finding the proper depth $d$ of a graph convolutional network (GCN) that provides strong representation ability has drawn significant attention, yet nonetheless largely remains an open problem for the graph learning community. Although noteworthy progress has been made, the depth or the number of layers of a corresponding GCN is realized by a series of graph convolution operations, which naturally makes $d$ a positive integer ($d \in \mathbb{N}+$). An interesting question is whether breaking the constraint of $\mathbb{N}+$ by making $d$ a real number ($d \in \mathbb{R}$) can bring new insights into graph learning mechanisms. In this work, by redefining GCN's depth $d$ as a trainable parameter continuously adjustable within $(-\infty,+\infty)$, we open a new door of controlling its signal processing capability to model graph homophily/heterophily (nodes with similar/dissimilar labels/attributes tend to be inter-connected). A simple and powerful GCN model TEDGCN, is proposed to retain the simplicity of GCN and meanwhile automatically search for the optimal $d$ without the prior knowledge regarding whether the input graph is homophilic or heterophilic. Negative-valued $d$ intrinsically enables high-pass frequency filtering functionality via augmented topology for graph heterophily. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of TEDGCN on node classification tasks for a variety of homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks usually express depth as a positive integer because they apply a sequence of graph convolutions. This paper asks what becomes possible when depth is instead a trainable real-valued parameter, including negative values. The goal is to adjust how the model processes graph signals rather than select a conventional layer count.

The proposed TEDGCN model learns this depth parameter without requiring advance knowledge of whether connected nodes tend to be similar or dissimilar. Those two patterns are called homophily and heterophily. Under the paper's formulation, negative depth enables high-pass frequency filtering through an augmented graph topology, providing a way to handle heterophilic relationships.

The significance is that one adjustable parameter governs behavior relevant to both types of graph structure while retaining the simplicity of a graph convolutional model. Experiments report superior node-classification performance across a variety of homophilic and heterophilic graphs. These findings support the usefulness of the continuous-depth formulation for the tested tasks; the learned quantity is a signal-processing control, not a literal negative number of network layers.
summary.tldr: TEDGCN learns a continuous depth parameter, including negative values, to adapt graph filtering to both similar and dissimilar connected nodes.

title: From Trainable Negative Depth to Edge Heterophily in Graphs

abstract: This paper studies the problem of Anytime-Competitive Markov Decision Process (A-CMDP). Existing works on Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) aim to optimize the expected reward while constraining the expected cost over random dynamics, but the cost in a specific episode can still be unsatisfactorily high. In contrast, the goal of A-CMDP is to optimize the expected reward while guaranteeing a bounded cost in each round of any episode against a policy prior. We propose a new algorithm, called Anytime-Competitive Reinforcement Learning (ACRL), which provably guarantees the anytime cost constraints. The regret analysis shows the policy asymptotically matches the optimal reward achievable under the anytime competitive constraints. Experiments on the application of carbon-intelligent computing verify the reward performance and cost constraint guarantee of ACRL.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system can satisfy an average cost limit while still incurring an unacceptable cost during a particular episode. This paper studies a stronger requirement: maintain a cost bound at every round of every episode, measured against a reference policy called a policy prior, while optimizing expected reward.

The authors formalize this requirement as an Anytime-Competitive Markov Decision Process and introduce the ACRL algorithm. Its central guarantee concerns costs throughout an episode, so compliance does not depend solely on averaging over random outcomes. The policy prior supplies the comparison used by the competitive constraint.

The paper proves that ACRL satisfies these anytime constraints. Its regret analysis also shows that the learned policy asymptotically reaches the best reward achievable under those constraints. This comparison is specifically with the constrained optimum, rather than an unrestricted reward maximum. Experiments in carbon-intelligent computing support both the algorithm's reward performance and its cost guarantees, connecting the formal objective to an application where costs matter during operation.
summary.tldr: ACRL learns to maximize reward while provably respecting cost constraints at every round relative to a reference policy.

title: Anytime-Competitive Reinforcement Learning with Policy Prior

abstract: The classical Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) identifies the correlations between two sets of multivariate variables based on their covariance, which has been widely applied in diverse fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and speech analysis. Despite its popularity, CCA can encounter challenges in explaining correlations between two variable sets within high-dimensional data contexts. Thus, this paper studies Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (SCCA) that enhances the interpretability of CCA. We first show that SCCA generalizes three well-known sparse optimization problems, sparse PCA, sparse SVD, and sparse regression, which are all classified as NP-hard problems. This result motivates us to develop strong formulations and efficient algorithms. Our main contributions include (i) the introduction of a combinatorial formulation that captures the essence of SCCA and allows the development of exact and approximation algorithms; (ii) the establishment of the complexity results for two low-rank special cases of SCCA; and (iii) the derivation of an equivalent mixed-integer semidefinite programming model that facilitates a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm with analytical cuts. The effectiveness of our proposed formulations and algorithms is validated through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis studies relationships between two sets of variables using their covariance. In high-dimensional data, those relationships can be difficult to interpret. Sparse canonical correlation analysis seeks more interpretable relationships through sparse solutions. This paper studies the optimization problem underlying that goal and develops formulations and algorithms for solving it.

The authors first show that sparse canonical correlation analysis generalizes sparse principal component analysis, sparse singular value decomposition, and sparse regression, all NP-hard problems. This establishes the computational challenge motivating their work. They introduce a combinatorial formulation that supports both exact and approximation algorithms, and determine complexity results for two special cases involving low-rank structure.

They also derive an equivalent mixed-integer semidefinite programming model and build a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm using analytical cuts. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed formulations and algorithms. The contribution connects the interpretability objective to explicit optimization machinery, while examining both the general problem's difficulty and the structure available in particular cases.
summary.tldr: The paper develops complexity results, optimization formulations, and exact and approximate algorithms for sparse canonical correlation analysis.

title: On Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: Performance on popular ML benchmarks is highly correlated with model scale, suggesting that most benchmarks tend to measure a similar underlying factor of general model capabilities. However, substantial research effort remains devoted to designing new benchmarks, many of which claim to measure novel phenomena. In the spirit of the Bitter Lesson, we leverage spectral analysis to measure an underlying capabilities component, the direction in benchmark-performance-space which explains most variation in model performance. In an extensive analysis of existing safety benchmarks, we find that variance in model performance on many safety benchmarks is largely explained by the capabilities component. In response, we argue that safety research should prioritize metrics which are not highly correlated with scale. Our work provides a lens to analyze both novel safety benchmarks and novel safety methods, which we hope will enable future work to make differential progress on safety.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether safety benchmark improvements distinguish safety progress from broader increases in model capability. Its starting observation is that performance on many machine-learning benchmarks correlates strongly with model scale. If safety scores follow the same underlying pattern, their improvement may be difficult to interpret as a distinct safety advance.

The authors use spectral analysis to extract a capabilities component from benchmark results. This component is the direction across benchmark scores that explains the greatest variation in model performance. They then examine existing safety benchmarks and find that this shared component explains much of the performance variation on many of them.

Based on that analysis, the authors argue for prioritizing safety metrics that are not highly correlated with scale. Their method provides a way to scrutinize both new benchmarks and proposed safety methods for progress distinguishable from general capability gains. The finding concerns many evaluated benchmarks; it does not establish that every safety measure is merely a capability test.
summary.tldr: Spectral analysis finds that general capabilities explain much of the variation on many safety benchmarks, complicating claims of distinct safety progress.

title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?

abstract: 3D human shape reconstruction under severe occlusion due to human-object or human-human interaction is a challenging problem. While implicit function methods capture detailed clothed shapes, they require aligned shape priors and or are weak at inpainting occluded regions given an image input. Parametric models i.e. SMPL, instead offer whole body shapes, however, are often misaligned with images. In this work, we propose a novel pipeline composed of a probabilistic SMPL model and point cloud diffusion for pixel-aligned detailed 3D human reconstruction under occlusion. Multiple hypotheses generated by the probabilistic SMPL method are conditioned via continuous 3D shape representations. Point cloud diffusion refines the distribution of 3D points fitted to both the multi-hypothesis shape condition and pixel-aligned image features, offering detailed clothed shapes and inpainting occluded parts of human bodies. In the experiments using the CAPE, MultiHuman and Hi4D datasets, the proposed method outperforms various SOTA methods based on SMPL, implicit functions, point cloud diffusion, and their combined, under synthetic and real occlusions. Our code is publicly available at https://donghwankim0101.github.io/projects/mhcdiff.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a clothed person in 3D becomes difficult when objects or other people hide much of the body. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing approaches: implicit methods can capture clothing detail but struggle with hidden regions or require aligned shape priors, while parametric body models provide complete shapes that may not align with the image.

The proposed pipeline combines a probabilistic SMPL body model with point-cloud diffusion. The body model generates several plausible shape hypotheses, which become conditioning information through continuous 3D representations. Diffusion then refines the distribution of 3D points using both those hypotheses and image features aligned to pixels, bringing body-shape guidance together with visible image evidence.

This combination produces detailed clothed reconstructions and fills in occluded body regions. Evaluations on CAPE, MultiHuman, and Hi4D report improvements over methods using SMPL, implicit functions, point-cloud diffusion, and combinations of them under synthetic and real occlusion. The approach uses multiple candidate shapes to guide reconstruction where the image alone provides incomplete evidence.
summary.tldr: Multiple probabilistic body-shape hypotheses guide point-cloud diffusion to reconstruct detailed clothed humans from heavily occluded images.

title: Multi-hypotheses Conditioned Point Cloud Diffusion for 3D Human Reconstruction from Occluded Images

abstract: Algorithmic monoculture arises when many decision-makers rely on the same algorithm to evaluate applicants. An emerging body of work investigates possible harms of this kind of homogeneity, but has been limited by the challenge of incorporating market effects in which the preferences and behavior of many applicants and decision-makers jointly interact to determine outcomes.Addressing this challenge, we introduce a tractable theoretical model of algorithmic monoculture in a two-sided matching market with many participants. We use the model to analyze outcomes under monoculture (when decision-makers all evaluate applicants using a common algorithm) and under polyculture (when decision-makers evaluate applicants independently). All else equal, monoculture (1) selects less-preferred applicants when noise is well-behaved, (2) matches more applicants to their top choice, though individual applicants may be worse off depending on their value to decision-makers and risk tolerance, and (3) is more robust to disparities in the number of applications submitted.

paragraphs: Algorithmic monoculture occurs when many decision-makers use the same algorithm to evaluate applicants. The paper studies its consequences in a two-sided matching market, where outcomes depend jointly on applicants' preferences and decision-makers' evaluations. This market perspective matters because changing evaluations can also change who competes for whom and which matches ultimately form.

The authors introduce a tractable theoretical model comparing a shared evaluation algorithm with independent evaluations, called polyculture. Holding other factors equal, monoculture selects applicants who are less preferred by decision-makers when evaluation noise is well-behaved. At the same time, it matches more applicants to their top choice. These results show that decision-maker selection quality and applicant choice satisfaction can move in different directions.

The increase in top-choice matches does not mean every applicant benefits. Individual outcomes depend on applicants' value to decision-makers and their tolerance for risk. The model also finds monoculture more robust to differences in the number of applications submitted. Together, the findings characterize several distinct consequences of shared evaluation, rather than assigning it a single market-wide benefit or harm.
summary.tldr: A matching-market model shows that shared evaluation algorithms can worsen selection quality while increasing top-choice matches and robustness to application-count disparities.

title: Monoculture in Matching Markets

abstract: Generating simulations to train intelligent agents in game-playing and robotics from natural language input, user input, or task documentation remains an open-ended challenge. Existing approaches focus on parts of this challenge, such as generating reward functions or task hyperparameters. Unlike previous work, we introduce FACTORSIM that generates full simulations in code from language input that can be used to train agents. Exploiting the structural modularity specific to coded simulations, we propose to use a factored partially observable Markov decision process representation that allows us to reduce context dependence during each step of the generation. For evaluation, we introduce a generative simulation benchmark that assesses the generated simulation code’s accuracy and effectiveness in facilitating zero-shot transfers in reinforcement learning settings. We show that FACTORSIM outperforms existing methods in generating simulations regarding prompt alignment (i.e., accuracy), zero-shot transfer abilities, and human evaluation. We also demonstrate its effectiveness in generating robotic tasks.

paragraphs: Training agents in games or robotics requires simulations that implement the intended task. Generating these from language is broader than writing a reward function or selecting task settings. FactorSim tackles the full simulation: it produces code from language input that can then be used to train an agent.

The method takes advantage of the modular structure of coded simulations. It uses a factored partially observable Markov decision process representation to reduce how much context each generation step depends on. Breaking the simulation into factors gives the generation process a structure aligned with the components of the environment being constructed.

The authors also introduce a benchmark that evaluates whether generated code matches the prompt and whether the resulting simulations support zero-shot transfer in reinforcement learning. FactorSim outperforms existing methods on prompt alignment, transfer ability, and human evaluation, and is demonstrated on robotic tasks. These findings assess the generated environments both as implementations of instructions and as training resources whose usefulness extends to agent behavior.
summary.tldr: FactorSim generates complete simulation code from language using a factored representation that reduces context dependence during generation.

title: FactorSim: Generative Simulation via Factorized Representation

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in the field of image generation due to their outstanding capabilities. However, these models require substantial computing resources because of the multi-step denoising process during inference. While traditional pruning methods have been employed to optimize these models, the retraining process necessitates large-scale training datasets and extensive computational costs to maintain generalization ability, making it neither convenient nor efficient. Recent studies attempt to utilize the similarity of features across adjacent denoising stages to reduce computational costs through simple and static strategies. However, these strategies cannot fully harness the potential of the similar feature patterns across adjacent timesteps. In this work, we propose a novel pruning method that derives an efficient diffusion model via a more intelligent and differentiable pruner. At the core of our approach is casting the model pruning process into a SubNet search process. Specifically, we first introduce a SuperNet based on standard diffusion via adding some backup connections built upon the similar features. We then construct a plugin pruner network and design optimization losses to identify redundant computation. Finally, our method can identify an optimal SubNet through few-step gradient optimization and a simple post-processing procedure. We conduct extensive experiments on various diffusion models including Stable Diffusion series and DiTs. Our DiP-GO approach achieves 4.4 x speedup for SD-1.5 without any loss of accuracy, significantly outperforming the previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: DiP-GO aims to reduce the cost of image generation with diffusion models, whose repeated denoising stages require substantial computation. Conventional pruning can demand expensive retraining, while simple strategies for reusing similar features across neighboring stages leave potential savings unexplored. The paper turns the choice of computations to retain into an optimization problem.

The method first expands a standard diffusion model into a SuperNet by adding backup connections based on similarities between features. A separate pruner network and specially designed losses then identify redundant computation. A small number of gradient optimization steps, followed by post-processing, selects a smaller SubNet from the available computational paths.

The authors test the approach on several diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion variants and diffusion transformers. For SD-1.5, they report a 4.4-fold speedup without accuracy loss in their evaluation, outperforming prior methods. This result supports learning how to remove redundant work across denoising stages, rather than relying only on fixed rules for exploiting feature similarity.
summary.tldr: DiP-GO learns which diffusion computations to remove, reporting a 4.4-fold SD-1.5 speedup without accuracy loss in its evaluation.

title: DiP-GO: A Diffusion Pruner via Few-step Gradient Optimization

abstract: Multimodal learning has gained increasing importance across various fields, offering the ability to integrate data from diverse sources such as images, text, and personalized records, which are frequently observed in medical domains. However, in scenarios where some modalities are missing, many existing frameworks struggle to accommodate arbitrary modality combinations, often relying heavily on a single modality or complete data. This oversight of potential modality combinations limits their applicability in real-world situations. To address this challenge, we propose Flex-MoE (Flexible Mixture-of-Experts), a new framework designed to flexibly incorporate arbitrary modality combinations while maintaining robustness to missing data. The core idea of Flex-MoE is to first address missing modalities using a new missing modality bank that integrates observed modality combinations with the corresponding missing ones. This is followed by a uniquely designed Sparse MoE framework. Specifically, Flex-MoE first trains experts using samples with all modalities to inject generalized knowledge through the generalized router ($\mathcal{G}$-Router). The $\mathcal{S}$-Router then specializes in handling fewer modality combinations by assigning the top-1 gate to the expert corresponding to the observed modality combination. We evaluate Flex-MoE on the ADNI dataset, which encompasses four modalities in the Alzheimer's Disease domain, as well as on the MIMIC-IV dataset. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of Flex-MoE, highlighting its ability to model arbitrary modality combinations in diverse missing modality scenarios. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/UNITES-Lab/flex-moe}.

paragraphs: Multimodal prediction combines information from sources such as images, text, and personal records. In practice, different examples may contain different subsets of those sources. Flex-MoE addresses this variation with a mixture-of-experts framework designed to handle arbitrary modality combinations, including cases where some inputs are missing.

The framework first uses a missing-modality bank to connect the observed combination with its missing modalities. It then applies a sparse mixture of experts with two routing roles. A generalized router trains experts on complete examples to establish shared knowledge. A specialized router handles reduced modality combinations by assigning the top-ranked gate to the expert associated with the observed combination.

This design makes input availability part of the routing decision, while retaining knowledge learned from complete data. The authors evaluate it on ADNI, with four modalities in the Alzheimer's disease domain, and on MIMIC-IV. Their results demonstrate effectiveness across diverse missing-modality scenarios. The evidence supports combining general expert knowledge with combination-specific routing for prediction when the available sources vary between examples.
summary.tldr: Flex-MoE combines a missing-modality bank with general and specialized expert routing to handle varying combinations of available inputs.

title: Flex-MoE: Modeling Arbitrary Modality Combination via the Flexible Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: It is customary to deploy uniform scalar quantization in the end-to-end optimized Neural image compression methods, instead of more powerful vector quantization, due to the high complexity of the latter. Lattice vector quantization (LVQ), on the other hand, presents a compelling alternative, which can exploit inter-feature dependencies more effectively while keeping computational efficiency almost the same as scalar quantization. However, traditional LVQ structures are designed/optimized for uniform source distributions, hence nonadaptive and suboptimal for real source distributions of latent code space for Neural image compression tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel learning method to overcome this weakness by designing the rate-distortion optimal lattice vector quantization (OLVQ) codebooks with respect to the sample statistics of the latent features to be compressed. By being able to better fit the LVQ structures to any given latent sample distribution, the proposed OLVQ method improves the rate-distortion performances of the existing quantization schemes in neural image compression significantly, while retaining the amenability of uniform scalar quantization.

paragraphs: Neural image compression must convert learned image features into discrete values that can be stored or transmitted. Uniform scalar quantization handles features individually and is commonly used because it is computationally manageable. Vector quantization can exploit relationships between features, but its greater complexity makes it harder to deploy.

Lattice vector quantization offers a structured alternative with computational efficiency close to scalar quantization. Its traditional structures, however, are optimized for uniformly distributed sources and may fit actual neural latent features poorly. The paper proposes learning lattice codebooks from the statistics of the features being compressed, adapting the quantization structure to their observed distribution.

The resulting optimal lattice vector quantization method targets the rate-distortion trade-off: balancing the amount of encoded data against reconstruction error. The authors report significant improvements over existing quantization schemes while retaining the practical manageability associated with uniform scalar quantization. The central contribution is making an efficient, structured quantizer responsive to the latent data it actually encounters, rather than relying on a distributional design that may be mismatched.
summary.tldr: Learning lattice quantization codebooks from latent-feature statistics improves the reported compression trade-off while retaining computational practicality.

title: Learning Optimal Lattice Vector Quantizers for End-to-end Neural Image Compression

abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to execute actions following human instructions. Existing VLN models are optimized through expert demonstrations by supervised behavioural cloning or incorporating manual reward engineering. While straightforward, these efforts overlook the accumulation of errors in the Markov decision process, and struggle to match the distribution of the expert policy. Going beyond this, we propose an Energy-based Navigation Policy (ENP) to model the joint state-action distribution using an energy-based model. At each step, low energy values correspond to the state-action pairs that the expert is most likely to perform, and vice versa. Theoretically, the optimization objective is equivalent to minimizing the forward divergence between the occupancy measure of the expert and ours. Consequently, ENP learns to globally align with the expert policy by maximizing the likelihood of the actions and modeling the dynamics of the navigation states in a collaborative manner. With a variety of VLN architectures, ENP achieves promising performances on R2R, REVERIE, RxR, and R2R-CE, unleashing the power of existing VLN models.

paragraphs: Vision-language navigation requires an agent to follow human instructions through a sequence of actions. Training through behavioral cloning or manually engineered rewards can struggle with accumulating errors and matching the expert's overall behavior. This paper proposes learning the joint distribution of navigation states and actions to address that broader alignment problem.

The Energy-based Navigation Policy assigns lower energy to state-action pairs that an expert is more likely to perform. Its training objective combines action likelihood with modeling how navigation states evolve. The authors show that the objective is equivalent to minimizing forward divergence between the expert's occupancy measure and the model's, connecting training to the distribution of state-action visits.

This gives the method an explicit route toward aligning behavior across navigation, rather than evaluating action imitation in isolation. Applied with several navigation architectures, ENP produces promising results on R2R, REVERIE, RxR, and R2R-CE. The evidence supports the usefulness of this policy formulation across the tested architectures and benchmarks, without establishing that accumulated navigation errors are eliminated.
summary.tldr: ENP models joint state-action behavior with an energy-based policy to better align instruction-following navigation with expert trajectories.

title: Vision-Language Navigation with Energy-Based Policy

abstract: In this paper, we study learning-augmented algorithms for the Bahncard problem. The Bahncard problem is a generalization of the ski-rental problem, where a traveler needs to irrevocably and repeatedly decide between a cheap short-term solution and an expensive long-term one with an unknown future. Even though the problem is canonical, only a primal-dual-based learning-augmented algorithm was explicitly designed for it. We develop a new learning-augmented algorithm, named PFSUM, that incorporates both history and short-term future to improve online decision making. We derive the competitive ratio of PFSUM as a function of the prediction error and conduct extensive experiments to show that PFSUM outperforms the primal-dual-based algorithm.

Even though the problem is canonical, only a primal-dual-based learning-augmented algorithm was explicitly designed for it. We develop a new learning-augmented algorithm, named PFSUM, that incorporates both history and short-term future to improve online decision making. We derive the competitive ratio of PFSUM as a function of the prediction error and conduct extensive experiments to show that PFSUM outperforms the primal-dual-based algorithm.

paragraphs: The Bahncard problem concerns repeated decisions between a cheaper short-term option and a more expensive long-term option when future demand is unknown. Each decision is irreversible, so a choice that looks economical now may turn out poorly as later needs become clear. It generalizes the classic ski-rental problem.

The paper introduces PFSUM, an algorithm that combines historical information with predictions about the near future. This makes it a learning-augmented online algorithm: decisions still arrive over time, but forecasts supplement what has already been observed. The approach gives both past activity and anticipated short-term activity a role in deciding when the long-term option is worthwhile.

The authors derive a competitive ratio that depends on prediction error, explicitly connecting the performance guarantee to forecast quality. Extensive experiments also show PFSUM outperforming the previously developed primal-dual learning-augmented algorithm. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: how the algorithm's guarantee changes with imperfect predictions, and how it compares with the existing approach in the evaluated cases.
summary.tldr: PFSUM combines past observations with short-term forecasts to improve online Bahncard decisions, with guarantees tied to prediction error.

title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms for the Bahncard Problem

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in generating realistic high-quality images, audios, and videos. They benefit significantly from extensive pre-training on large-scale datasets, including web-crawled data with paired data and conditions, such as image-text and image-class pairs.Despite rigorous filtering, these pre-training datasets often inevitably contain corrupted pairs where conditions do not accurately describe the data. This paper presents the first comprehensive study on the impact of such corruption in pre-training data of DMs.We synthetically corrupt ImageNet-1K and CC3M to pre-train and evaluate over $50$ conditional DMs. Our empirical findings reveal that various types of slight corruption in pre-training can significantly enhance the quality, diversity, and fidelity of the generated images across different DMs, both during pre-training and downstream adaptation stages. Theoretically, we consider a Gaussian mixture model and prove that slight corruption in the condition leads to higher entropy and a reduced 2-Wasserstein distance to the ground truth of the data distribution generated by the corruptly trained DMs.Inspired by our analysis, we propose a simple method to improve the training of DMs on practical datasets by adding condition embedding perturbations (CEP).CEP significantly improves the performance of various DMs in both pre-training and downstream tasks.We hope that our study provides new insights into understanding the data and pre-training processes of DMs.

paragraphs: Conditional diffusion models learn from data paired with descriptions or labels, but these pairings can be imperfect. This paper investigates what happens when the conditioning information is slightly wrong. The authors synthetically corrupt ImageNet-1K and CC3M and train and evaluate more than 50 conditional diffusion models to study the effects.

The experiments find that several forms of slight corruption can improve generated-image quality, diversity, and fidelity during pretraining and downstream adaptation. A theoretical analysis under a Gaussian mixture model offers a related explanation: slight condition corruption increases the generated distribution's entropy and reduces its 2-Wasserstein distance from the true data distribution.

Motivated by that analysis, the authors introduce condition embedding perturbations, or CEP, which deliberately perturb the conditioning representation during training. They report improvements across multiple diffusion models in pretraining and downstream tasks. The result gives slight conditioning corruption a potentially useful role in training; both the empirical emphasis on slight corruption and the Gaussian-mixture setting of the proof are central to the claims.
summary.tldr: Slight conditioning corruption improves diffusion models in reported experiments and motivates a practical condition-embedding perturbation method.

title: Slight Corruption in Pre-training Data Makes Better Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce a new class of generative models for music called live music models that produce a continuous stream of music in real-time with synchronized user control. We release Magenta RealTime, an open-weights live music model that can be steered using text or audio prompts to control acoustic style. On automatic metrics of music quality, Magenta RealTime outperforms other open-weights music generation models, despite using fewer parameters and offering first-of-its-kind live generation capabilities. We also release Lyria RealTime, an API-based model with extended controls, offering access to our most powerful model with wide prompt coverage. These models demonstrate a new paradigm for AI-assisted music creation that emphasizes human-in-the-loop interaction for live music performance.

paragraphs: Live Music Models introduces music generators that produce a continuous stream while accepting synchronized user control. The central idea is to make interaction part of the music’s ongoing creation. This places the human participant inside the generation process and makes the models relevant to live musical performance.

The authors release Magenta RealTime with open weights. Users can steer its acoustic style through text or audio prompts. On automatic measures of music quality, it outperforms other open-weights music generation models despite having fewer parameters. The paper also presents its live generation capability as a first of its kind.

A second release, Lyria RealTime, provides API access to the authors’ most powerful model, with broader prompt coverage and additional controls. Together, the models illustrate an approach to AI-assisted music making organized around continuous generation and human direction. The reported quality comparison concerns automatic metrics for Magenta RealTime; the broader creative contribution is the ability to shape a musical stream as it unfolds.
summary.tldr: Magenta RealTime and Lyria RealTime generate continuous music streams that users can steer during live creation.

title: Live Music Models

abstract: Event cameras offer a promising avenue for multi-view stereo depth estimation and Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) due to their ability to detect blur-free 3D edges at high-speed and over broad illumination conditions. However, traditional deep learning frameworks designed for conventional cameras struggle with the asynchronous, stream-like nature of event data, as their architectures are optimized for discrete, image-like inputs. We propose a scalable, flexible and adaptable framework for pixel-wise depth estimation with event cameras in both monocular and stereo setups. The 3D scene structure is encoded into disparity space images (DSIs), representing spatial densities of rays obtained by back-projecting events into space via known camera poses. Our neural network processes local subregions of the DSIs combining 3D convolutions and a recurrent structure to recognize valuable patterns for depth prediction. Local processing enables fast inference with full parallelization and ensures constant ultra-low model complexity and memory costs, regardless of camera resolution. Experiments on standard benchmarks (MVSEC and DSEC datasets) demonstrate unprecedented effectiveness: (i) using purely monocular data, our method achieves comparable results to existing stereo methods; (ii) when applied to stereo data, it strongly outperforms all state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, reducing the mean absolute error by at least 42\%; (iii) our method also allows for increases in depth completeness by more than 3-fold while still yielding a reduction in median absolute error of at least 30\%. Given its remarkable performance and effective processing of event-data, our framework holds strong potential to become a standard approach for using deep learning for event-based depth estimation and SLAM.

paragraphs: Event cameras produce asynchronous streams, which fit poorly into neural architectures designed around conventional image frames. DERD-Net estimates depth from these streams in both monocular and stereo setups. It uses the geometric structure of event observations to create a representation that a neural network can process locally.

Given known camera poses, the method back-projects events into space and records ray densities in disparity space images. A network combines 3D convolutions with recurrence to recognize depth-related patterns in local subregions. This local design supports parallel inference and, according to the paper, keeps model complexity and memory costs constant and very low regardless of camera resolution.

With stereo input, the authors report at least a 42% reduction in mean absolute error relative to state-of-the-art approaches. They also report more than threefold greater depth completeness while reducing median absolute error by at least 30%. These findings support event-ray densities as an effective representation for depth learning under the stated camera-pose requirement.
summary.tldr: DERD-Net learns depth from local event-ray densities using known camera poses, reporting substantial stereo accuracy and depth-completeness gains.

title: DERD-Net: Learning Depth from Event-based Ray Densities

abstract: Learned Image Compression (LIC) models face critical challenges in real-world scenarios due to various environmental degradations, such as fog and rain. Due to the distribution mismatch between degraded inputs and clean training data, well-trained LIC models suffer from reduced compression efficiency, while retraining dedicated models for diverse degradation types is costly and impractical. Our method addresses the above issue by leveraging prompt learning under the information bottleneck principle, enabling compact extraction of shared components between degraded and clean images for improved latent alignment and compression efficiency. In detail, we propose an Information Bottleneck-constrained Latent Representation Unifying (IB-LRU) scheme, in which a Probabilistic Prompt Generator (PPG) is deployed to simultaneously capture the distribution of different degradations. Such a design dynamically guides the latent-representation process at the encoder through a gated modulation process. Moreover, to promote the degradation distribution capture process, the probabilistic prompt learning is guided by the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle. That is,IB constrains the information encoded in the prompt to focus solely on degradation characteristics while avoiding the inclusion of redundant image contextual information. We apply our IB-LRU method to a variety of state-of-the-art LIC backbones, and extensive experiments under various degradation scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of our design. Our code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Learned image compressors trained on clean pictures can lose efficiency when their inputs contain degradations such as fog or rain. Training a separate compressor for every degradation is costly. This paper instead adapts the formation of compressed representations through learned prompts, aiming to align degraded inputs with the useful content represented in clean images.

The proposed IB-LRU scheme includes a probabilistic prompt generator that captures distributions of different degradations. Its prompts dynamically influence the encoder through gated modulation. An information bottleneck constrains prompt learning so that prompts focus on degradation characteristics while avoiding redundant image context. This gives the prompts a specific role: describing the corruption that the representation process should account for.

At the representation level, the method seeks compact information shared by degraded and clean images, connecting compression with restoration. The authors apply it to several leading learned-compression backbones and report effective results across different degradation scenarios. The contribution is a reusable adaptation scheme for handling varied degraded inputs, with experiments supporting its usefulness across the tested compressor architectures.
summary.tldr: Information-constrained prompts help learned image compressors handle degradations by aligning degraded and clean latent representations.

title: Prompt-Guided Alignment with Information Bottleneck Makes Image Compression Also a Restorer

abstract: Neural networks learn effective feature representations, which can be transferred to new tasks without additional training. While larger datasets are known to improve feature transfer, the theoretical conditions for the success of such transfer remain unclear. This work investigates feature transfer in networks trained for classification to identify the conditions that enable effective clustering in unseen classes. We first reveal that higher similarity between training and unseen distributions leads to improved Cohesion and Separability. We then show that feature expressiveness is enhanced when inputs are similar to the training classes, while the features of irrelevant inputs remain indistinguishable. We validate our analysis on synthetic and benchmark datasets, including CAR, CUB, SOP, ISC, and ImageNet. Our analysis highlights the importance of the similarity between training classes and the input distribution for successful feature transfer.

We first reveal that higher similarity between training and unseen distributions leads to improved Cohesion and Separability. We then show that feature expressiveness is enhanced when inputs are similar to the training classes, while the features of irrelevant inputs remain indistinguishable. Our analysis highlights the importance of the similarity between training classes and the input distribution for successful feature transfer.

paragraphs: Features learned for classification often support clustering of previously unseen classes, but the conditions for successful transfer are not fully understood. This paper analyzes that transfer in a two-layer model, focusing on how training and target distributions relate.

The authors show that greater distributional similarity improves cohesion within classes and separation between them. Inputs resembling training classes obtain more expressive features, while irrelevant inputs can remain indistinguishable in the learned representation. Thus, additional data help only through the structure they teach the feature extractor.

Synthetic experiments and benchmarks including CAR, CUB, SOP, ISC, and ImageNet support the analysis. The results offer a concrete explanation for uneven transfer: a strong source classifier need not organize every unfamiliar input usefully. The relevant question is how much the new task shares with the distinctions learned during source training.
summary.tldr: A two-layer analysis connects feature transfer to similarity between training and unseen data.

title: How Classifier Features Transfer to Downstream: An Asymptotic Analysis in a Two-Layer Model

abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative training while preserving the privacy of all participants. However, the heterogeneity in data distribution across multiple training nodes poses significant challenges to the construction of federated models. Prior studies were dedicated to mitigating the effects of data heterogeneity by using global information as a blueprint and restricting the local update of the model for reaching a "hard consensus". But this practice makes it difficult to balance local and global information, and it neglects to negotiate amicably between local and global models to reach mutually agreeable results, called ``soft consensus". In this paper, a multiple-path solving method is proposed to balance global and local features and combine these two feature preference paths to reach a soft consensus. Rather than relying on global information as the sole criterion, a negotiation process is employed to address the same objective by accommodating diverse feature preferences, thereby facilitating the discovery of a more plausible solution through multiple distinct pathways. Considering the overwhelming power of local features during local training, a swapping strategy is applied to weaken them to balance the solution paths. Moreover, to minimize the additional communication cost caused by the introduction of multiple paths, the solution of the task network is converted into data adaptation to reduce the amount of parameter transmission. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method.

However, the heterogeneity in data distribution across multiple training nodes poses significant challenges to the construction of federated models. Prior studies were dedicated to mitigating the effects of data heterogeneity by using global information as a blueprint and restricting the local update of the model for reaching a "hard consensus". But this practice makes it difficult to balance local and global information, and it neglects to negotiate amicably between local and global models to reach mutually agreeable results, called ``soft consensus". In this paper, a multiple-path solving method is proposed to balance global and local features and combine these two feature preference paths to reach a soft consensus. Rather than relying on global information as the sole criterion, a negotiation process is employed to address the same objective by accommodating diverse feature preferences, thereby facilitating the discovery of a more plausible solution through multiple distinct pathways. Considering the overwhelming power of local features during local training, a swapping strategy is applied to weaken them to balance the solution paths. Moreover, to minimize the additional communication cost caused by the introduction of multiple paths, the solution of the task network is converted into data adaptation to reduce the amount of parameter transmission. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine training across participants whose data distributions can differ substantially. Prior approaches often restrict local updates using global information as the standard for agreement. This paper argues that such hard consensus can make it difficult to balance useful local features with information shared across participants.

The proposed method pursues soft consensus through multiple solution paths that accommodate different preferences for local and global features. These paths are combined through a negotiation process directed at the same objective. Because local features can dominate local training, the method uses a swapping strategy to weaken that dominance and better balance the paths.

Multiple paths could increase communication requirements. To reduce parameter transmission, the authors convert the task-network solution into data adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate advantages for the proposed method. Its contribution is a coordinated approach to heterogeneous federated learning: negotiate between local and global feature preferences, counteract local dominance, and address the additional communication introduced by pursuing multiple paths.
summary.tldr: The method balances local and global information through multiple negotiated solution paths while reducing their added communication cost.

title: Soft-consensual Federated Learning for Data Heterogeneity via Multiple Paths

abstract: Does vision-and-language (VL) training change the linguistic representations of language models in meaningful ways? In terms of downstream task performance on text-only tasks, most results in the literature have shown marginal differences. In this work, we start from the hypothesis that the domain in which VL training could have a significant effect is lexical-conceptual knowledge, in particular its taxonomic organization. Through comparing minimal pairs of text-only LMs and their VL-trained counterparts, we first show that the VL models often outperform their text-only counterparts on a text-only question-answering task that requires taxonomic understanding of concepts mentioned in the questions. Using an array of targeted behavioral and representational analyses, we show that the LMs and VLMs do not differ significantly in terms of their taxonomic knowledge itself, but they differ in how they represent questions that contain concepts in a taxonomic relation vs. a non-taxonomic relation. This implies that the taxonomic knowledge itself does not change substantially through additional VL training, but VL training does improve the deployment of this knowledge in the context of a specific task, even when the presentation of the task is purely linguistic.
