paragraphs: This paper asks whether adding vision-and-language training changes a language model's conceptual knowledge. It focuses on taxonomy: how concepts relate through categories and category membership. The authors compare closely matched text-only models and their vision-language counterparts, then test them on text-only questions that require understanding these relationships.

Vision-language models often answer these questions better. To investigate why, the researchers combine targeted behavioral tests with analyses of internal representations. They find no significant difference in the models' taxonomic knowledge itself. Instead, the models differ in how they represent questions containing taxonomically related concepts compared with questions containing concepts without that relationship.

The findings suggest that additional vision-language training improves access to, or use of, existing taxonomic knowledge within this task, without substantially changing the knowledge itself. This distinction matters when interpreting better task scores: improved performance can reflect better deployment of stored knowledge. The observed benefit also appears when the question is entirely linguistic, showing that the effect of multimodal training can carry into a text-only setting.
summary.tldr: Vision-language training often improves taxonomic question answering by helping models use existing knowledge, without substantially changing that knowledge.

title: Vision-and-Language Training Helps Deploy Taxonomic Knowledge but Does Not Fundamentally Alter It

abstract: Visual geo-localization for drones faces critical degradation under weather perturbations, \eg, rain and fog, where existing methods struggle with two inherent limitations: 1) Heavy reliance on limited weather categories that constrain generalization, and 2) Suboptimal disentanglement of entangled scene-weather features through pseudo weather categories. We present WeatherPrompt, a multi-modality learning paradigm that establishes weather-invariant representations through fusing the image embedding with the text context. Our framework introduces two key contributions: First, a Training-free Weather Reasoning mechanism that employs off-the-shelf large multi-modality models to synthesize multi-weather textual descriptions through human-like reasoning. It improves the scalability to unseen or complex weather, and could reflect different weather strength. Second, to better disentangle the scene and weather features, we propose a multi-modality framework with the dynamic gating mechanism driven by the text embedding to adaptively reweight and fuse visual features across modalities. The framework is further optimized by the cross-modal objectives, including image-text contrastive learning and image-text matching, which maps the same scene with different weather conditions closer in the representation space. Extensive experiments validate that, under diverse weather conditions, our method achieves competitive recall rates compared to state-of-the-art drone geo-localization methods. Notably, it improves Recall@1 by 13.37\% under night conditions and by 18.69\% under fog and snow conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jahawn-Wen/WeatherPrompt.

A training-free weather-reasoning component uses existing large multimodal models to generate descriptions covering multiple weather conditions. These descriptions can express complex or previously unseen weather and may reflect its intensity. A text-driven dynamic gate then reweights and combines visual features. Image-text contrastive and matching objectives encourage observations of the same scene under different weather to occupy nearby locations in representation space.

Experiments report competitive retrieval recall across diverse weather conditions. Specifically, the abstract states Recall@1 improvements of 13.37% at night and 18.69% under fog and snow conditions. title: WeatherPrompt: Multi-modality Representation Learning for All-Weather Drone Visual Geo-Localization

abstract: Self-supervised pre-training is essential for 3D point cloud representation learning, as annotating their irregular, topology-free structures is costly and labor-intensive. Masked autoencoders (MAEs) offer a promising framework but rely on explicit positional embeddings, such as patch center coordinates, which leak geometric information and limit data-driven structural learning. In this work, we propose Point-MaDi, a novel Point cloud Masked autoencoding Diffusion framework for pre-training that integrates a dual-diffusion pretext task into an MAE architecture to address this issue. Specifically, we introduce a center diffusion mechanism in the encoder, noising and predicting the coordinates of both visible and masked patch centers without ground-truth positional embeddings. These predicted centers are processed using a transformer with self-attention and cross-attention to capture intra- and inter-patch relationships. In the decoder, we design a conditional patch diffusion process, guided by the encoder's latent features and predicted centers to reconstruct masked patches directly from noise. This dual-diffusion design drives comprehensive global semantic and local geometric representations during pre-training, eliminating external geometric priors. Extensive experiments on ScanObjectNN, ModelNet40, ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and ScanNet demonstrate that Point-MaDi achieves superior performance across downstream tasks, surpassing Point-MAE by 5.51\% on OBJ-BG, 5.17\% on OBJ-ONLY, and 4.34\% on PB-T50-RS for 3D object classification on the ScanObjectNN dataset.

paragraphs: Learning from unlabeled point clouds can reduce dependence on costly three-dimensional annotations. However, masked autoencoders often receive patch-center coordinates as positional information, exposing geometry that the model could otherwise learn to infer. Point-MaDi changes the pretraining task so that recovering spatial structure becomes part of the learning problem.

Self-attention and cross-attention process the predicted centers to capture relationships within and between patches. The decoder then reconstructs masked patches from noise, conditioned on the encoder's features and predicted centers. These two diffusion processes target global semantic structure and local geometry together.

Experiments across ScanObjectNN, ModelNet40, ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and ScanNet report superior downstream performance. For ScanObjectNN classification, the reported gains over Point-MAE are 5.51% on OBJ-BG, 5.17% on OBJ-ONLY, and 4.34% on PB-T50-RS. The results support making center prediction and patch reconstruction complementary pretraining tasks, reducing reliance on externally supplied geometric priors.
summary.tldr: Point-MaDi learns point-cloud structure by jointly denoising patch centers and reconstructing masked patches, improving downstream three-dimensional recognition.

title: Point-MaDi: Masked Autoencoding with Diffusion for Point Cloud Pre-training

abstract: Gaussian sketching, which consists of pre-multiplying the data with a random Gaussian matrix, is a widely used technique in data science and machine learning. Beyond computational benefits, this operation also provides differential privacy guarantees due to its inherent randomness. In this work, we revisit this operation through the lens of \Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP), providing a refined privacy analysis that yields significantly tighter bounds than prior results. We then demonstrate how this improved analysis leads to performance improvement in different linear regression settings, establishing theoretical utility guarantees. Empirically, our methods improve performance across multiple datasets and, in several cases, reduce runtime.

paragraphs: Gaussian sketching transforms data by multiplying it by a random Gaussian matrix. Besides its computational benefits, the randomness can provide differential privacy guarantees. This paper revisits the privacy analysis of that operation, asking how tightly its privacy properties can be characterized using Rényi differential privacy.

The main contribution is a refined analysis that gives significantly tighter privacy bounds than previous results. Those bounds provide a sharper account of the protection supplied by the random transformation. The authors then use the improved analysis in several linear regression settings and establish theoretical guarantees for the resulting utility. This links the privacy calculation to the quality of the statistical task performed on the transformed data.

Experiments across multiple datasets report improved performance, with runtime reductions in several cases. The stated gains therefore extend beyond a tighter mathematical bound: the revised analysis supports better regression methods in the evaluated settings. Runtime improvements are reported for some cases, while performance improvements span multiple datasets.
summary.tldr: A tighter Rényi differential privacy analysis of Gaussian sketching yields improved linear regression utility and, in several cases, lower runtime.

title: The Gaussian Mixing Mechanism: Renyi Differential Privacy via Gaussian Sketches

abstract: Biological function arises through the dynamical interactions of multiple subsystems, including those between brain areas, within gene regulatory networks, and more. A common approach to understanding these systems is to model the dynamics of each subsystem and characterize communication between them. An alternative approach is through the lens of control theory: how the subsystems control one another. This approach involves inferring the directionality, strength, and contextual modulation of control between subsystems. However, methods for understanding subsystem control are typically linear and cannot adequately describe the rich contextual effects enabled by nonlinear complex systems. To bridge this gap, we devise a data-driven nonlinear control-theoretic framework to characterize subsystem interactions via the Jacobian of the dynamics. We address the challenge of learning Jacobians from time-series data by proposing the JacobianODE, a deep learning method that leverages properties of the Jacobian to directly estimate it for arbitrary dynamical systems from data alone. We show that JacobianODE models outperform existing Jacobian estimation methods on challenging systems, including high-dimensional chaos. Applying our approach to a multi-area recurrent neural network (RNN) trained on a working memory selection task, we show that the “sensory” area gains greater control over the “cognitive” area over learning. Furthermore, we leverage the JacobianODE to directly control the trained RNN, enabling precise manipulation of its behavior. Our work lays the foundation for a theoretically grounded and data-driven understanding of interactions among biological subsystems.

The paper approaches this through control theory, emphasizing that influence can change with context. Linear methods cannot adequately capture the contextual effects of nonlinear dynamics, motivating a framework based on the dynamics’ Jacobian.

These demonstrations connect estimation of nonlinear interactions with both interpreting and controlling a learned dynamical system.

title: Characterizing control between interacting subsystems with deep Jacobian estimation

abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) is a promising compute paradigm to improve speed and power efficiency of neural network inference beyond the limits of conventional von Neumann-based architectures. However, AIMC introduces fundamental challenges such as noisy computations and strict constraints on input and output quantization. Because of these constraints and imprecisions, off-the-shelf LLMs are not able to achieve 4-bit-level performance when deployed on AIMC-based hardware. While researchers previously investigated recovering this accuracy gap on small, mostly vision-based models, a generic method applicable to LLMs pre-trained on trillions of tokens does not yet exist. In this work, we introduce a general and scalable method to robustly adapt LLMs for execution on noisy, low-precision analog hardware. Our approach enables state-of-the-art models — including Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct — to retain performance comparable to 4-bit weight, 8-bit activation baselines, despite the presence of analog noise and quantization constraints. Additionally, we show that as a byproduct of our training methodology, analog foundation models can be quantized for inference on low-precision digital hardware. Finally, we show that our models also benefit from test-time compute scaling, showing better scaling behavior than models trained with 4-bit weight and 8-bit static input quantization. Our work bridges the gap between high-capacity LLMs and efficient analog hardware, offering a path toward energy-efficient foundation models. Code is available at [github.com/IBM/analog-foundation-models](https://github.com/IBM/analog-foundation-models).

summary.tldr: A scalable adaptation method helps language models retain performance under the noise and precision constraints of analog computing.

title: Analog Foundation Models

abstract: Achieving generalization in neural approaches across different scales and distributions remains a significant challenge for routing problems. A key obstacle is that neural networks often fail to learn robust principles for identifying universal patterns and deriving optimal solutions from diverse instances. In this paper, we first uncover Purity Law, a fundamental structural principle for optimal solutions of routing problems, defining that edge prevalence grows exponentially with the sparsity of surrounding vertices. Statistically and theoretically validated across diverse instances, Purity Law reveals a consistent bias toward local sparsity in global optima. Building on this insight, we propose Purity Policy Optimization (PUPO), a novel training paradigm that explicitly aligns characteristics of neural solutions with Purity Law during the solution construction process to enhance generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PUPO can be seamlessly integrated with popular neural solvers, significantly enhancing their generalization performance without incurring additional computational overhead during inference.

paragraphs: Neural routing solvers can struggle when applied to problems with different sizes or distributions from their training data. The paper links this difficulty to learning reusable structural principles of good routes. It identifies a pattern called Purity Law: an edge's prevalence in optimal solutions grows exponentially with the sparsity of nearby vertices.

The authors support this relationship with statistical and theoretical analysis across diverse instances. It describes a consistent preference associated with local sparsity within globally optimal routes. They then introduce Purity Policy Optimization, a training method that aligns characteristics of a neural solver's constructed solutions with this structural pattern.

Experiments show that the training approach can be integrated with popular neural routing solvers and substantially improve their generalization. The reported gains require no additional computation during inference. The contribution therefore connects an analyzed property of optimal routes to the training process, giving solvers a structural guide that can remain useful across changes in problem scale and distribution.
summary.tldr: Purity Policy Optimization trains routing solvers to follow a structural pattern in optimal routes, improving generalization without extra inference computation.

title: Purity Law for Neural Routing Problem Solvers with Enhanced Generalizability

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve superior performance through training-time scaling, and test-time scaling further enhances their capabilities by conducting effective reasoning during inference. However, as the scale of reasoning increases, existing test-time scaling methods suffer from accumulated historical information, which not only wastes computational resources but also interferes with effective reasoning. To address this issue, we observe that complex reasoning can be achieved by solving a series of independent and self-contained subquestions. These subquestions are essentially \textit{atomic questions}, exhibiting the memoryless property similar to Markov processes. Based on this observation, we propose Atom of Thoughts (\our), where each state transition consists of decomposing the current question into a dependency-based directed acyclic graph and contracting its subquestions, forming a simplified question that maintains answer equivalence with the original problem. This answer preservation enables the iterative \textit{decomposition-contraction} process to naturally form a meaningful Markov reasoning process. Furthermore, these atomic states can be seamlessly integrated into existing test-time scaling methods, enabling \our to serve as a plug-in enhancement for improving reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more reasoning time can improve its answers, but extended reasoning also accumulates historical information. The paper argues that this growing history can consume computation and interfere with subsequent reasoning. Atom of Thoughts addresses the problem by organizing reasoning around self-contained questions that carry what the next step needs.

Each transition starts by decomposing the current question into a directed acyclic graph of subquestions and their dependencies. The method then contracts those subquestions into a simplified question that preserves the original answer. Repeating this decomposition and contraction produces a sequence of progressively reformulated problems, with answer preservation connecting the successive states.

The Markov analogy concerns how these states carry information: a self-contained current question supports the next transition without requiring the full accumulated history. The contribution is therefore a way to structure inference around compact reasoning states. The abstract also presents those states as compatible with existing test-time scaling methods, allowing Atom of Thoughts to enhance other reasoning procedures as a plug-in.
summary.tldr: Atom of Thoughts repeatedly decomposes and simplifies questions into answer-preserving, self-contained states to organize language-model reasoning.

title: Atom of Thoughts for Markov LLM Test-Time Scaling

abstract: Characterizing interactions between brain areas is a fundamental goal of systems neuroscience. While such analyses are possible when areas are recorded simultaneously, it is rare to observe all combinations of areas of interest within a single animal or recording session. How can we leverage multi-animal datasets to better understand multi-area interactions? Building on recent progress in large-scale, multi-animal models, we introduce NeuroPaint, a masked autoencoding approach for inferring the dynamics of unobserved brain areas. By training across animals with overlapping subsets of recorded areas, NeuroPaint learns to reconstruct activity in missing areas based on shared structure across individuals. We train and evaluate our approach on both synthetic data and two multi-animal, multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Our results demonstrate that models trained across animals with partial observations can successfully in-paint the dynamics of unrecorded areas, enabling multi-area analyses that transcend the limitations of any single experiment.

paragraphs: Understanding interactions among brain areas is difficult when experiments do not record all relevant areas simultaneously. Different animals or recording sessions may provide different pieces of the picture. NeuroPaint investigates whether combining those partial observations can support inference about activity in areas that were not recorded.

The method uses masked autoencoding to reconstruct missing brain-area dynamics. It trains across animals whose recorded areas overlap, learning shared structure across individuals. That overlap is central to the approach: recordings collectively provide relationships that a single experiment may not contain. The resulting model uses available activity to infer the dynamics of unobserved areas.

The authors train and evaluate NeuroPaint on synthetic data and two multi-animal, multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Their results show successful reconstruction of unrecorded area dynamics from models trained on partial observations across animals. These inferred dynamics enable multi-area analyses that extend beyond the coverage of any individual experiment. The contribution is a way to draw on the combined structure of a dataset while preserving the distinction between recorded activity and model-inferred activity.
summary.tldr: NeuroPaint learns from overlapping brain recordings across animals to infer the dynamics of areas missing from individual experiments.

title: Inpainting the Neural Picture: Inferring Unrecorded Brain Area Dynamics from Multi-Animal Datasets

abstract: Long-horizon tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and dynamic re-planning remain challenging for large language models (LLMs). Sequential prompting methods are prone to context drift, loss of goal information, and recurrent failure cycles, while hierarchical prompting methods often weaken cross-level continuity or incur substantial runtime overhead. We introduce ReCAP (Recursive Context-Aware Reasoning and Planning), a hierarchical framework with shared context for reasoning and planning in LLMs. ReCAP combines three key mechanisms: (i) plan-ahead decomposition, in which the model generates a full subtask list, executes the first item, and refines the remainder; (ii) structured re-injection of parent plans, maintaining consistent multi-level context during recursive return; and (iii) memory-efficient execution, bounding the active prompt so costs scale linearly with task depth. Together these mechanisms align high-level goals with low-level actions, reduce redundant prompting, and preserve coherent context updates across recursion. Experiments demonstrate that ReCAP substantially improves subgoal alignment and success rates on various long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, achieving a 32\% gain on synchronous Robotouille and a 29\% improvement on asynchronous Robotouille under the strict pass@1 protocol.
originalAbstract: Long-horizon tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and dynamic re-planning remain challenging for large language models (LLMs). Sequential prompting methods are prone to context drift, loss of goal information, and recurrent failure cycles, while hierarchical prompting methods often weaken cross-level continuity or incur substantial runtime overhead. We introduce ReCAP (Recursive Context-Aware Reasoning and Planning), a hierarchical framework with shared context for reasoning and planning in LLMs. ReCAP combines three key mechanisms: (i) plan-ahead decomposition, in which the model generates a full subtask list, executes the first item, and refines the remainder; (ii) structured re-injection of parent plans, maintaining consistent multi-level context during recursive return; and (iii) memory-efficient execution, bounding the active prompt so costs scale linearly with task depth. Together these mechanisms align high-level goals with low-level actions, reduce redundant prompting, and preserve coherent context updates across recursion. Experiments demonstrate that ReCAP substantially improves subgoal alignment and success rates on various long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, achieving a 32\% gain on synchronous Robotouille and a 29\% improvement on asynchronous Robotouille under the strict pass@1 protocol.

paragraphs: Long tasks require language-model agents to keep their overall goal in view while revising individual steps. Sequential prompting can lose that connection, and hierarchical prompting can weaken continuity between planning levels or add substantial overhead. ReCAP introduces a recursive planning framework that shares context across those levels.

The model first creates a complete list of subtasks, executes the first item, and revises the remaining plan. When execution returns from a deeper level, structured parent-plan information is reintroduced so the local result remains connected to the broader objective. The framework also bounds the active prompt, making costs scale linearly with task depth.

Together, these mechanisms aim to reduce redundant prompting and maintain coherent updates as plans change. Experiments report improved subgoal alignment and success on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks, including gains of 32% on synchronous Robotouille and 29% on asynchronous Robotouille under strict pass@1 evaluation. The findings support explicit management of planning context as a way to improve sustained, multi-step agent behavior.
summary.tldr: ReCAP combines recursive planning, parent-plan context, and bounded prompts to improve long-horizon agent success.

title: ReCAP: Recursive Context-Aware Reasoning and Planning for Large Language Model Agents

abstract: Score-based generative models (SGMs) have emerged as one of the most popular classes of generative models. A substantial body of work now exists on the analysis of SGMs, focusing either on discretization aspects or on their statistical performance. In the latter case, bounds have been derived, under various metrics, between the true data distribution and the distribution induced by the SGM, often demonstrating polynomial convergence rates with respect to the number of training samples. However, these approaches adopt a largely approximation theory viewpoint, which tends to be overly pessimistic and relatively coarse. In particular, they fail to fully explain the empirical success of SGMs or capture the role of the optimization algorithm used in practice to train the score network. To support this observation, we first present simple experiments illustrating the concrete impact of optimization hyperparameters on the generalization ability of the generated distribution. Then, this paper aims to bridge this theoretical gap by providing the first algorithmic- and data-dependent generalization analysis for SGMs. In particular, we establish bounds that explicitly account for the optimization dynamics of the learning algorithm, offering new insights into the generalization behavior of SGMs. Our theoretical findings are supported by empirical results on several datasets.

paragraphs: A generative model should learn a distribution that resembles the underlying data distribution beyond the particular examples used for training. Existing analyses of score-based generative models often bound this discrepancy through approximation theory and the number of training samples. The authors argue that these bounds can be too coarse and pessimistic, especially because they do not adequately represent how the score network is actually optimized.

The paper first presents simple experiments showing that optimization hyperparameters affect how well the generated distribution generalizes. It then develops a theoretical analysis whose bounds depend on both the data and the learning algorithm. In particular, the bounds explicitly incorporate optimization dynamics, connecting generalization to the process that produces the trained network.

Empirical results on several datasets support the theoretical findings. The main significance is a more training-sensitive account of diffusion-model generalization: sample size and approximation capacity alone leave out relevant information. The analysis brings the optimization procedure into the explanation of why a learned generator does or does not match the data distribution.
summary.tldr: New generalization bounds for score-based generative models explicitly incorporate the training algorithm, optimization dynamics, and data.

title: Algorithm- and Data-Dependent Generalization Bounds for Diffusion Models

abstract: Recent work has formalized the reward hypothesis through the lens of expected utility theory, by interpreting reward as utility. Hausner's foundational work showed that dropping the continuity axiom leads to a generalization of expected utility theory where utilities are lexicographically ordered vectors of arbitrary dimension. In this paper, we extend this result by identifying a simple and practical condition under which preferences in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) cannot be represented by scalar rewards, necessitating a 2-dimensional reward function. We provide a full characterization of such reward functions, as well as the general d-dimensional case under a memorylessness assumption on preferences. Furthermore, we show that optimal policies in this setting retain many desirable properties of their scalar-reward counterparts, while in the Constrained MDP (CMDP) setting — another common multiobjective setting — they do not.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly expresses an agent's preferences through a single numerical reward. This paper studies preferences that require a richer representation: vectors whose components have a strict priority order. With lexicographic ordering, a higher-priority component is considered before lower-priority components. The question is when such preferences cannot be captured by a scalar reward.

The work builds on a result from expected utility theory: removing the continuity axiom allows utilities to take the form of lexicographically ordered vectors. It extends this perspective to Markov Decision Processes by identifying a practical condition under which scalar rewards cannot represent the preferences and a two-dimensional reward function is needed. The authors characterize these functions and the general higher-dimensional case under a memorylessness assumption on preferences.

The paper also establishes that optimal policies retain many desirable properties associated with scalar-reward policies. It contrasts this with constrained Markov Decision Processes, where those properties do not carry over in the same way. The contribution is a formal foundation for expressing ordered priorities while preserving useful policy structure.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when ordered priorities require vector rewards and shows that their optimal policies preserve useful scalar-reward properties.

title: Beyond Scalar Rewards: An Axiomatic Framework for Lexicographic MDPs

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong abilities in general language tasks, yet adapting them to specific domains remains a challenge. Current method like Domain Adaptive Pretraining (DAPT) requires costly full-parameter training and suffers from catastrophic forgetting. Meanwhile, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) introduces substantial inference latency due to expensive nearest-neighbor searches and longer context. This paper introduces \textit{Memory Decoder}, a plug-and-play pretrained memory that enables efficient domain adaptation without changing the original model's parameters. Memory Decoder employs a small transformer decoder that learns to imitate the behavior of an external non-parametric retriever. Once trained, Memory Decoder can be seamlessly integrated with any pretrained language model that shares the same tokenizer, requiring no model-specific modifications. Experimental results demonstrate that Memory Decoder enables effective adaptation of various Qwen and Llama models to three distinct specialized domains: biomedicine, finance, and law, reducing perplexity by an average of 6.17 points. Overall, Memory Decoder introduces a novel paradigm centered on a specially pretrained memory component designed for domain-specific adaptation. This memory architecture can be integrated in a plug-and-play manner, consistently enhancing performance across multiple models within the target domain.

The paper reports an average perplexity reduction of 6.17 points, indicating improved prediction of domain text in those evaluations. The contribution is a reusable adaptation component that captures retrieval behavior through pretraining and consistently improves performance across multiple tested models within the target domains.
summary.tldr: Memory Decoder adapts compatible language models through a separate retriever-imitating component, reducing domain perplexity without changing their original parameters.

title: Memory Decoder: A Pretrained, Plug-and-Play Memory for Large Language Models

abstract: Modeling the inherent hierarchical structure of 3D objects and 3D scenes is highly desirable, as it enables a more holistic understanding of environments for autonomous agents. Accomplishing this with implicit representations, such as Neural Radiance Fields, remains an unexplored challenge. Existing methods that explicitly model hierarchical structures often face significant limitations: they either require multiple rendering passes to capture embeddings at different levels of granularity, significantly increasing inference time, or rely on predefined, closed-set discrete hierarchies that generalize poorly to the diverse and nuanced structures encountered by agents in the real world. To address these challenges, we propose OpenHype, a novel approach that represents scene hierarchies using a continuous hyperbolic latent space. By leveraging the properties of hyperbolic geometry, OpenHype naturally encodes multi-scale relationships and enables smooth traversal of hierarchies through geodesic paths in latent space. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on standard benchmarks, demonstrating superior efficiency and adaptability in 3D scene understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding a 3D environment involves relationships at multiple levels of detail, including the hierarchical organization of objects and scenes. Representing those relationships within implicit scene models such as neural radiance fields is challenging. Existing explicit approaches described in the paper either require repeated rendering at different granularities or depend on predefined discrete hierarchies with limited adaptability.

OpenHype represents scene hierarchies in a continuous hyperbolic latent space. The geometry of that space supports encoding relationships across scales. Geodesic paths through the representation allow smooth movement through the hierarchy, making changes in granularity part of the learned space. This offers a way to represent nuanced hierarchical structure without restricting it to a predefined closed set of levels.

The authors report that OpenHype outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks, with better efficiency and adaptability in 3D scene understanding. The approach matters because it brings hierarchical organization into implicit scene representations while addressing the costs and rigidity associated with the alternatives discussed in the paper.
summary.tldr: OpenHype uses a continuous hyperbolic representation to encode and traverse 3D scene hierarchies efficiently.

title: OpenHype: Hyperbolic Embeddings for Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Radiance Fields

abstract: We propose the task of knowledge distillation detection, which aims to determine whether a student model has been distilled from a given teacher, under a practical setting where only the student’s weights and the teacher’s API are available. This problem is motivated by growing concerns about model provenance and unauthorized replication through distillation. To address this task, we introduce a model-agnostic framework that combines data-free input synthesis and statistical score computation for detecting distillation. Our approach is applicable to both classification and generative models. Experiments on diverse architectures for image classification and text-to-image generation show that our method improves detection accuracy over the strongest baselines by 59.6\% on CIFAR-10, 71.2\% on ImageNet, and 20.0\% for text-to-image generation. The code is available at https://github.com/shqii1j/distillation_detection.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the task of detecting whether one model was distilled from a particular teacher. The setting reflects a specific access pattern: the suspected student’s weights are available, but the teacher can only be queried through an API. The motivation is model provenance, including concerns about replication through knowledge distillation.

The proposed framework combines data-free input synthesis with statistical score computation. It generates inputs for the detection process and uses computed scores to assess the possible teacher–student relationship. The framework is model-agnostic and applies to both classification and generation, giving the same broad detection strategy relevance across different kinds of model outputs.

Experiments cover diverse architectures for image classification and text-to-image generation. The authors report detection-accuracy improvements over their strongest baselines of 59.6% on CIFAR-10, 71.2% on ImageNet, and 20.0% for text-to-image generation. These findings provide empirical support for investigating distillation provenance under the stated access constraints, extending the problem beyond classification to generative models as well.
summary.tldr: A data-free statistical framework detects possible teacher–student distillation relationships using student weights and teacher API access.

title: Knowledge Distillation Detection for Open-weights Models

abstract: High-quality supervised finetuning (SFT) data are essential for unlocking pretrained LLMs’ capabilities. Typically, instructions are paired with responses from various sources—by human annotators or other LMs—which are often out of the distribution of the target model to be finetuned. At scale, this mismatch can lead to diminishing returns and even hurt model performance and robustness. We hypothesize that SFT is most effective when the data is aligned with the model’s pretrained distribution, and propose **GRAPE**—a novel SFT framework that tailors supervision to the target model. For each instruction, it **g**athers **r**esponses from various sources and selects the one that **a**ligns most closely to the model’s **pre**trained distribution, as measured by the normalized probability. Standard SFT is then performed on these selected responses. We first evaluate GRAPE in a controlled experiment, sampling multiple responses per question in the UltraInteract dataset from diverse models. We finetune using GRAPE-selected data on LMs from different families, including LLaMA-1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B. GRAPE significantly outperforms strong baselines—including distilling from the strongest model—with absolute gains up to **13.8%** averaged across benchmarks, and outperforms a 3× larger data baseline with improvements up to **17.3%**. GRAPE's benefits generalize to off-the-shelf SFT data. When used to subsample from the post-training data of Tulu3 and Olmo-2, GRAPE surpasses strong baselines trained on 4.5× more data by **6.1%**, and outperforms state-of-the-art selection methods by **3.9%** on average. Notably, with only **1/3 the data** and **half the training epochs**, GRAPE enables LLaMA-1-8B to **exceed Tulu3-SFT performance by 3.5%**. Our findings highlight that aligning supervision with the pretrained distribution provides a simple yet powerful strategy to improve both the **efficiency** and **effectiveness** of SFT.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning commonly uses responses written by people or generated by other models. GRAPE tests the hypothesis that supervision works better when it fits the model being trained.

For each instruction, GRAPE gathers candidate responses from several sources and selects the one with the highest alignment to the target model’s pretrained distribution, measured through normalized probability. It then applies ordinary supervised fine-tuning to the selected responses. The intervention lies in choosing supervision, making the same pool of candidate answers usable in a model-specific way.

Benefits also extend to existing tuning datasets: selected subsets outperform baselines using substantially more data. These results support distributional fit as a useful selection principle for improving both the efficiency and effectiveness of instruction tuning.
summary.tldr: GRAPE improves instruction tuning by selecting responses that fit the target model’s pretrained distribution, often outperforming baselines trained on more data.

title: The Best Instruction-Tuning Data are Those That Fit

abstract: In single-cell perturbation prediction, a central task is to forecast the effects of perturbing a gene unseen in the training data. The efficacy of such predictions depends on two factors: (1) the similarity of the target gene to those covered in the training data, which informs model (epistemic) uncertainty, and (2) the quality of the corresponding training data, which reflects data (aleatoric) uncertainty. Both factors are critical for determining the reliability of a prediction, particularly as gene perturbation is an inherently stochastic biochemical process. In this paper, we propose PRESCRIBE (PREdicting Single-Cell Response wIth Bayesian Estimation), a multivariate deep evidential regression framework designed to measure both sources of uncertainty jointly. Our analysis demonstrates that PRESCRIBE effectively estimates a confidence score for each prediction, which strongly correlates with its empirical accuracy. This capability enables the filtering of untrustworthy results, and in our experiments, it achieves steady accuracy improvements of over 3% compared to comparable baselines.

paragraphs: PRESCRIBE predicts how individual cells respond when a gene is perturbed, focusing on genes whose perturbations were absent from training. Reliability depends on how similar that gene is to those already studied and on the quality of the relevant training measurements. The paper treats these as distinct sources of uncertainty that should inform confidence together.

Its multivariate deep evidential regression framework jointly measures model uncertainty and data uncertainty using Bayesian estimation. Model uncertainty reflects the evidence available for extending predictions to an unfamiliar gene. Data uncertainty reflects the quality and stochasticity of the observations themselves. Accounting for both matters because gene perturbation is an inherently variable biochemical process, so unfamiliarity alone cannot explain unreliable predictions.

The resulting confidence score is strongly correlated with empirical prediction accuracy in the authors' analysis. This makes it useful for filtering out predictions that are less trustworthy. Experiments report steady accuracy gains exceeding 3% relative to comparable baselines. The contribution therefore combines response prediction with an assessment of reliability that can help determine which predicted responses deserve greater confidence.
summary.tldr: PRESCRIBE jointly estimates model and data uncertainty to identify reliable predictions of cellular responses to unseen gene perturbations.

title: PRESCRIBE: Predicting Single-Cell Responses with Bayesian Estimation

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) excel in image generation, but suffer from slow inference and the training-inference discrepancies. Although gradient-based solvers like DPM-Solver accelerate the denoising inference, they lack theoretical foundations in information transmission efficiency. In this work, we introduce an information-theoretic perspective on the inference processes of DMs, revealing that successful denoising fundamentally reduces conditional entropy in reverse transitions. This principle leads to our key insights into the inference processes: (1) data prediction parameterization outperforms its noise counterpart, and (2) optimizing conditional variance offers *a reference-free way* to minimize both transition and reconstruction errors. Based on these insights, we propose an entropy-aware variance optimized method for the generative process of DMs, called *EVODiff*, which systematically reduces uncertainty by optimizing conditional entropy during denoising. Extensive experiments on DMs validate our insights and demonstrate that our method significantly and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) gradient-based solvers. For example, compared to the DPM-Solver++, EVODiff reduces the reconstruction error by up to *45.5\%* (FID improves from 5.10 to 2.78) at 10 function evaluations (NFE) on CIFAR-10, cuts the NFE cost by *25\%* (from 20 to 15 NFE) for high-quality samples on ImageNet-256, and improves text-to-image generation while reducing artifacts. Code is available at https://github.com/ShiguiLi/EVODiff.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through repeated denoising, making inference speed and accumulated error central concerns. EVODiff studies this process through information theory. The paper argues that successful reverse transitions reduce conditional entropy, meaning that each transition should reduce uncertainty about the cleaner result given the current state.

This perspective leads to two stated insights: predicting clean data performs better than predicting noise, and optimizing conditional variance provides a reference-free way to reduce transition and reconstruction errors. EVODiff turns these ideas into a denoising method that optimizes conditional entropy. The aim is to improve the information gained during the generation process while reducing uncertainty.

Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art gradient-based solvers. Against DPM-Solver++, the abstract reports up to 45.5% lower reconstruction error on CIFAR-10 at ten function evaluations, with FID changing from 5.10 to 2.78. On ImageNet-256, high-quality sampling uses fifteen rather than twenty evaluations. Text-to-image results also show improvements and fewer artifacts, supporting the method across multiple image-generation settings.
summary.tldr: EVODiff improves diffusion inference by using conditional entropy and variance to guide more accurate, efficient denoising.

title: EVODiff: Entropy-aware Variance Optimized Diffusion Inference

abstract: Modern precipitation forecasting systems, including reanalysis datasets, numerical models, and AI-based approaches, typically produce coarse-resolution gridded outputs. The process of converting these outputs to station-level predictions often introduces substantial spatial biases relative to station-level observations, especially in complex terrains or under extreme conditions. These biases stem from two core challenges: (i) $\textbf{station-level heterogeneity}$, with site-specific temporal and spatial dynamics; and (ii) $\textbf{oversmoothing}$, which blurs fine-scale variability in graph-based models. To address these issues, we propose $\textbf{DiffLiG}$ ($\underline{Diff}$usion-enhanced $\underline{Li}$quid $\underline{G}$raph with Attention Propagation), a graph neural network designed for precise spatial correction from gridded forecasts to station observations. DiffLiG integrates a GeoLiquidNet that adapts temporal encoding via site-aware OU dynamics, a graph neural network with a dynamic edge modulator that learns spatially adaptive connectivity, and a Probabilistic Diffusion Selector that generates and refines ensemble forecasts to mitigate oversmoothing. Experiments across multiple datasets show that DiffLiG consistently outperforms other methods, delivering more accurate and robust corrections across diverse geographic and climatic settings. Moreover, it achieves notable gains on other key meteorological variables, underscoring its generalizability and practical utility.

paragraphs: Precipitation forecasts commonly describe broad grid cells, while weather stations measure conditions at particular locations. Converting between these scales can introduce spatial biases, especially in difficult terrain or extreme conditions. This paper targets two contributing problems: stations have distinct patterns over space and time, and graph models can smooth away the local variability needed for accurate correction.

DiffLiG combines three components to address these problems. GeoLiquidNet adapts its representation of temporal behavior to each site using site-aware OU dynamics. A graph network learns spatially adaptive connections through a dynamic edge modulator. A probabilistic diffusion selector then generates and refines forecast ensembles, helping counter the loss of fine-scale variation caused by oversmoothing.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report more accurate and robust corrections than competing methods in diverse geographic and climatic settings. They also report improvements for other meteorological variables. Together, these findings support a correction strategy that adapts both temporal behavior and spatial relationships to individual stations while using ensemble refinement to preserve variability.
summary.tldr: DiffLiG improves grid-to-station weather correction by combining site-specific temporal modeling, adaptive graph connections, and diffusion-based ensemble refinement.

title: DiffLiG: Diffusion-enhanced Liquid Graph with Attention Propagation for Grid-to-Station Precipitation Correction

abstract: Matrix approximation is a common tool in recommendation systems, text mining, and computer vision. A prevalent assumption in constructing matrix approximations is that the partially observed matrix is of low-rank. We propose a new matrix approximation model where we assume instead that the matrix is locally of low-rank, leading to a representation of the observed matrix as a weighted sum of low-rank matrices. We analyze the accuracy of the proposed local low-rank modeling. Our experiments show improvements in prediction accuracy over classical approaches for recommendation tasks.

paragraphs: Matrix approximation uses observed entries to build a compact account of a larger matrix. It appears in recommendation, text mining, and computer vision. A common modeling assumption is that the partially observed matrix has low rank, meaning that its overall structure can be represented through a limited number of underlying components.

This paper replaces the global assumption with a local one: the matrix is assumed to have low-rank structure locally. The resulting model represents the observed matrix as a weighted sum of low-rank matrices. This allows several component approximations to contribute to the overall representation, rather than requiring one low-rank approximation to describe the entire matrix.

The authors analyze the accuracy of this local modeling approach and evaluate it on recommendation tasks. Their experiments show improved prediction accuracy over classical approaches. The findings support the usefulness of the local low-rank assumption in those tasks, where combining simpler component models provides a more effective approximation of the observed data.
summary.tldr: Modeling a matrix as a weighted combination of locally low-rank components improves recommendation prediction accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Local Low-Rank Matrix Approximation

abstract: We propose an algorithmic framework for convex minimization problems of composite functions with two terms: a self-concordant part and a possibly nonsmooth regularization part. Our method is a new proximal Newton algorithm with local quadratic convergence rate. As a specific problem instance, we consider sparse precision matrix estimation problems in graph learning. Via a careful dual formulation and a novel analytic step-size selection, we instantiate an algorithm within our framework for graph learning that avoids Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions, making it attractive for parallel and distributed implementations.

Via a careful dual formulation and a novel analytic step-size selection, we instantiate an algorithm within our framework for graph learning that avoids Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions, making it attractive for parallel and distributed implementations.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex optimization objectives that combine two components: a self-concordant term and a regularization term that may be nonsmooth. These components create a need for an algorithm that can use the structure of the first term while accommodating the possible lack of smoothness in the second.

The authors propose a proximal Newton framework for this setting. Their method has local quadratic convergence, meaning that sufficiently near a solution, the error can shrink at a rate governed by its square. The word local matters: the stated convergence rate describes behavior near the solution rather than promising that speed from every starting point.

The paper then applies the framework to estimating sparse precision matrices for graph learning. A carefully constructed dual formulation and an analytic choice of step size produce an algorithm that avoids both Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions. Removing these operations makes the method attractive for parallel and distributed implementation, connecting the general optimization result to a concrete computational concern in graph learning.
summary.tldr: A proximal Newton framework offers local quadratic convergence and a graph-learning implementation that avoids Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions.

title: A proximal Newton framework for composite minimization: Graph learning without Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions

abstract: We develop an efficient algorithm to learn a Mahalanobis distance metric by directly optimizing a ranking loss. Our approach focuses on optimizing the top of the induced rankings, which is desirable in tasks such as visualization and nearest-neighbor retrieval. We further develop and justify a simple technique to reduce training time significantly with minimal impact on performance. Our proposed method significantly outperforms alternative methods on several real-world tasks, and can scale to large and high-dimensional data.

Our proposed method significantly outperforms alternative methods on several real-world tasks, and can scale to large and high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: This paper learns a distance function with the quality of the resulting rankings as its direct objective. A Mahalanobis metric determines how differences between data points contribute to their distance, allowing the learned notion of closeness to reflect the task. Changing that metric changes which examples appear nearest to a query or another point.

The algorithm concentrates on the top of those rankings. This emphasis matters in nearest-neighbor retrieval, where the first returned items are especially consequential, and in visualization, where nearby relationships help determine what users see. By optimizing a ranking loss directly, the method connects distance learning to the ordering it is intended to produce.

The authors also develop and justify a simple training acceleration technique. They report a substantial reduction in training time with little effect on performance, alongside significant improvements over alternative methods on several real-world tasks. The approach is described as scaling to large, high-dimensional datasets. Together, these findings make both ranking quality and the cost of learning the metric central contributions.
summary.tldr: The paper efficiently learns Mahalanobis distances by directly optimizing ranking quality, with particular emphasis on the highest-ranked results.

title: Efficient Learning of Mahalanobis Metrics for Ranking

abstract: Common statistical practice has shown that the full power of Bayesian methods is not realized until hierarchical priors are used, as these allow for greater “robustness” and the ability to “share statistical strength.” Yet it is an ongoing challenge to provide a learning-theoretically sound formalism of such notions that: offers practical guidance concerning when and how best to utilize hierarchical models; provides insights into what makes for a good hierarchical prior; and, when the form of the prior has been chosen, can guide the choice of hyperparameter settings. We present a set of analytical tools for understanding hierarchical priors in both the online and batch learning settings. We provide regret bounds under log-loss, which show how certain hierarchical models compare, in retrospect, to the best single model in the model class. We also show how to convert a Bayesian log-loss regret bound into a Bayesian risk bound for any bounded loss, a result which may be of independent interest. Risk and regret bounds for Student’s t and hierarchical Gaussian priors allow us to formalize the concepts of “robustness” and “sharing statistical strength.” Priors for feature selection are investigated as well. Our results suggest that the learning-theoretic benefits of using hierarchical priors can often come at little cost on practical problems.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Bayesian priors are valued for robustness and for allowing related learning problems to share statistical information. This paper seeks a learning-theoretic account of those benefits. Its analytical tools address both sequential online learning and batch learning, with the aim of informing prior design and hyperparameter choices.

The authors derive log-loss regret bounds that compare certain hierarchical learners with the best single model selected in hindsight from the model class. They also show how a Bayesian log-loss regret bound can be converted into a Bayesian risk bound for any bounded loss. This connects sequential predictive comparisons with guarantees expressed through other loss functions.

Its results suggest that hierarchical priors can often provide learning-theoretic advantages at little practical cost. That conclusion is qualified: the contribution supplies analytical support for particular prior families, rather than a blanket guarantee that every hierarchy improves every learning problem.
summary.tldr: Risk and regret bounds explain how particular hierarchical Bayesian priors can provide robustness and share statistical strength.

title: Risk and Regret of Hierarchical Bayesian Learners

abstract: A widely applied approach to causal inference from a time series X, often referred to as “(linear) Granger causal analysis”, is to simply regress present on past and interpret the regression matrix \hatB causally. However, if there is an unmeasured time series Z that influences X, then this approach can lead to wrong causal conclusions, i.e., distinct from those one would draw if one had additional information such as Z. In this paper we take a different approach: We assume that X together with some hidden Z forms a first order vector autoregressive (VAR) process with transition matrix A, and argue why it is more valid to interpret A causally instead of \hatB. Then we examine under which conditions the most important parts of A are identifiable or almost identifiable from only X. Essentially, sufficient conditions are (1) non-Gaussian, independent noise or (2) no influence from X to Z. We present two estimation algorithms that are tailored towards conditions (1) and (2), respectively, and evaluate them on synthetic and real-world data. We discuss how to check the model using X.

In this paper we take a different approach: We assume that X together with some hidden Z forms a first order vector autoregressive (VAR) process with transition matrix A, and argue why it is more valid to interpret A causally instead of \hatB. paragraphs: Regressing a time series' present values on its past is a common route to Granger causal analysis. However, an unmeasured series that influences the observed one can change the causal conclusions drawn from this regression. This paper explicitly models that hidden influence instead of interpreting the observed regression matrix directly.

The authors assume that the observed series X and a hidden series Z jointly follow a first-order vector autoregressive process. They argue that this joint process's transition matrix is a more appropriate object for causal interpretation. The main question becomes which important parts of that matrix can be identified, or almost identified, using observations of X alone.

The paper gives sufficient conditions based on either independent non-Gaussian noise or an absence of influence from X to Z. These are alternative routes to the stated identification results, not requirements claimed to cover every possible case. Two estimation algorithms address the respective conditions and are evaluated on synthetic and real-world data. The authors also discuss checking the model using the observed series.
summary.tldr: Modeling observed and hidden time series jointly can make important causal parameters identifiable under specified sufficient conditions.

title: Causal Inference by Identification of Vector Autoregressive Processes with Hidden Components

abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved great successes on various machine learning tasks, however, there are many open fundamental questions to be answered. In this paper, we tackle the problem of quantifying the quality of learned wights of different networks with possibly different architectures, going beyond considering the final classification error as the only metric. We introduce \emphExtended Data Jacobian Matrix to help analyze properties of networks of various structures, finding that, the spectrum of the extended data jacobian matrix is a strong discriminating factor for networks of different structures and performance. Based on such observation, we propose a novel regularization method, which manages to improve the network performance comparably to dropout, which in turn verifies the observation.

In this paper, we tackle the problem of quantifying the quality of learned wights of different networks with possibly different architectures, going beyond considering the final classification error as the only metric. We introduce \emphExtended Data Jacobian Matrix to help analyze properties of networks of various structures, finding that, the spectrum of the extended data jacobian matrix is a strong discriminating factor for networks of different structures and performance. Based on such observation, we propose a novel regularization method, which manages to improve the network performance comparably to dropout, which in turn verifies the observation.

paragraphs: Classification error gives a direct measure of a neural network's predictions, but the authors seek an additional way to assess its learned weights. Their question includes comparisons between networks with different architectures. The paper introduces the Extended Data Jacobian Matrix as a tool for analyzing properties of these differently structured networks.

The analysis focuses on the matrix's spectrum, a collection of numerical characteristics that summarizes aspects of the matrix. The authors find that this spectrum strongly distinguishes networks with different structures and performance. This supplies an additional perspective on learned networks, connecting an internal mathematical description with differences observed in their predictive behavior.

The authors then use that observation to design a regularization method. They report improvements in network performance comparable to those obtained with dropout, interpreting this result as support for the spectral observation. The work therefore moves from analyzing trained weights to using that analysis during learning. Its stated evidence concerns the discriminating value of the spectrum and the effectiveness of the resulting regularizer.
summary.tldr: The Extended Data Jacobian Matrix provides a spectral view of learned networks and motivates a regularizer with improvements comparable to dropout.

title: Analysis of Deep Neural Networks with Extended Data Jacobian Matrix

abstract: In this paper we consider nonconvex optimization and learning over a network of distributed nodes. We develop a Proximal Primal-Dual Algorithm (Prox-PDA), which enables the network nodes to distributedly and collectively compute the set of first-order stationary solutions in a global sublinear manner [with a rate of $O(1/r)$, where $r$ is the iteration counter]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that enables distributed nonconvex optimization with global rate guarantees. Our numerical experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
originalAbstract: In this paper we consider nonconvex optimization and learning over a network of distributed nodes. We develop a Proximal Primal-Dual Algorithm (Prox-PDA), which enables the network nodes to distributedly and collectively compute the set of first-order stationary solutions in a global sublinear manner [with a rate of $O(1/r)$, where $r$ is the iteration counter]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that enables distributed nonconvex optimization with global rate guarantees. Our numerical experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper considers nonconvex optimization and learning carried out by a network of distributed nodes. The nodes must collectively solve an optimization problem through a distributed procedure. The proposed method, the Proximal Primal-Dual Algorithm or Prox-PDA, supplies a convergence-rate guarantee for this network setting.

The target is first-order stationarity, a condition expressing that first-order information no longer provides a direction of improvement. In a nonconvex problem, this is distinct from identifying a globally optimal solution. The authors establish global sublinear convergence toward the set of first-order stationary solutions, with a rate of O(1/r), where r counts iterations.

This rate quantifies how the algorithm progresses as distributed computation continues. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first distributed nonconvex optimization algorithm with a global rate guarantee. Numerical experiments also demonstrate effectiveness. The main contribution is thus a theoretically controlled distributed procedure for seeking stationary solutions, supported by numerical evidence; the word global in the rate claim should not be read as a guarantee of global optimality.
summary.tldr: Prox-PDA enables distributed nonconvex optimization with an O(1/r) convergence rate toward first-order stationary solutions.

title: Prox-PDA: The Proximal Primal-Dual Algorithm for Fast Distributed Nonconvex Optimization and Learning Over Networks

abstract: Motivated by electricity consumption reconstitution, we propose a new matrix recovery method using nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF). The task tackled here is to reconstitute electricity consumption time series at a fine temporal scale from measures that are temporal aggregates of individual consumption. Contrary to existing NMF algorithms, the proposed method uses temporal aggregates as input data, instead of matrix entries. Furthermore, the proposed method is extended to take into account individual autocorrelation to provide better estimation, using a recent convex relaxation of quadratically constrained quadratic programs. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world electricity consumption datasets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
originalAbstract: Motivated by electricity consumption reconstitution, we propose a new matrix recovery method using nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF). The task tackled here is to reconstitute electricity consumption time series at a fine temporal scale from measures that are temporal aggregates of individual consumption. Contrary to existing NMF algorithms, the proposed method uses temporal aggregates as input data, instead of matrix entries. Furthermore, the proposed method is extended to take into account individual autocorrelation to provide better estimation, using a recent convex relaxation of quadratically constrained quadratic programs. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world electricity consumption datasets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Electricity records may provide consumption totals over intervals when the desired output is a much finer time series. This paper studies reconstruction from those temporal aggregates. It proposes a matrix recovery method based on nonnegative matrix factorization, adapting the method to observations that combine multiple times rather than directly reveal individual entries.

That observation model is central to the approach. Existing NMF algorithms typically take matrix entries as input, whereas this method works with aggregated measurements of individual consumption. The recovery procedure therefore addresses the form of data actually available in the stated electricity-consumption problem, instead of treating interval totals as fine-scale observations.

The authors also extend the method to incorporate individual autocorrelation, using relationships across time to improve estimation. This extension uses a convex relaxation of quadratically constrained quadratic programs. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real electricity datasets illustrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines aggregate-aware factorization with temporal information to reconstruct finer consumption patterns from coarser measurements.
summary.tldr: An aggregate-aware NMF method reconstructs fine-scale electricity consumption and incorporates autocorrelation to improve estimation.

title: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization for Time Series Recovery From a Few Temporal Aggregates

abstract: The task of representing entire graphs has seen a surge of prominent results, mainly due to learning convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on graph-structured data. While CNNs demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in graph classification task, such methods are supervised and therefore steer away from the original problem of network representation in task-agnostic manner. Here, we coherently propose an approach for embedding entire graphs and show that our feature representations with SVM classifier increase classification accuracy of CNN algorithms and traditional graph kernels. For this we describe a recently discovered graph object, anonymous walk , on which we design task-independent algorithms for learning graph representations in explicit and distributed way. Overall, our work represents a new scalable unsupervised learning of state-of-the-art representations of entire graphs.
originalAbstract: The task of representing entire graphs has seen a surge of prominent results, mainly due to learning convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on graph-structured data. While CNNs demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in graph classification task, such methods are supervised and therefore steer away from the original problem of network representation in task-agnostic manner. Here, we coherently propose an approach for embedding entire graphs and show that our feature representations with SVM classifier increase classification accuracy of CNN algorithms and traditional graph kernels. For this we describe a recently discovered graph object, anonymous walk , on which we design task-independent algorithms for learning graph representations in explicit and distributed way. Overall, our work represents a new scalable unsupervised learning of state-of-the-art representations of entire graphs.

paragraphs: Representing an entire graph means turning its structure into features that another learning method can use. The paper distinguishes this goal from training a graph classifier directly. A supervised graph neural network learns representations around the labels supplied during training, whereas a task-independent representation is learned without organizing the embedding around a particular classification objective.

The authors build their approach around a graph object called an anonymous walk. They use this object to design unsupervised algorithms that learn whole-graph representations in both explicit and distributed forms. The contribution is therefore a way to construct reusable graph features, with scalability presented as a central property of the approach.

To evaluate the representations, the authors combine them with a support vector machine classifier. They report higher classification accuracy than the convolutional graph methods and traditional graph kernels considered. These results show that learning graph representations without task labels can still produce features that work well for downstream supervised classification.
summary.tldr: Anonymous walks support scalable, unsupervised whole-graph representations that improve classification accuracy in the reported comparisons.

title: Anonymous Walk Embeddings

abstract: One of the most compelling features of Gaussian process (GP) regression is its ability to provide well-calibrated posterior distributions. Recent advances in inducing point methods have sped up GP marginal likelihood and posterior mean computations, leaving posterior covariance estimation and sampling as the remaining computational bottlenecks. In this paper we address these shortcomings by using the Lanczos algorithm to rapidly approximate the predictive covariance matrix. Our approach, which we refer to as LOVE (LanczOs Variance Estimates), substantially improves time and space complexity. In our experiments, LOVE computes covariances up to 2,000 times faster and draws samples 18,000 times faster than existing methods, all without sacrificing accuracy.

In this paper we address these shortcomings by using the Lanczos algorithm to rapidly approximate the predictive covariance matrix. Our approach, which we refer to as LOVE (LanczOs Variance Estimates), substantially improves time and space complexity. In our experiments, LOVE computes covariances up to 2,000 times faster and draws samples 18,000 times faster than existing methods, all without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression provides a distribution over predictions, making uncertainty a central part of its output. Improvements in inducing point methods had accelerated marginal likelihood calculations and posterior means, but estimating posterior covariance and drawing samples remained expensive. This paper targets those remaining operations, which are needed to work with the predictive distribution beyond its mean.

The proposed method, LOVE, uses the Lanczos algorithm to approximate the predictive covariance matrix efficiently. Covariance describes how uncertainty in different predictions varies together, so accelerating its calculation supports a richer predictive output. The authors report substantial improvements in both time and memory complexity through this approximation approach.

In their experiments, covariance calculations are up to 2,000 times faster and sample generation is 18,000 times faster than existing methods, without observed loss of accuracy. These are reported experimental speedups. The contribution is to make distributional prediction and sampling more computationally accessible, extending efficiency improvements to the uncertainty calculations that remained bottlenecks.
summary.tldr: LOVE approximates Gaussian process predictive covariance with Lanczos, delivering large experimental speedups for covariance estimation and sampling.

title: Constant-Time Predictive Distributions for Gaussian Processes

abstract: Policy gradient methods are a widely used class of model-free reinforcement learning algorithms where a state-dependent baseline is used to reduce gradient estimator variance. Several recent papers extend the baseline to depend on both the state and action and suggest that this significantly reduces variance and improves sample efficiency without introducing bias into the gradient estimates. To better understand this development, we decompose the variance of the policy gradient estimator and numerically show that learned state-action-dependent baselines do not in fact reduce variance over a state-dependent baseline in commonly tested benchmark domains. We confirm this unexpected result by reviewing the open-source code accompanying these prior papers, and show that subtle implementation decisions cause deviations from the methods presented in the papers and explain the source of the previously observed empirical gains. Furthermore, the variance decomposition highlights areas for improvement, which we demonstrate by illustrating a simple change to the typical value function parameterization that can significantly improve performance.
