To better understand this development, we decompose the variance of the policy gradient estimator and numerically show that learned state-action-dependent baselines do not in fact reduce variance over a state-dependent baseline in commonly tested benchmark domains. We confirm this unexpected result by reviewing the open-source code accompanying these prior papers, and show that subtle implementation decisions cause deviations from the methods presented in the papers and explain the source of the previously observed empirical gains. Furthermore, the variance decomposition highlights areas for improvement, which we demonstrate by illustrating a simple change to the typical value function parameterization that can significantly improve performance.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods commonly use a state-dependent baseline to reduce the variability of their gradient estimates. Earlier work proposed adding action dependence to the baseline, claiming lower variance and improved sample efficiency without bias. This paper investigates which parts of those reported gains actually follow from the proposed baseline design.

The authors decompose the variance of the policy gradient estimator and numerically examine commonly used benchmark domains. They find that the learned state-action baselines do not reduce variance relative to state-only baselines in those settings. Reviewing the accompanying open-source implementations reveals subtle choices that differ from the published methods and explain the previously observed empirical improvements.

The variance decomposition also suggests productive changes to the learning system. The authors demonstrate that a simple modification to the usual value-function parameterization can significantly improve performance. The paper therefore combines a reassessment of an existing explanation with an alternative improvement, grounding both in an analysis of where gradient-estimator variance comes from.
summary.tldr: Variance analysis and code review attribute reported action-dependent baseline gains to implementation choices and motivate a value-function improvement.

title: The Mirage of Action-Dependent Baselines in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: With an eye toward understanding complexity control in deep learning, we study how infinitesimal regularization or gradient descent optimization lead to margin maximizing solutions in both homogeneous and non homogeneous models, extending previous work that focused on infinitesimal regularization only in homogeneous models. To this end we study the limit of loss minimization with a diverging norm constraint (the “constrained path”), relate it to the limit of a “margin path” and characterize the resulting solution. For non-homogeneous ensemble models, which output is a sum of homogeneous sub-models, we show that this solution discards the shallowest sub-models if they are unnecessary. For homogeneous models, we show convergence to a “lexicographic max-margin solution”, and provide conditions under which max-margin solutions are also attained as the limit of unconstrained gradient descent.
originalAbstract: With an eye toward understanding complexity control in deep learning, we study how infinitesimal regularization or gradient descent optimization lead to margin maximizing solutions in both homogeneous and non homogeneous models, extending previous work that focused on infinitesimal regularization only in homogeneous models. To this end we study the limit of loss minimization with a diverging norm constraint (the “constrained path”), relate it to the limit of a “margin path” and characterize the resulting solution. For non-homogeneous ensemble models, which output is a sum of homogeneous sub-models, we show that this solution discards the shallowest sub-models if they are unnecessary. For homogeneous models, we show convergence to a “lexicographic max-margin solution”, and provide conditions under which max-margin solutions are also attained as the limit of unconstrained gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how regularization and optimization can favor particular solutions in deep models. Its focus is margin maximization and its connection to complexity control. The analysis covers both homogeneous and non-homogeneous models, extending earlier work that examined infinitesimal regularization only for homogeneous models.

The authors study a constrained path: the limiting behavior of loss minimization as the allowed parameter norm grows without bound. They connect this path to a margin-based path and characterize the selected solution. For non-homogeneous ensembles formed by adding homogeneous sub-models, the limiting solution discards the shallowest sub-models when they are unnecessary. This gives a depth-sensitive description of the preference induced by the optimization formulation.

For homogeneous models, the paper establishes convergence to a lexicographic maximum-margin solution, which refines how margin solutions are selected. It also gives conditions under which unconstrained gradient descent reaches maximum-margin solutions in the limit. The gradient-descent conclusion is conditional, while the overall analysis clarifies how model structure affects the solutions selected by limiting optimization procedures.
summary.tldr: Limiting optimization paths reveal margin-based solution preferences that depend on model homogeneity and depth.

title: Lexicographic and Depth-Sensitive Margins in Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Deep Models

abstract: This paper shows that every sublevel set of the loss function of a class of deep over-parameterized neural nets with piecewise linear activation functions is connected and unbounded. This implies that the loss has no bad local valleys and all of its global minima are connected within a unique and potentially very large global valley.
originalAbstract: This paper shows that every sublevel set of the loss function of a class of deep over-parameterized neural nets with piecewise linear activation functions is connected and unbounded. This implies that the loss has no bad local valleys and all of its global minima are connected within a unique and potentially very large global valley.

paragraphs: This paper examines the geometry of neural-network loss functions through their sublevel sets. A sublevel set collects all parameter choices whose loss is at or below a selected threshold. Studying these sets asks whether solutions with sufficiently low loss occupy one connected region or separate regions divided by higher-loss territory.

For a class of deep, over-parameterized networks with piecewise linear activation functions, the paper proves that every sublevel set is connected and unbounded. Connectedness rules out disconnected regions at a given loss threshold. Unboundedness describes a different feature: these regions are not confined to a bounded portion of parameter space. Both properties concern the loss landscape of the network class covered by the result.

The authors conclude that this landscape has no bad local valleys and that all global minima belong to a single connected global valley, which may be very large. The result gives a structural explanation of how optimal solutions relate to one another. Its scope is the stated network class, rather than deep learning architectures in general.
summary.tldr: A class of over-parameterized, piecewise-linear networks has connected, unbounded loss sublevel sets and one connected global valley.

title: On Connected Sublevel Sets in Deep Learning

abstract: Variational inference transforms posterior inference into parametric optimization thereby enabling the use of latent variable models where otherwise impractical. However, variational inference can be finicky when different variational parameters control variables that are strongly correlated under the model. Traditional natural gradients based on the variational approximation fail to correct for correlations when the approximation is not the true posterior. To address this, we construct a new natural gradient called the Variational Predictive Natural Gradient (VPNG). Unlike traditional natural gradients for variational inference, this natural gradient accounts for the relationship between model parameters and variational parameters. We demonstrate the insight with a simple example as well as the empirical value on a classification task, a deep generative model of images, and probabilistic matrix factorization for recommendation.

However, variational inference can be finicky when different variational parameters control variables that are strongly correlated under the model. Traditional natural gradients based on the variational approximation fail to correct for correlations when the approximation is not the true posterior. To address this, we construct a new natural gradient called the Variational Predictive Natural Gradient (VPNG). Unlike traditional natural gradients for variational inference, this natural gradient accounts for the relationship between model parameters and variational parameters. We demonstrate the insight with a simple example as well as the empirical value on a classification task, a deep generative model of images, and probabilistic matrix factorization for recommendation.

paragraphs: Variational inference makes posterior inference manageable by turning it into optimization over a parameterized approximation. That optimization can become difficult when different variational parameters control variables that the model strongly correlates. This paper studies how the choice of optimization direction can account for those relationships.

Traditional natural gradients use information from the variational approximation. The authors identify a problem when that approximation differs from the true posterior: its natural gradient can fail to correct for the relevant correlations. Their Variational Predictive Natural Gradient instead accounts for relationships between model parameters and variational parameters. The change broadens the information used to determine how optimization should move.

A simple example illustrates the underlying insight. The paper also demonstrates empirical value in classification, deep generative modeling of images, and probabilistic matrix factorization for recommendation. These examples support the usefulness of the proposed gradient across different latent variable applications. The contribution targets optimization difficulties arising from correlations that the current variational approximation does not adequately capture.
summary.tldr: The Variational Predictive Natural Gradient accounts for relationships between model and variational parameters to address correlation related optimization difficulties.

title: The Variational Predictive Natural Gradient

abstract: Consequential decision-making incentivizes individuals to strategically adapt their behavior to the specifics of the decision rule. While a long line of work has viewed strategic adaptation as gaming and attempted to mitigate its effects, recent work has instead sought to design classifiers that incentivize individuals to improve a desired quality. Key to both accounts is a cost function that dictates which adaptations are rational to undertake. In this work, we develop a causal framework for strategic adaptation. Our causal perspective clearly distinguishes between gaming and improvement and reveals an important obstacle to incentive design. We prove any procedure for designing classifiers that incentivize improvement must inevitably solve a non-trivial causal inference problem. We show a similar result holds for designing cost functions that satisfy the requirements of previous work. Key to both accounts is a cost function that dictates which adaptations are rational to undertake. In this work, we develop a causal framework for strategic adaptation. Our causal perspective clearly distinguishes between gaming and improvement and reveals an important obstacle to incentive design. We prove any procedure for designing classifiers that incentivize improvement must inevitably solve a non-trivial causal inference problem. paragraphs: People may change their behavior in response to a classifier that makes consequential decisions about them. Such adaptation can improve a desired quality, or it can merely improve the chance of receiving a favorable decision. This paper develops a causal framework that distinguishes these two possibilities in strategic classification.

Existing approaches often describe adaptation through a cost function that determines which changes are rational for an individual. The authors show that encouraging genuine improvement involves a deeper requirement: any procedure that designs classifiers with such incentives must solve a non-trivial causal inference problem. The result identifies causal reasoning as a necessary component of that design task.

A related theorem applies to constructing cost functions that satisfy requirements used in previous work. Thus, specifying how difficult changes are does not remove the underlying causal challenge. The contribution explains why designing incentives requires understanding how behavioral changes affect the desired outcome, and reveals causal modeling assumptions within approaches previously framed primarily as strategic classification.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that designing classifiers to incentivize genuine improvement necessarily entails a non-trivial causal inference problem.

title: Strategic Classification is Causal Modeling in Disguise

abstract: Extreme multi-label classification (XMC) is the problem of finding the relevant labels for an input, from a very large universe of possible labels. We consider XMC in the setting where labels are available only for groups of samples - but not for individual ones. Current XMC approaches are not built for such multi-instance multi-label (MIML) training data, and MIML approaches do not scale to XMC sizes. We develop a new and scalable algorithm to impute individual-sample labels from the group labels; this can be paired with any existing XMC method to solve the aggregated label problem. We characterize the statistical properties of our algorithm under mild assumptions, and provide a new end-to-end framework for MIML as an extension. Experiments on both aggregated label XMC and MIML tasks show the advantages over existing approaches.

The authors introduce a scalable algorithm that imputes individual-example labels from the aggregated group labels. Those inferred labels can then be used with any existing extreme multi-label classifier. This creates a bridge between the supervision that is available and the training format that established large-scale classifiers expect.

The paper characterizes the imputation algorithm’s statistical properties under mild assumptions and extends the approach into an end-to-end framework for multi-instance multi-label learning. Experiments on both problem types show advantages over existing approaches. The contribution therefore addresses both compatibility and scale: it makes group-level supervision usable by extreme classifiers and provides a related framework for learning directly in the grouped setting.
summary.tldr: A scalable label-imputation algorithm turns group-level annotations into training labels usable by existing extreme multi-label classifiers.

title: Extreme Multi-label Classification from Aggregated Labels

abstract: We introduce kernels with random Fourier features in the meta-learning framework for few-shot learning. We propose meta variational random features (MetaVRF) to learn adaptive kernels for the base-learner, which is developed in a latent variable model by treating the random feature basis as the latent variable. We formulate the optimization of MetaVRF as a variational inference problem by deriving an evidence lower bound under the meta-learning framework. To incorporate shared knowledge from related tasks, we propose a context inference of the posterior, which is established by an LSTM architecture. The LSTM-based inference network can effectively integrate the context information of previous tasks with task-specific information, generating informative and adaptive features. The learned MetaVRF can produce kernels of high representational power with a relatively low spectral sampling rate and also enables fast adaptation to new tasks. Experimental results on a variety of few-shot regression and classification tasks demonstrate that MetaVRF delivers much better, or at least competitive, performance compared to existing meta-learning alternatives.

It uses random Fourier features to represent kernels and treats the feature basis as a latent variable, allowing the representation to be inferred rather than held fixed across tasks.

The authors formulate training as variational inference and derive an evidence lower bound for the meta-learning setting. An LSTM-based inference network combines information from previous tasks with information about the current task. This context-dependent posterior inference provides a mechanism for sharing knowledge across related tasks while producing features suited to the task being solved.

The learned features can represent expressive kernels with a relatively low spectral sampling rate and enable fast adaptation to new tasks. Experiments cover both few-shot regression and classification. MetaVRF performs substantially better than existing meta-learning alternatives in some comparisons and competitively in others. The findings support adaptive kernel learning as a useful route to transferring knowledge while retaining task-specific flexibility.
summary.tldr: MetaVRF learns task-adaptive kernels through variational random features and context shared across related few-shot tasks.

title: Learning to Learn Kernels with Variational Random Features

abstract: Regression, as a counterpart to classification, is a major paradigm with a wide range of applications. Domain adaptation regression extends it by generalizing a regressor from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Existing domain adaptation regression methods have achieved positive results limited only to the shallow regime. A question arises: Why learning invariant representations in the deep regime less pronounced? A key finding of this paper is that classification is robust to feature scaling but regression is not, and aligning the distributions of deep representations will alter feature scale and impede domain adaptation regression. Based on this finding, we propose to close the domain gap through orthogonal bases of the representation spaces, which are free from feature scaling. Inspired by Riemannian geometry of Grassmann manifold, we define a geometrical distance over representation subspaces and learn deep transferable representations by minimizing it. To avoid breaking the geometrical properties of deep representations, we further introduce the bases mismatch penalization to match the ordering of orthogonal bases across representation subspaces. Our method is evaluated on three domain adaptation regression benchmarks, two of which are introduced in this paper. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods significantly, forming early positive results in the deep regime.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation regression transfers a numerical predictor from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. The paper investigates why aligning deep representations has been less successful for regression. Its central finding is that regression is sensitive to feature scaling, and distribution alignment can alter that scale in ways that impede transfer.

The proposed method compares representation spaces through orthogonal bases, avoiding dependence on feature scale. Drawing on the geometry of the Grassmann manifold, the authors define a distance between representation subspaces and minimize it during learning. This targets a geometric relationship between domains rather than directly forcing their full representation distributions to match.

The method also includes a basis-mismatch penalty that aligns the ordering of orthogonal bases across the two spaces while preserving the intended geometry. Evaluation covers three domain-adaptation regression benchmarks, two introduced by the paper. The authors report significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods compared. These findings provide early positive evidence for deep regression transfer through subspace alignment and identify feature scale as a consequential design consideration.
summary.tldr: Aligning the geometry of representation subspaces improves domain-adaptation regression while avoiding the feature-scaling problem of distribution alignment.

title: Representation Subspace Distance for Domain Adaptation Regression

abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) are a class of generative models which have recently been shown to produce excellent samples. We show that with a few simple modifications, DDPMs can also achieve competitive log-likelihoods while maintaining high sample quality. Additionally, we find that learning variances of the reverse diffusion process allows sampling with an order of magnitude fewer forward passes with a negligible difference in sample quality, which is important for the practical deployment of these models. We additionally use precision and recall to compare how well DDPMs and GANs cover the target distribution. Finally, we show that the sample quality and likelihood of these models scale smoothly with model capacity and training compute, making them easily scalable. We release our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/openai/improved-diffusion.

This paper shows that a few modifications also make their log-likelihoods competitive while preserving that sample quality. The contribution therefore concerns both the quality of generated examples and how well the model assigns probability to data.

One practical change is to learn the variances used in the reverse diffusion process. The authors find that this allows sampling with roughly ten times fewer network forward passes, with a negligible difference in sample quality. Reducing the number of passes directly addresses the computational work required to generate samples.

The paper also uses precision and recall to compare the target-distribution coverage of diffusion models and GANs. Separately, it finds that sample quality and likelihood improve smoothly as model capacity and training computation increase. These findings present diffusion models as a scalable generative approach whose sampling cost can be substantially reduced while retaining the reported quality.
summary.tldr: Simple diffusion-model changes improve likelihoods and enable roughly tenfold fewer sampling passes with negligible loss of sample quality.

title: Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

abstract: Standard deep reinforcement learning algorithms use a shared representation for the policy and value function, especially when training directly from images. However, we argue that more information is needed to accurately estimate the value function than to learn the optimal policy. Consequently, the use of a shared representation for the policy and value function can lead to overfitting. To alleviate this problem, we propose two approaches which are combined to create IDAAC: Invariant Decoupled Advantage Actor-Critic. First, IDAAC decouples the optimization of the policy and value function, using separate networks to model them. Second, it introduces an auxiliary loss which encourages the representation to be invariant to task-irrelevant properties of the environment. IDAAC shows good generalization to unseen environments, achieving a new state-of-the-art on the Procgen benchmark and outperforming popular methods on DeepMind Control tasks with distractors. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/rraileanu/idaac.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often uses a shared representation for choosing actions and estimating their long-term value, especially with image inputs. The authors argue that accurate value estimation can require more information than learning the optimal policy. Sharing a representation can therefore encourage the policy to depend on information that contributes to overfitting.

Their method, Invariant Decoupled Advantage Actor-Critic, or IDAAC, combines two changes. Separate networks model the policy and value function, decoupling their optimization. An auxiliary loss also encourages the learned representation to remain insensitive to properties of the environment that are irrelevant to the task. These changes target both shared training demands and dependence on distracting details.

IDAAC generalizes well to unseen environments in the reported evaluations. It achieves a new state-of-the-art result on Procgen and outperforms popular methods on DeepMind Control tasks containing distractors. These empirical findings support the combined design as a way to improve generalization. The underlying argument is that learning to act effectively and learning to predict value need not impose identical representational requirements.
summary.tldr: IDAAC separates policy and value learning and encourages invariance to irrelevant details, improving generalization in the reported reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

title: Decoupling Value and Policy for Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Pixelizations of Platonic solids such as the cube and icosahedron have been widely used to represent spherical data, from climate records to Cosmic Microwave Background maps. Platonic solids have well-known global symmetries. Once we pixelize each face of the solid, each face also possesses its own local symmetries in the form of Euclidean isometries. One way to combine these symmetries is through a hierarchy. However, this approach does not adequately model the interplay between the two levels of symmetry transformations. We show how to model this interplay using ideas from group theory, identify the equivariant linear maps, and introduce equivariant padding that respects these symmetries. Deep networks that use these maps as their building blocks generalize gauge equivariant CNNs on pixelized spheres. These deep networks achieve state-of-the-art results on semantic segmentation for climate data and omnidirectional image processing. Code is available at https://git.io/JGiZA.

paragraphs: Spherical data can be represented by dividing the faces of a cube or another Platonic solid into pixels. This creates two interacting kinds of symmetry: transformations of the whole solid and local geometric transformations within each face. The paper argues that treating them as a simple hierarchy does not adequately capture how they interact.

The authors use group theory to describe that interaction and identify linear operations that are equivariant to it. Such operations make network representations transform consistently with the modeled symmetries. They also introduce equivariant padding, so the treatment of boundaries respects the same structure. Together, these components provide building blocks for deep networks on pixelized spheres.

The resulting networks generalize gauge equivariant convolutional networks for this representation of spherical data. They achieve state-of-the-art results on the reported climate semantic segmentation and omnidirectional image processing tasks. The contribution links a more complete treatment of global and local symmetries to concrete network operations, with empirical evidence that those operations are useful for spherical prediction problems.
summary.tldr: The paper builds networks for pixelized spheres that respect interacting global and local symmetries, improving results on climate and omnidirectional image tasks.

title: Equivariant Networks for Pixelized Spheres

abstract: Despite recent successes, most contrastive self-supervised learning methods are domain-specific, relying heavily on data augmentation techniques that require knowledge about a particular domain, such as image cropping and rotation. To overcome such limitation, we propose a domain-agnostic approach to contrastive learning, named DACL, that is applicable to problems where domain-specific data augmentations are not readily available. Key to our approach is the use of Mixup noise to create similar and dissimilar examples by mixing data samples differently either at the input or hidden-state levels. We theoretically analyze our method and show advantages over the Gaussian-noise based contrastive learning approach. To demonstrate the effectiveness of DACL, we conduct experiments across various domains such as tabular data, images, and graphs. Our results show that DACL not only outperforms other domain-agnostic noising methods, such as Gaussian-noise, but also combines well with domain-specific methods, such as SimCLR, to improve self-supervised visual representation learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive self-supervised learning often depends on domain-specific transformations that create useful related examples. Image cropping and rotation are examples of choices that require knowledge of the data. DACL addresses situations where such transformations are not readily available, seeking a way to construct contrastive training examples across different kinds of data.

Its central ingredient is Mixup noise: samples are mixed differently to create similar and dissimilar examples. Mixing can take place at the input level or within a model's hidden representations. This gives the contrastive learning process a source of variation that does not depend on designing a separate augmentation procedure for each domain.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing advantages over Gaussian-noise-based contrastive learning. Experiments span tabular data, images, and graphs, with DACL outperforming other domain-agnostic noising approaches in the reported results. It also combines with domain-specific methods such as SimCLR to improve visual representations. The findings support both its use where tailored augmentations are unavailable and its compatibility with existing image-specific approaches.
summary.tldr: DACL uses sample mixing for contrastive learning across domains and can also improve representations when combined with domain-specific augmentations.

title: Towards Domain-Agnostic Contrastive Learning

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a decentralized machine-learning paradigm, in which a global server iteratively averages the model parameters of local users without accessing their data. User heterogeneity has imposed significant challenges to FL, which can incur drifted global models that are slow to converge. Knowledge Distillation has recently emerged to tackle this issue, by refining the server model using aggregated knowledge from heterogeneous users, other than directly averaging their model parameters. This approach, however, depends on a proxy dataset, making it impractical unless such a prerequisite is satisfied. Moreover, the ensemble knowledge is not fully utilized to guide local model learning, which may in turn affect the quality of the aggregated model. Inspired by the prior art, we propose a data-free knowledge distillation approach to address heterogeneous FL, where the server learns a lightweight generator to ensemble user information in a data-free manner, which is then broadcasted to users, regulating local training using the learned knowledge as an inductive bias. Empirical studies powered by theoretical implications show that our approach facilitates FL with better generalization performance using fewer communication rounds, compared with the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines learning from users whose data remain local. When users differ substantially, directly averaging their model parameters can produce a drifting global model that converges slowly. Knowledge distillation offers another way to combine their knowledge, but existing approaches can require a proxy dataset and may not fully use the combined knowledge to improve local training.

This paper proposes a data-free distillation method in which the server learns a lightweight generator that brings together information from users. The generator is then sent back to users, where its learned knowledge guides local model training. This creates a path for aggregated information to influence subsequent learning on individual devices.

The approach addresses both the need for a proxy dataset and the limited use of shared knowledge in local updates. Empirical studies, supported by theoretical implications, show better generalization with fewer communication rounds than the compared leading methods. The findings suggest that exchanging a learned source of guidance can improve how heterogeneous users contribute to and benefit from federated learning.
summary.tldr: A server-trained generator shares distilled user knowledge to improve heterogeneous federated learning without requiring a proxy dataset.

title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Heterogeneous Federated Learning

abstract: We develop a new approach to multi-label conformal prediction in which we aim to output a precise set of promising prediction candidates with a bounded number of incorrect answers. Standard conformal prediction provides the ability to adapt to model uncertainty by constructing a calibrated candidate set in place of a single prediction, with guarantees that the set contains the correct answer with high probability. In order to obey this coverage property, however, conformal sets can become inundated with noisy candidates—which can render them unhelpful in practice. This is particularly relevant to practical applications where there is a limited budget, and the cost (monetary or otherwise) associated with false positives is non-negligible. We propose to trade coverage for a notion of precision by enforcing that the presence of incorrect candidates in the predicted conformal sets (i.e., the total number of false positives) is bounded according to a user-specified tolerance. Subject to this constraint, our algorithm then optimizes for a generalized notion of set coverage (i.e., the true positive rate) that allows for any number of true answers for a given query (including zero). We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a number of classification tasks in natural language processing, computer vision, and computational chemistry.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction can express uncertainty by returning a set of candidate answers instead of one prediction. Standard coverage guarantees aim to include the correct answer with high probability. However, meeting that objective can produce a set crowded with incorrect candidates, reducing its usefulness when checking or acting on each candidate has a cost.

This paper changes the priority for multi-label prediction. The user specifies a tolerance for false positives, and the method constrains the number of incorrect candidates accordingly. Subject to that constraint, it seeks to recover as many true answers as possible through a generalized coverage objective based on the true positive rate.

The formulation accommodates queries with several correct answers and queries with none. Its central tradeoff is explicit: coverage can be sacrificed to limit unwanted candidates. Experiments across natural language processing, computer vision, and computational chemistry demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The result makes prediction sets responsive to a practical resource constraint, rather than treating inclusion of a correct answer as the sole criterion for usefulness.
summary.tldr: The method trades conformal coverage for user-controlled false-positive limits while maximizing recovery of true answers.

title: Conformal Prediction Sets with Limited False Positives

abstract: Offline RL algorithms must account for the fact that the dataset they are provided may leave many facets of the environment unknown. The most common way to approach this challenge is to employ pessimistic or conservative methods, which avoid behaviors that are too dissimilar from those in the training dataset. However, relying exclusively on conservatism has drawbacks: performance is sensitive to the exact degree of conservatism, and conservative objectives can recover highly suboptimal policies. In this work, we propose that offline RL methods should instead be adaptive in the presence of uncertainty. We show that acting optimally in offline RL in a Bayesian sense involves solving an implicit POMDP. As a result, optimal policies for offline RL must be adaptive, depending not just on the current state but rather all the transitions seen so far during evaluation. We present a model-free algorithm for approximating this optimal adaptive policy, and demonstrate the efficacy of learning such adaptive policies in offline RL benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from an existing dataset that may leave important parts of the environment uncertain. Conservative methods address this by avoiding behavior too different from the recorded data. The paper argues that relying exclusively on conservatism can be problematic: results depend on its strength, and conservative objectives can yield highly suboptimal policies.

The authors show that Bayesian-optimal behavior in offline reinforcement learning involves an implicit partially observable decision problem. Under this formulation, an optimal policy must adapt using the transitions observed during evaluation. Its decisions therefore depend on the accumulated interaction history as well as the current state. Experience collected while acting provides information relevant to the uncertainty left by the offline dataset.

The paper presents a model-free algorithm that approximates this adaptive policy and evaluates it on offline reinforcement learning benchmarks. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of training for adaptation. The central implication is that handling uncertainty can involve learning how to respond to new evidence during evaluation, alongside the choices made during offline training.
summary.tldr: Bayesian-optimal offline RL requires history-dependent adaptation, motivating a model-free algorithm that learns to use evaluation-time experience.

title: Offline RL Policies Should Be Trained to be Adaptive

abstract: Label-specific features serve as an effective strategy to facilitate multi-label classification, which account for the distinct discriminative properties of each class label via tailoring its own features. Existing approaches implement this strategy in a quite straightforward way, i.e. finding the most pertinent and discriminative features for each class label and directly inducing classifiers on constructed label-specific features. In this paper, we propose a dual perspective for label-specific feature learning, where label-specific discriminative properties are considered by identifying each label’s own non-informative features and making the discrimination process immutable to variations of these features. To instantiate it, we present a perturbation-based approach DELA to provide classifiers with label-specific immutability on simultaneously identified non-informative features, which is optimized towards a probabilistically-relaxed expected risk minimization problem. Comprehensive experiments on 10 benchmark data sets show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art counterparts.

Existing label-specific feature methods typically identify the features most useful for each label and train a classifier using those features. This paper develops another way to express the same need for label-dependent discrimination.

Its approach identifies features that are uninformative for a particular label and makes that label's prediction insensitive to changes in them. The proposed method, DELA, uses perturbations to encourage this stability while also identifying the non-informative features. Training is formulated through a probabilistically relaxed expected-risk objective, linking feature identification and classifier behavior within one optimization problem.

This perspective matters because relevance can be expressed through what a classifier should ignore as well as through what it should use. The invariance is label-specific: the method does not require every label to disregard the same features. Experiments on ten benchmark datasets show better performance than the state-of-the-art comparison methods. Those results support learning label-specific resistance to irrelevant variation as an effective strategy for multi-label prediction.
summary.tldr: DELA improves multi-label classification by learning which features each label should ignore and making predictions insensitive to their variation.

title: Dual Perspective of Label-Specific Feature Learning for Multi-Label Classification

abstract: This work introduces a diffusion model for molecule generation in 3D that is equivariant to Euclidean transformations. Our E(3) Equivariant Diffusion Model (EDM) learns to denoise a diffusion process with an equivariant network that jointly operates on both continuous (atom coordinates) and categorical features (atom types). In addition, we provide a probabilistic analysis which admits likelihood computation of molecules using our model. Experimentally, the proposed method significantly outperforms previous 3D molecular generative methods regarding the quality of generated samples and the efficiency at training time.

Atom positions are continuous quantities, while atom identities are categorical, so the model’s denoising network jointly operates on different types of features.

The network is equivariant to Euclidean transformations. In practical terms, changing the spatial placement or orientation of a molecular configuration produces a corresponding transformation in the model’s spatial behavior. This builds geometric consistency into the generation process. The approach learns to remove the noise introduced by a diffusion process while respecting that structure.

The authors also provide a probabilistic analysis that permits likelihood computation for molecules under the model. Their experiments report significantly better generated-sample quality and training efficiency than previous three-dimensional molecular generation methods. The contribution combines joint modeling of atom types and coordinates, geometric symmetry, and a probabilistic treatment that supports both generation and likelihood evaluation.
summary.tldr: EDM jointly denoises atom types and coordinates with geometric equivariance, improving molecular sample quality and training efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Equivariant Diffusion for Molecule Generation in 3D

abstract: Meta-learning has emerged as a potent paradigm for quick learning of few-shot tasks, by leveraging the meta-knowledge learned from meta-training tasks. Well-generalized meta-knowledge that facilitates fast adaptation in each task is preferred; however, recent evidence suggests the undesirable memorization effect where the meta-knowledge simply memorizing all meta-training tasks discourages task-specific adaptation and poorly generalizes. There have been several solutions to mitigating the effect, including both regularizer-based and augmentation-based methods, while a systematic understanding of these methods in a single framework is still lacking. In this paper, we offer a novel causal perspective of meta-learning. Through the lens of causality, we conclude the universal label space as a confounder to be the causing factor of memorization and frame the two lines of prevailing methods as different deconfounder approaches. Remarkably, derived from the causal inference principle of front-door adjustment, we propose two frustratingly easy but effective deconfounder algorithms, i.e., sampling multiple versions of the meta-knowledge via Dropout and grouping the meta-knowledge into multiple bins. The proposed causal perspective not only brings in the two deconfounder algorithms that surpass previous works in four benchmark datasets towards combating memorization, but also opens a promising direction for meta-learning.

paragraphs: Meta-learning seeks reusable knowledge that helps a model adapt quickly to tasks with few examples. It can instead memorize the training tasks so strongly that task-specific adaptation becomes less effective. Existing regularization and augmentation methods address this problem, but the paper seeks a common explanation of why these different interventions can help.

The authors develop a causal perspective that identifies the universal label space as a confounding factor behind memorization. Within this account, regularization-based and augmentation-based methods become different approaches to deconfounding. This reframes the issue as a problem with how shared task information influences learning and adaptation, providing a framework for interpreting existing remedies.

One samples multiple versions of meta-knowledge through Dropout; the other groups meta-knowledge into multiple bins. Both aim to counter the identified confounding effect. Results across four benchmark datasets show improvements over previous methods for combating memorization, supporting the usefulness of this causal perspective for designing meta-learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: A causal account of meta-learning memorization motivates two simple deconfounding methods that improve results across four benchmarks.

title: The Role of Deconfounding in Meta-learning

abstract: Learning robust models that generalize well under changes in the data distribution is critical for real-world applications. To this end, there has been a growing surge of interest to learn simultaneously from multiple training domains - while enforcing different types of invariance across those domains. Yet, all existing approaches fail to show systematic benefits under controlled evaluation protocols. In this paper, we introduce a new regularization - named Fishr - that enforces domain invariance in the space of the gradients of the loss: specifically, the domain-level variances of gradients are matched across training domains. Our approach is based on the close relations between the gradient covariance, the Fisher Information and the Hessian of the loss: in particular, we show that Fishr eventually aligns the domain-level loss landscapes locally around the final weights. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Fishr for out-of-distribution generalization. Notably, Fishr improves the state of the art on the DomainBed benchmark and performs consistently better than Empirical Risk Minimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexrame/fishr.

paragraphs: Training on several domains can expose a model to different data distributions, but that alone does not ensure it will generalize to a new one. Fishr adds a regularizer that asks those training domains to agree in a specific way: the variances of their loss gradients should match. The focus is therefore on how training examples affect parameter updates.

The paper motivates this choice through relationships among gradient covariance, Fisher information, and the Hessian, which describes local loss curvature. Its analysis shows that Fishr eventually brings domain-level loss landscapes into local alignment around the final model weights. This gives the variance-matching objective an interpretation in terms of the geometry of learning across domains.

Experiments show benefits for out-of-distribution generalization, including an improvement over the previous state of the art on DomainBed and consistently better performance than empirical risk minimization in the reported evaluations. These findings connect a concrete gradient-based regularizer with improved performance under distribution changes. The landscape alignment result is local around the final weights, rather than a claim that all domains become equivalent everywhere.
summary.tldr: Fishr matches gradient variances across training domains, locally aligning their loss landscapes and improving out-of-distribution performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Fishr: Invariant Gradient Variances for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Tabular data is arguably one of the most commonly used data structures in various practical domains, including finance, healthcare and e-commerce. The inherent heterogeneity allows tabular data to store rich information. However, based on a recently published tabular benchmark, we can see deep neural networks still fall behind tree-based models on tabular datasets. In this paper, we propose Trompt–which stands for Tabular Prompt–a novel architecture inspired by prompt learning of language models. The essence of prompt learning is to adjust a large pre-trained model through a set of prompts outside the model without directly modifying the model. Based on this idea, Trompt separates the learning strategy of tabular data into two parts. The first part, analogous to pre-trained models, focus on learning the intrinsic information of a table. The second part, analogous to prompts, focus on learning the variations among samples. Trompt is evaluated with the benchmark mentioned above. The experimental results demonstrate that Trompt outperforms state-of-the-art deep neural networks and is comparable to tree-based models.

paragraphs: Tabular datasets combine heterogeneous kinds of information, and deep networks have struggled to match tree-based models on the benchmark motivating this paper. Trompt proposes a neural architecture tailored to this setting. Its design borrows the idea of prompts from language modeling to organize how the model learns from a table.

The architecture separates learning into two parts. One captures information intrinsic to the table, playing a role analogous to a pretrained model. The other captures variation among individual samples, playing a role analogous to prompts. This analogy guides a division between shared information and sample-specific variation within the tabular learning architecture.

The authors evaluate Trompt on the same published benchmark that highlighted the gap between deep networks and tree methods. They report performance above state-of-the-art deep neural networks and comparable to tree-based models. The findings support the proposed architectural separation as a useful way to improve neural learning on tabular data. The comparison establishes competitiveness on the evaluated benchmark, with parity rather than superiority claimed against tree-based approaches.
summary.tldr: Trompt separates table-wide information from sample variation, outperforming deep tabular models and matching tree-based performance on the evaluated benchmark.

title: Trompt: Towards a Better Deep Neural Network for Tabular Data

abstract: This paper studies the fundamental limits of reinforcement learning (RL) in the challenging partially observable setting. While it is well-established that learning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) requires exponentially many samples in the worst case, a surge of recent work shows that polynomial sample complexities are achievable under the revealing condition —A natural condition that requires the observables to reveal some information about the unobserved latent states. However, the fundamental limits for learning in revealing POMDPs are much less understood, with existing lower bounds being rather preliminary and having substantial gaps from the current best upper bounds. We establish strong PAC and regret lower bounds for learning in revealing POMDPs. Our lower bounds scale polynomially in all relevant problem parameters in a multiplicative fashion, and achieve significantly smaller gaps against the current best upper bounds, providing a solid starting point for future studies. In particular, for multi-step revealing POMDPs, we show that (1) the latent state-space dependence is at least $\Omega(S^{1.5})$ in the PAC sample complexity, which is notably harder than the $\widetilde{\Theta}(S)$ scaling for fully-observable MDPs; (2) Any polynomial sublinear regret is at least $\Omega(T^{2/3})$, suggesting its fundamental difference from the single-step case where $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret is achievable. Technically, our hard instance construction adapts techniques in distribution testing , which is new to the RL literature and may be of independent interest. We also complement our results with new sharp regret upper bounds for strongly B-stable PSRs , which include single-step revealing POMDPs as a special case.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, an agent receives observations without directly seeing the underlying state. Revealing conditions require those observations to expose some information about hidden states, making polynomial sample guarantees possible. This paper investigates the difficulty that remains by establishing stronger lower bounds on sample complexity and regret.

For multi-step revealing problems, the authors show that PAC sample complexity has at least an S to the three-halves dependence on the number of latent states. This exceeds the roughly linear state dependence of fully observable problems. They also show that any polynomial sublinear regret must be at least of order T to the two-thirds, contrasting with achievable square-root dependence in the single-step revealing case.

The lower bounds combine relevant problem parameters multiplicatively and narrow gaps with existing upper bounds. Their hard-instance construction adapts distribution-testing techniques. The paper additionally provides sharp regret upper bounds for strongly B-stable predictive state representations, a class including single-step revealing problems, sharpening the distinction between different forms of partial observability.
summary.tldr: Stronger lower bounds show that multi-step revealing POMDPs retain substantial learning difficulty despite allowing polynomial sample complexity.

title: Lower Bounds for Learning in Revealing POMDPs

abstract: In this paper, we study the role of feedback in online learning with switching costs. It has been shown that the minimax regret is $\widetilde{\Theta}(T^{2/3})$ under bandit feedback and improves to $\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{T})$ under full-information feedback, where $T$ is the length of the time horizon. However, it remains largely unknown how the amount and type of feedback generally impact regret. To this end, we first consider the setting of bandit learning with extra observations; that is, in addition to the typical bandit feedback, the learner can freely make a total of $B_{\mathrm{ex}}$ extra observations . We fully characterize the minimax regret in this setting, which exhibits an interesting phase-transition phenomenon : when $B_{\mathrm{ex}} = O(T^{2/3})$, the regret remains $\widetilde{\Theta}(T^{2/3})$, but when $B_{\mathrm{ex}} = \Omega(T^{2/3})$, it becomes $\widetilde{\Theta}(T/\sqrt{B_{\mathrm{ex}}})$, which improves as the budget $B_{\mathrm{ex}}$ increases. To design algorithms that can achieve the minimax regret, it is instructive to consider a more general setting where the learner has a budget of $B$ total observations. We fully characterize the minimax regret in this setting as well and show that it is $\widetilde{\Theta}(T/\sqrt{B})$, which scales smoothly with the total budget $B$. Furthermore, we propose a generic algorithmic framework, which enables us to design different learning algorithms that can achieve matching upper bounds for both settings based on the amount and type of feedback. One interesting finding is that while bandit feedback can still guarantee optimal regret when the budget is relatively limited, it no longer suffices to achieve optimal regret when the budget is relatively large.

paragraphs: Online learners must balance improving their choices against the cost of switching actions. Feedback determines how much they can learn without changing their behavior. This paper characterizes how both the quantity and type of observations affect the best achievable worst-case regret in that setting.

With ordinary bandit feedback plus a budget of extra observations, the authors identify a transition around T^(2/3) extra observations. Below that scale, regret remains of order T^(2/3), ignoring logarithmic factors. Above it, regret scales as T divided by the square root of the extra-observation budget, so additional feedback begins to improve the rate.

When the budget instead counts all observations, the optimal regret scales smoothly as T divided by the square root of that total budget, again up to logarithmic factors. A generic algorithmic framework achieves matching upper bounds in both settings. The results also distinguish feedback types: bandit feedback can remain optimal with a limited budget, but becomes insufficient for optimal regret when the available budget is relatively large.
summary.tldr: The paper precisely characterizes how observation budgets and feedback types control regret in online learning with switching costs.

title: Understanding the Role of Feedback in Online Learning with Switching Costs

abstract: One of the fundamental quests of AI is to produce agents that coordinate well with humans. This problem is challenging, especially in domains that lack high quality human behavioral data, because multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) often converges to different equilibria from the ones that humans prefer. We propose a novel framework, instructRL, that enables humans to specify what kind of strategies they expect from their AI partners through natural language instructions. We use pretrained large language models to generate a prior policy conditioned on the human instruction and use the prior to regularize the RL objective. This leads to the RL agent converging to equilibria that are aligned with human preferences. We show that instructRL converges to human-like policies that satisfy the given instructions in a proof-of-concept environment as well as the challenging Hanabi benchmark. Finally, we show that knowing the language instruction significantly boosts human-AI coordination performance in human evaluations in Hanabi.

The paper attributes part of this challenge to multi-agent reinforcement learning converging on equilibria different from those humans prefer. This is particularly difficult when high-quality examples of human behavior are unavailable to guide learning.

The proposed instructRL framework lets people describe their expected partner strategies in natural language. A pretrained large language model converts an instruction into a prior policy, which then regularizes the reinforcement-learning objective. The prior supplies guidance about the desired behavior while the agent learns, steering the training process toward strategies aligned with the instruction.

The authors show instruction-following, human-like policies in both a proof-of-concept environment and Hanabi. Human evaluations in Hanabi also find that knowing the language instruction significantly improves human–AI coordination. The findings connect language guidance during policy training with a shared understanding during interaction: an instruction can help shape the agent's strategy and help a human partner anticipate that strategy.
summary.tldr: instructRL uses language-model policy priors derived from human instructions to guide reinforcement learning toward better human–AI coordination.

title: Language Instructed Reinforcement Learning for Human-AI Coordination

abstract: Behavior constrained policy optimization has been demonstrated to be a successful paradigm for tackling Offline Reinforcement Learning. By exploiting historical transitions, a policy is trained to maximize a learned value function while constrained by the behavior policy to avoid a significant distributional shift. In this paper, we propose our closed-form policy improvement operators. We make a novel observation that the behavior constraint naturally motivates the use of first-order Taylor approximation, leading to a linear approximation of the policy objective. Additionally, as practical datasets are usually collected by heterogeneous policies, we model the behavior policies as a Gaussian Mixture and overcome the induced optimization difficulties by leveraging the LogSumExp’s lower bound and Jensen’s Inequality, giving rise to a closed-form policy improvement operator. We instantiate both one-step and iterative offline RL algorithms with our novel policy improvement operators and empirically demonstrate their effectiveness over state-of-the-art algorithms on the standard D4RL benchmark. Our code is available at https://cfpi-icml23.github.io/.

One successful approach maximizes a learned value function while keeping the new policy close to the behavior that generated the data. That constraint limits distributional shift, reducing the mismatch between the data available for learning and the actions selected by the improved policy.

These steps produce closed-form policy improvement operators, which the authors incorporate into both one-step and iterative offline learning algorithms. Experiments on D4RL demonstrate their effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution connects an existing constraint on behavioral change to an approximation and mixture-model treatment that yields explicit policy updates.
summary.tldr: Behavior-constrained approximations and Gaussian mixture modeling yield closed-form policy improvement operators for offline reinforcement learning.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Closed-Form Policy Improvement Operators

abstract: Designing machine learning architectures for processing neural networks in their raw weight matrix form is a newly introduced research direction. Unfortunately, the unique symmetry structure of deep weight spaces makes this design very challenging. If successful, such architectures would be capable of performing a wide range of intriguing tasks, from adapting a pre-trained network to a new domain to editing objects represented as functions (INRs or NeRFs). As a first step towards this goal, we present here a novel network architecture for learning in deep weight spaces. It takes as input a concatenation of weights and biases of a pre-trained MLP and processes it using a composition of layers that are equivariant to the natural permutation symmetry of the MLP’s weights: Changing the order of neurons in intermediate layers of the MLP does not affect the function it represents. We provide a full characterization of all affine equivariant and invariant layers for these symmetries and show how these layers can be implemented using three basic operations: pooling, broadcasting, and fully connected layers applied to the input in an appropriate manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture and its advantages over natural baselines in a variety of learning tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies neural networks that take another neural network's weights as input. A central difficulty is that different weight arrangements can represent the same function: consistently reordering intermediate neurons leaves an MLP's behavior unchanged. A model processing raw weights should therefore account for this symmetry rather than attach meaning to an arbitrary neuron ordering.

The proposed architecture processes the concatenated weights and biases of a pretrained MLP through layers that respect these permutations. The authors fully characterize the affine equivariant and invariant layers for the relevant symmetries. They also show that these layers can be implemented using pooling, broadcasting, and appropriately applied fully connected operations.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness and advantages over natural baselines across several learning tasks. The broader motivation includes adapting pretrained networks to new domains and editing objects represented by neural functions, although those are presented as potential capabilities of this research direction. The concrete contribution is a principled architecture whose treatment of raw weights matches the functional equivalences already present in an MLP.
summary.tldr: The paper builds networks that process MLP weights while respecting neuron-permutation symmetries, with a complete characterization of the relevant affine layers.

title: Equivariant Architectures for Learning in Deep Weight Spaces

abstract: The recent integration of deep learning and pairwise similarity annotation-based constrained clustering—i.e., deep constrained clustering (DCC)—has proven effective for incorporating weak supervision into massive data clustering: Less than 1% of pair similarity annotations can often substantially enhance the clustering accuracy. However, beyond empirical successes, there is a lack of understanding of DCC. In addition, many DCC paradigms are sensitive to annotation noise, but performance-guaranteed noisy DCC methods have been largely elusive. This work first takes a deep look into a recently emerged logistic loss function of DCC, and characterizes its theoretical properties. Our result shows that the logistic DCC loss ensures the identifiability of data membership under reasonable conditions, which may shed light on its effectiveness in practice. Building upon this understanding, a new loss function based on geometric factor analysis is proposed to fend against noisy annotations. It is shown that even under unknown annotation confusions, the data membership can still be provably identified under our proposed learning criterion. The proposed approach is tested over multiple datasets to validate our claims.

paragraphs: Deep constrained clustering uses annotations about whether pairs of examples are similar to help organize large datasets into groups. Even a small fraction of such annotations can often improve clustering substantially. However, successful experiments have outpaced theoretical understanding, and incorrect pair annotations can undermine methods that depend on this weak supervision.

The paper first analyzes a logistic loss used in deep constrained clustering. It shows that this loss makes data membership identifiable under reasonable conditions. In this context, identifiability concerns whether the learning formulation can distinguish the underlying group memberships. The result supplies a theoretical explanation for why the loss can work in practice.

Building on that analysis, the authors propose a new loss based on geometric factor analysis to handle noisy annotations. They establish that membership remains identifiable under their proposed criterion even when annotation confusions are unknown. Tests across multiple datasets support the claims. The contribution combines an explanation of an existing objective with a new objective designed to preserve recoverability when pairwise supervision is unreliable.
summary.tldr: A geometric clustering loss supports provable membership identification despite unknown annotation confusions, building on an analysis of logistic clustering loss.

title: Deep Clustering with Incomplete Noisy Pairwise Annotations: A Geometric Regularization Approach

abstract: In federated learning (FL), a cluster of local clients are chaired under the coordination of the global server and cooperatively train one model with privacy protection. Due to the multiple local updates and the isolated non-iid dataset, clients are prone to overfit into their own optima, which extremely deviates from the global objective and significantly undermines the performance. Most previous works only focus on enhancing the consistency between the local and global objectives to alleviate this prejudicial client drifts from the perspective of the optimization view, whose performance would be prominently deteriorated on the high heterogeneity. In this work, we propose a novel and general algorithm FedSMOO by jointly considering the optimization and generalization targets to efficiently improve the performance in FL. Concretely, FedSMOO adopts a dynamic regularizer to guarantee the local optima towards the global objective, which is meanwhile revised by the global Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) optimizer to search for the consistent flat minima. Our theoretical analysis indicates that FedSMOO achieves fast $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ convergence rate with low generalization bound. Extensive numerical studies are conducted on the real-world dataset to verify its peerless efficiency and excellent generality.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model through clients whose data remain separate. When their data distributions differ, repeated local updates can pull clients toward solutions that fit their own data but deviate from the global objective. The paper argues that approaches focused mainly on aligning local and global optimization can deteriorate when this heterogeneity is high.

FedSMOO combines alignment with an explicit concern for generalization. A dynamic regularizer directs local optima toward the global objective, while a global sharpness-aware minimization procedure seeks consistent flat minima. The two components address related goals: keeping clients oriented toward the shared problem and shaping the kinds of solutions that training reaches.

The theoretical analysis gives an O(1/T) convergence rate and a low generalization bound. Numerical studies on real-world data report strong efficiency and generality. The paper's central contribution is this joint treatment of optimization consistency and generalization, supported by both analysis and experiments, rather than treating client drift as the only consideration in federated training.
summary.tldr: FedSMOO combines dynamic regularization and global sharpness-aware optimization to improve consistency and generalization in federated learning.

title: Dynamic Regularized Sharpness Aware Minimization in Federated Learning: Approaching Global Consistency and Smooth Landscape

abstract: Dataset Condensation has emerged as a technique for compressing large datasets into smaller synthetic counterparts, facilitating downstream training tasks. In this paper, we study the impact of bias inside the original dataset on the performance of dataset condensation. With a comprehensive empirical evaluation on canonical datasets with color, corruption and background biases, we found that color and background biases in the original dataset will be amplified through the condensation process, resulting in a notable decline in the performance of models trained on the condensed dataset, while corruption bias is suppressed through the condensation process. To reduce bias amplification in dataset condensation, we introduce a simple yet highly effective approach based on a sample reweighting scheme utilizing kernel density estimation. Empirical results on multiple real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Notably, on CMNIST with 5% bias-conflict ratio and IPC 50, our method achieves 91.5% test accuracy compared to 23.8% from vanilla DM, boosting the performance by 67.7%, whereas applying state-of-the-art debiasing method on the same dataset only achieves 53.7% accuracy. Our findings highlight the importance of addressing biases in dataset condensation and provide a promising avenue to address bias amplification in the process.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation compresses a large training dataset into a small synthetic dataset for training other models. This paper asks what happens when the original data contain misleading associations. Its evaluations distinguish color, background, and corruption biases, showing that compression can affect different kinds of bias differently rather than simply preserving the original dataset’s behavior.

In the studied settings, condensation amplifies color and background biases, reducing the performance of models trained on the synthetic data. Corruption bias, however, is suppressed. To address the harmful amplification, the authors introduce a sample reweighting approach based on kernel density estimation. The method changes how samples contribute to condensation, and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support its effectiveness.

A highlighted CMNIST result uses a 5% bias-conflict ratio and 50 images per class. The proposed method reaches 91.5% test accuracy, compared with 23.8% for vanilla DM and 53.7% for the cited debiasing method. The improvement over vanilla DM is 67.7 percentage points. This example illustrates how addressing bias during condensation can materially affect the usefulness of the resulting training data.
summary.tldr: Dataset condensation can amplify color and background biases, and density-based sample reweighting substantially reduces this problem in the reported experiments.

title: Ameliorate Spurious Correlations in Dataset Condensation

abstract: WebAssembly enables near-native execution in web applications and is increasingly adopted for tasks that demand high performance and robust security. However, its assembly-like syntax, implicit stack machine, and low-level data types make it extremely difficult for human developers to understand, spurring the need for effective WebAssembly reverse engineering techniques. In this paper, we propose StackSight, a novel neurosymbolic approach that combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with advanced program analysis to decompile complex WebAssembly code into readable C++ snippets. StackSight visualizes and tracks virtual stack alterations via a static analysis algorithm and then applies chain-of-thought prompting to harness LLM’s complex reasoning capabilities. Evaluation results show that StackSight significantly improves WebAssembly decompilation. Our user study also demonstrates that code snippets generated by StackSight have significantly higher win rates and enable a better grasp of code semantics.

paragraphs: WebAssembly supports fast execution in web applications, but its low-level form is difficult for developers to interpret. Its assembly-like instructions, implicit stack operations, and low-level data types obscure what a program is doing. StackSight addresses this reverse-engineering problem by translating complex WebAssembly into readable C++ snippets.

The approach combines program analysis with a large language model. A static analysis algorithm tracks and visualizes changes to the virtual stack, making an otherwise implicit part of execution explicit. Chain-of-thought prompting then guides the language model's reasoning about the code. This combination brings structured information about program behavior into the decompilation process.

The authors report significant improvements in WebAssembly decompilation. Their user study also finds that StackSight's generated snippets achieve significantly higher win rates and help people understand code semantics more effectively. These findings matter because the intended outcome is readable code that communicates program meaning to developers. The paper therefore evaluates both decompilation improvements and the usefulness of the resulting snippets to human readers.
summary.tldr: StackSight combines static stack analysis with language-model reasoning to turn WebAssembly into C++ snippets that developers can understand more easily.

title: StackSight: Unveiling WebAssembly through Large Language Models and Neurosymbolic Chain-of-Thought Decompilation

abstract: Precipitation nowcasting based on radar data plays a crucial role in extreme weather prediction and has broad implications for disaster management. Despite progresses have been made based on deep learning, two key challenges of precipitation nowcasting are not well-solved: (i) the modeling of complex precipitation system evolutions with different scales, and (ii) accurate forecasts for extreme precipitation. In this work, we propose CasCast, a cascaded framework composed of a deterministic and a probabilistic part to decouple the predictions for mesoscale precipitation distributions and small-scale patterns. Then, we explore training the cascaded framework at the high resolution and conducting the probabilistic modeling in a low dimensional latent space with a frame-wise-guided diffusion transformer for enhancing the optimization of extreme events while reducing computational costs. Extensive experiments on three benchmark radar precipitation datasets show that CasCast achieves competitive performance. Especially, CasCast significantly surpasses the baseline (up to +91.8%) for regional extreme-precipitation nowcasting.

paragraphs: Radar-based precipitation nowcasting must follow weather systems that evolve at different spatial scales. Forecasting extreme rain adds another challenge: a model needs to capture localized patterns as well as the broader precipitation distribution. CasCast addresses these linked problems by dividing prediction into two connected stages.

The framework combines a deterministic component with a probabilistic component, separating mesoscale precipitation distributions from smaller-scale patterns. It explores high-resolution training while carrying out probabilistic modeling in a lower-dimensional latent representation. A diffusion transformer guided frame by frame supports this stage. The design aims to improve optimization for extreme events while reducing the computational cost of probabilistic prediction.

Experiments on three radar precipitation benchmarks show competitive overall performance. For regional extreme precipitation, the authors report improvements over the baseline reaching 91.8%. That figure is a reported maximum for this evaluation setting. The broader finding is that separating large-scale evolution from smaller probabilistic detail can help address the particular demands of high-resolution extreme-rain forecasting.
summary.tldr: CasCast separates broad precipitation evolution from small-scale probabilistic patterns to improve high-resolution nowcasting, especially for extreme rain.

title: CasCast: Skillful High-resolution Precipitation Nowcasting via Cascaded Modelling

abstract: We propose Unsupervised Episode Generation method called Neighbors as Queries (NaQ) to solve the Few-Shot Node-Classification (FSNC) task by unsupervised Graph Meta-learning. Doing so enables full utilization of the information of all nodes in a graph, which is not possible in current supervised meta-learning methods for FSNC due to the label-scarcity problem. In addition, unlike unsupervised Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) methods that overlook the downstream task to be solved at the training phase resulting in vulnerability to class imbalance of a graph, we adopt the episodic learning framework that allows the model to be aware of the downstream task format, i.e., FSNC. The proposed NaQ is a simple but effective unsupervised episode generation method that randomly samples nodes from a graph to make a support set, followed by similarity-based sampling of nodes to make the corresponding query set. Since NaQ is model-agnostic, any existing supervised graph meta-learning methods can be trained in an unsupervised manner, while not sacrificing much of their performance or sometimes even improving them. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed unsupervised episode generation method for graph meta-learning towards the FSNC task. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JhngJng/NaQ-PyTorch.
