To address this limitation, we introduce Mem-T, an autonomous memory agent that interfaces with a lightweight hierarchical memory database to perform dynamic updates and multi-turn retrieval over streaming inputs. To effectively train long-horizon memory management capabilities, we further propose MoT-GRPO, a tree-guided reinforcement learning framework that transforms sparse terminal feedback into dense, step-wise supervision via memory operation tree backpropagation and hindsight credit assignment, thereby enabling the joint optimization of memory construction and retrieval. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mem-T is (1) high-performing, surpassing frameworks such as A-Mem and Mem0 by up to $14.94%$, and **(2) economical**, operating on a favorable accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier and reducing inference tokens per query by $\sim24.45%$ relative to GAM without sacrificing performance.

paragraphs: Memory agents decide how to process, store, and retrieve information instead of following a fixed memory pipeline. Training these decisions is difficult when the agent performs many operations before receiving feedback. A final success or failure signal provides little immediate guidance about which earlier memory decisions contributed to the outcome.

Mem-T combines an autonomous agent with a lightweight hierarchical memory database for updating memories and retrieving them through multiple turns over streaming inputs. Its training framework, MoT-GRPO, uses a tree of memory operations to propagate final feedback back to individual steps. Hindsight credit assignment supplies denser supervision, supporting joint optimization of memory construction and retrieval.

Experiments report improvements of up to 14.94% over frameworks such as A-Mem and Mem0. Mem-T also occupies a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off and uses approximately 24.45% fewer inference tokens per query than GAM without sacrificing performance. These findings suggest that better feedback for intermediate memory decisions can improve both answer quality and the cost of using memory.
summary.tldr: Mem-T turns delayed memory-task feedback into step-level training signals, improving reported performance while reducing retrieval-related inference costs.

title: Mem-T: Densifying Rewards for Long-Horizon Memory Agents

abstract: Cross multi-domain log anomaly detection aims to train a unified model applying in multiple heterogeneous systems, alleviating the annotation cost and scalability bottlenecks of traditional cross single-domain approaches. However, existing methods face two fundamental challenges: (i) geometric proximity alone is insufficient to certify normality, and (ii) forcibly aligning distributions across domains can induce negative transfer. To address these issues, we propose MPFM (Cross Multi-Domain Prototype Flow Matching for Log Anomaly Detection), grounded in the principle that anomalies are samples that cannot be stably generated by the normal data-generating mechanism. Specifically, MPFM employs a shared–private prototype system to disentangle cross-domain commonalities from domain-specific patterns, introduces domain-conditioned flow matching to perform anomaly detection by integrating structural and dynamical evidence, and further leverages prototype-drift-driven hard example mining to improve robustness near decision boundaries. Experiments on HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, and Spirit demonstrate that MPFM delivers substantial gains under multi-domain joint training.

To address these issues, we propose MPFM (Cross Multi-Domain Prototype Flow Matching for Log Anomaly Detection), grounded in the principle that anomalies are samples that cannot be stably generated by the normal data-generating mechanism. Specifically, MPFM employs a shared–private prototype system to disentangle cross-domain commonalities from domain-specific patterns, introduces domain-conditioned flow matching to perform anomaly detection by integrating structural and dynamical evidence, and further leverages prototype-drift-driven hard example mining to improve robustness near decision boundaries. paragraphs: A unified log anomaly detector must handle systems with different normal behaviors. The paper highlights two problems: closeness to normal examples does not by itself establish normality, and forcing different systems into matching distributions can harm learning. MPFM approaches detection through whether a sample can be stably generated by the mechanism representing normal data.

Its shared–private prototype system separates patterns common across domains from patterns specific to each domain. Domain-conditioned flow matching then combines structural evidence with evidence about generation dynamics. This allows the detector to use information beyond geometric proximity while retaining distinctions among the systems it learns from.

MPFM also uses prototype drift to identify difficult examples for additional learning, aiming to improve robustness near decision boundaries. Experiments jointly train across HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, and Spirit and report substantial gains in the multi-domain setting. The contribution is a coordinated approach to sharing knowledge, preserving domain-specific behavior, and detecting anomalies through both structure and dynamics. Its stated results support this combination for the evaluated log datasets.
summary.tldr: MPFM improves multi-domain log anomaly detection by combining shared and domain-specific prototypes with generation-based structural and dynamical evidence.

title: MPFM: Cross Multi-Domain Prototype Flow Matching for Log Anomaly Detection

abstract: Existing voice deepfake detection and localization models rely heavily on representations extracted from speech foundation models (SFMs). However, downstream finetuning has now reached a state of diminishing returns. In this paper, we shift the focus to pretraining and propose a novel recipe that combines bottleneck masked embedding prediction with flow-matching based spectrogram reconstruction. The outcome, Alethia, is the first foundational audio encoder for various voice deepfake detection and localization tasks. We evaluate on 5 different tasks with 56 benchmark datasets, and note Alethia significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SFMs with superior robustness to real-world perturbations and zero-shot generalization to unseen domains (e.g., singing deepfakes). We also demonstrate the limitation of discrete targets in masked token prediction, and show the importance of continuous embedding prediction and generative pretraining for capturing deepfake artifacts.

In this paper, we shift the focus to pretraining and propose a novel recipe that combines bottleneck masked embedding prediction with flow-matching based spectrogram reconstruction. The outcome, Alethia, is the first foundational audio encoder for various voice deepfake detection and localization tasks. We evaluate on 5 different tasks with 56 benchmark datasets, and note Alethia significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SFMs with superior robustness to real-world perturbations and zero-shot generalization to unseen domains (e.g., singing deepfakes). paragraphs: Voice deepfake detection depends on finding traces of synthetic audio, while localization also requires identifying where those traces occur. Existing systems often reuse representations from general speech foundation models. This paper argues that further fine-tuning of those representations is yielding diminishing returns and instead changes how the underlying audio encoder is pretrained.

Alethia combines two learning tasks: predicting masked continuous embeddings through a bottleneck and reconstructing spectrograms using flow matching. These tasks train the encoder to recover missing representations and generate an audio-related signal representation. The paper connects this combination to learning features that capture deepfake artifacts, emphasizing continuous embedding prediction and generative pretraining.

The authors evaluate Alethia on five tasks across 56 benchmark datasets and report significant improvements over state-of-the-art speech foundation models. They also report stronger robustness to real-world perturbations and zero-shot generalization to unseen domains, including singing deepfakes. Their analysis identifies limitations of discrete prediction targets, supporting the importance of the pretraining objective for learning useful forensic audio representations.
summary.tldr: Alethia uses continuous prediction and generative audio pretraining to improve voice deepfake detection, localization, and generalization.

abstract: We propose a general framework for learning from labeled and unlabeled data on a directed graph in which the structure of the graph including the directionality of the edges is considered. The time complexity of the algorithm derived from this framework is nearly linear due to recently developed numerical techniques. In the absence of labeled instances, this framework can be utilized as a spectral clustering method for directed graphs, which generalizes the spectral clustering approach for undirected graphs. We have applied our framework to real-world web classification problems and obtained encouraging results.

The time complexity of the algorithm derived from this framework is nearly linear due to recently developed numerical techniques. In the absence of labeled instances, this framework can be utilized as a spectral clustering method for directed graphs, which generalizes the spectral clustering approach for undirected graphs. We have applied our framework to real-world web classification problems and obtained encouraging results.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when examples are connected by a directed graph and only some examples have labels. A directed connection distinguishes a link from one example to another from a link going the other way. The proposed framework uses both the graph structure and this direction information when learning from labeled and unlabeled data.

The framework also covers the case in which no labels are available. In that setting, it becomes a spectral clustering method for directed graphs, extending the corresponding approach for undirected graphs. This connects classification with partial supervision and clustering without supervision within one framework, while retaining the distinction between the two directions of a relationship.

The algorithm derived from the framework has nearly linear time complexity through the use of numerical techniques. That computational property matters for applying graph-based learning to large collections of linked examples. The authors apply the framework to real-world web classification problems and report encouraging results, providing empirical support for the approach in the application they studied.
summary.tldr: A nearly linear-time framework uses directed graph structure for semi-supervised classification and, without labels, spectral clustering.

title: Learning from labeled and unlabeled data on a directed graph

abstract: Hierarchical models have been extensively studied in various domains. However, existing models assume fixed model structures or incorporate structural uncertainty generatively. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields (DHMRFs) to incorporate structural uncertainty in a discriminative manner. DHMRFs consist of two parts – structure model and class label model. Both are defined as exponential family distributions. Conditioned on observations, DHMRFs relax the independence assumption as made in directed models. As exact inference is intractable, a variational method is developed to learn parameters and to find the MAP model structure and label assignment. We apply the model to a real-world web data extraction task, which automatically extracts product items for sale on the Web. The results show promise.

In this paper, we propose Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields (DHMRFs) to incorporate structural uncertainty in a discriminative manner. DHMRFs consist of two parts – structure model and class label model. Both are defined as exponential family distributions. Conditioned on observations, DHMRFs relax the independence assumption as made in directed models. As exact inference is intractable, a variational method is developed to learn parameters and to find the MAP model structure and label assignment. We apply the model to a real-world web data extraction task, which automatically extracts product items for sale on the Web. The results show promise.

paragraphs: A hierarchical model represents relationships at multiple levels, but deciding how those levels connect can itself be uncertain. This paper introduces Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields to handle that uncertainty while predicting class labels from observations. The contribution is a discriminative treatment of structure: the model uses the observed data to assess both the hierarchy and its labels.

The framework separates a structure model from a class label model, expressing both through exponential family distributions. This makes the arrangement of the hierarchy an explicit part of the learning problem. Conditioned on observations, the framework also relaxes independence assumptions made by directed models, allowing a less restrictive account of dependencies.

Exact inference is intractable, so the authors develop a variational approximation for learning parameters and finding a maximum a posteriori structure and label assignment. They apply it to extracting product items offered for sale on web pages. The reported results are promising, supporting the potential usefulness of jointly reasoning about structure and labels in this extraction task.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Hierarchical Markov Random Fields jointly infer uncertain hierarchies and labels, with promising results for extracting products from web pages.

title: Dynamic hierarchical Markov random fields and their application to web data extraction

abstract: Clustering data in high dimensions is believed to be a hard problem in general. A number of efficient clustering algorithms developed in recent years address this problem by projecting the data into a lower-dimensional subspace, e.g.~via Principal Components Analysis (PCA) or random projections, before clustering. Here, we consider constructing such projections using multiple views of the data, via Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA). Under the assumption that the views are uncorrelated given the cluster label, we show that the separation conditions required for the algorithm to be successful are significantly weaker than prior results in the literature. We provide results for mixtures of Gaussians and mixtures of log concave distributions. We also provide empirical support from audio-visual speaker clustering (where we desire the clusters to correspond to speaker ID) and from hierarchical Wikipedia document clustering (where one view is the words in the document and other is the link structure).
originalAbstract: Clustering data in high dimensions is believed to be a hard problem in general. A number of efficient clustering algorithms developed in recent years address this problem by projecting the data into a lower-dimensional subspace, e.g.~via Principal Components Analysis (PCA) or random projections, before clustering. Here, we consider constructing such projections using multiple views of the data, via Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA). Under the assumption that the views are uncorrelated given the cluster label, we show that the separation conditions required for the algorithm to be successful are significantly weaker than prior results in the literature. We provide results for mixtures of Gaussians and mixtures of log concave distributions. We also provide empirical support from audio-visual speaker clustering (where we desire the clusters to correspond to speaker ID) and from hierarchical Wikipedia document clustering (where one view is the words in the document and other is the link structure).

paragraphs: Clustering high-dimensional data often begins by projecting it into fewer dimensions. This paper considers how multiple views of the same data can guide that projection. It uses canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, to construct a lower-dimensional representation from the relationships between views before clustering.

The theoretical results assume that the views are uncorrelated once the cluster label is given. Under this assumption, the algorithm succeeds under significantly weaker separation conditions than those in prior results. The authors establish results for mixtures of Gaussian distributions and mixtures of log-concave distributions. The assumption is central to the claimed improvement in required cluster separation.

Empirical support comes from two settings with naturally different views. Audio-visual speaker clustering aims to group observations by speaker identity. Hierarchical Wikipedia clustering uses document words as one view and link structure as another. These examples connect the theory to data with complementary descriptions. The paper's contribution is to show how cross-view information can support useful projections and, under the stated condition, improve clustering guarantees.
summary.tldr: CCA-based projections yield weaker sufficient cluster-separation requirements when views are uncorrelated conditional on the cluster label.

title: Multi-view clustering via canonical correlation analysis

abstract: Numerous semi-supervised learning methods have been proposed to augment Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB) using unlabeled documents, but their use in practice is often limited due to implementation difficulty, inconsistent prediction performance, or high computational cost. In this paper, we propose a new, very simple semi-supervised extension of MNB, called Semi-supervised Frequency Estimate (SFE). Our experiments show that it consistently improves MNB with additional data (labeled or unlabeled) in terms of AUC and accuracy, which is not the case when combining MNB with Expectation Maximization (EM). We attribute this to the fact that SFE consistently produces better conditional log likelihood values than both EM+MNB and MNB in labeled training data.
originalAbstract: Numerous semi-supervised learning methods have been proposed to augment Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB) using unlabeled documents, but their use in practice is often limited due to implementation difficulty, inconsistent prediction performance, or high computational cost. In this paper, we propose a new, very simple semi-supervised extension of MNB, called Semi-supervised Frequency Estimate (SFE). Our experiments show that it consistently improves MNB with additional data (labeled or unlabeled) in terms of AUC and accuracy, which is not the case when combining MNB with Expectation Maximization (EM). We attribute this to the fact that SFE consistently produces better conditional log likelihood values than both EM+MNB and MNB in labeled training data.

paragraphs: Unlabeled documents can supplement labeled training data for text classification, but incorporating them is not automatically helpful in practice. The paper identifies implementation difficulty, inconsistent prediction quality, and computational cost as obstacles facing existing semi-supervised extensions of multinomial naive Bayes. It proposes a simple alternative called Semi-supervised Frequency Estimate, or SFE.

SFE extends multinomial naive Bayes to use additional labeled or unlabeled data. In the reported experiments, this consistently improves both accuracy and AUC. The comparison with expectation maximization is significant: combining EM with multinomial naive Bayes does not show the same consistent benefit from extra data in those experiments.

The authors attribute SFE's predictive improvements to its better conditional log likelihood on labeled training examples, compared with both ordinary multinomial naive Bayes and EM combined with that model. This is their explanation of the observed results, rather than a universal guarantee that more data always helps. The contribution is a simple semi-supervised extension whose empirical behavior addresses a practical weakness of an established alternative.
summary.tldr: SFE is a simple semi-supervised extension of multinomial naive Bayes that consistently benefits from additional data in the reported experiments.

title: Large Scale Text Classification using Semisupervised Multinomial Naive Bayes

abstract: This paper introduces a general multi-class approach to weakly supervised classification. Inferring the labels and learning the parameters of the model is usually done jointly through a block-coordinate descent algorithm such as expectation-maximization (EM), which may lead to local minima. To avoid this problem, we propose a cost function based on a convex relaxation of the soft-max loss. We then propose an algorithm specifically designed to efficiently solve the corresponding semidefinite program (SDP). Empirically, our method compares favorably to standard ones on different datasets for multiple instance learning and semi-supervised learning as well as on clustering tasks.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces a general multi-class approach to weakly supervised classification. Inferring the labels and learning the parameters of the model is usually done jointly through a block-coordinate descent algorithm such as expectation-maximization (EM), which may lead to local minima. To avoid this problem, we propose a cost function based on a convex relaxation of the soft-max loss. We then propose an algorithm specifically designed to efficiently solve the corresponding semidefinite program (SDP). Empirically, our method compares favorably to standard ones on different datasets for multiple instance learning and semi-supervised learning as well as on clustering tasks.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised classification requires learning when the available supervision does not fully specify the training labels. A common strategy alternates between inferring labels and updating model parameters, as in expectation-maximization. The difficulty is that this joint learning process can settle into local minima. The paper proposes a general approach that supports multiple classes while addressing that optimization problem.

Its central step is to replace the original learning objective with a convex relaxation of the soft-max loss. A relaxation changes the optimization problem into a more tractable form. Here, the resulting problem is a semidefinite program, and the authors design an algorithm specifically to solve it efficiently. The contribution therefore includes both the formulation and a solver tailored to its structure.

Experiments compare the method with standard approaches across multiple instance learning, semi-supervised learning, and clustering tasks. The reported comparisons are favorable across these different settings. They support the usefulness of a shared convex framework for several forms of incomplete supervision, without establishing that the relaxation exactly solves every original classification problem.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation of soft-max loss provides a multi-class framework for weak supervision with a tailored semidefinite-program solver.

title: A convex relaxation for weakly supervised classifiers
